anchor_text: glow'd like plated Mars
summary: Mars was the Roman god of war. 'Plated' means armoured in metal plate. Philo remembers Antony's eyes blazing in battle like the gleaming war-god himself — a contrast with what they are doing now (gazing at Cleopatra).

sources.name: Classical commonplace
sources.citation: Mars (Roman god of war) figured as the armoured, gleaming war-god is a standard Roman and Elizabethan figure for a great general's martial radiance; cf. Virgil and Ovid passim (no single fixed locus).

anchor_text: Upon a tawny front
summary: 'Tawny' meant dark-complexioned or sun-browned; 'front' means face or forehead. Philo is describing Cleopatra, mocking Antony for fixing his soldier's gaze on an Egyptian queen rather than on a battlefield.
detail: Elizabethan texts applied 'tawny' to people of North African, Middle Eastern, and Mediterranean complexion — it was a value-neutral descriptor in some contexts but could also carry contempt. Here it works with 'gipsy's lust' (TLN 10) to mark Cleopatra as foreign and 'other' from Philo's Roman viewpoint. The playwright does not endorse that viewpoint; later scenes systematically undercut Roman dismissals of Cleopatra.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'tawny': 'of a dark and yellowish colour; applied to persons of dark complexion.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'tawny' adj. 1: 'Of a warm sandy or brownish-yellow colour'; applied to complexion from the 14th century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 6

Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'tawny' and OED s.v. 'tawny' are real reference works whose definitions (dark/yellowish complexion, attested from the 14th century) support the archaic-vocab gloss exactly.

'Front' as forehead/face and 'tawny' for dark North African complexion are both well-attested Elizabethan usages, and the note that the play later undercuts Philo's Roman framing is a defensible interpretive observation rather than an overreach.

anchor_text: triple pillar of the world transform'd
summary: After Julius Caesar's assassination, three men divided the Roman world between them: Mark Antony, Octavius Caesar, and Lepidus. They were called a triumvirate ('rule of three'). 'Triple pillar of the world' means Antony as one of those three supports. Philo is saying Antony, one of Rome's three rulers, has made himself 'a strumpet's fool.'
detail: The Second Triumvirate was established by law in 43 BCE and divided the Roman empire into three administrative zones. Antony held the east (including Egypt and the Greek world), Octavius the west, and the politically weak Lepidus north Africa. 'Three-nook'd world' (used later in the play) means the three-cornered world of Europe, Asia, and Africa — each corner held by one triumvir. The phrase 'triple pillar' collapses high political status into the image of something structural and load-bearing, then collapses that in turn into 'a strumpet's fool' — the fall is enormous.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 19 (the Second Triumvirate), trans. Sir Thomas North, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 13

Plutarch Life of Antony chapter 19 (North 1579) does describe the Second Triumvirate meeting on an island where Antony, Octavius, and Lepidus divided the empire — the citation accurately supports the summary.

The Second Triumvirate reading is unambiguous in context, the zone-distribution (east/west/north Africa) is historically accurate, and the structural-then-abased image ('pillar' collapsed to 'strumpet's fool') is the mainstream dramatic reading.

anchor_text: find out new heaven, new earth
summary: Cleopatra says she will put a limit on how much Antony may love her; he replies that she would have to discover a whole new creation to do it. The phrase 'new heaven, new earth' echoes Revelation 21:1, the promised transformed world at the end of time — Antony is saying their love is boundless enough to fill a universe that does not yet exist.
detail: The Book of Revelation (21:1) reads: 'And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away' (Geneva 1599). For a Protestant Elizabethan audience, 'new heaven and new earth' was the language of the ultimate divine promise — the eschatological remaking of creation. Antony takes the most absolute image of totality he can find and makes it the measure of his love. The allusion is one of the play's many moments in which the lovers' rhetoric strains toward the cosmic and the divine — a grandiosity Philo has already framed as delusion.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Revelation 21:1 (Geneva 1599): 'And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 18
Revelation 21:1 in the Geneva Bible 1599 reads exactly 'And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away' — the quoted text and citation are accurate.

The Revelation 21:1 allusion is the most commonly cited parallel in commentary; the interpretation that Antony uses cosmic eschatological language as the measure of boundless love correctly captures the line's logic ('Then must thou needs find out' means the limit would require a new creation).

anchor_text: scarce-bearded Caesar have not sent His powerful mandate
summary: The Caesar Cleopatra mocks here is Octavius Caesar — Antony's fellow triumvir and political rival — not the dead Julius Caesar. 'Scarce-bearded' means barely old enough to grow a beard, a jab at Octavius's youth; he was about 23 when Antony left for Egypt. Cleopatra is taunting Antony by imagining that a young upstart back in Rome is already ordering him around.
detail: Octavius Caesar (later Augustus) was the great-nephew and adopted heir of Julius Caesar. At the time the play's action begins (c. 41 BCE), Octavius was indeed in his early twenties and had not yet consolidated power. Calling him 'scarce-bearded' is both a literal comment on his age and a rhetorical diminishment — Cleopatra paints him as a beardless boy giving commands to Rome's greatest soldier. The audience must distinguish between two 'Caesars' throughout the play: Octavius (alive and threatening) and Julius (dead but repeatedly invoked, including as Cleopatra's former lover, 'broad-fronted Caesar').

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 26-28 (Antony and Octavius's rivalry in 41 BCE, when Octavius was approximately 22-23 years old), trans. Sir Thomas North (1579).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 23

Plutarch Life of Antony chapters 26-28 (North 1579) cover Antony's time in Egypt and the rivalry with Octavius; Octavian was born 63 BCE and was approximately 22 years old in 41 BCE, consistent with the annotation's 'approximately 22-23.'

The identification of 'Caesar' as Octavius (not Julius) is unambiguous from dramatic context, and the age detail (~23 in 41 BCE) and the reading of 'scarce-bearded' as a youth-taunt are both historically grounded and textually sound.

anchor_text: Let Rome in Tiber melt, and the wide arch Of the rang'd empire fall
summary: The Tiber is the river that flows through Rome; 'rang'd empire' means the Roman empire with its ordered ranks of conquered territories. Antony is saying he does not care if Rome dissolves into its own river and the whole empire collapses. This hyperbole — deliberate massive overstatement — declares that Cleopatra and the present moment ('here is my space') matter more to him than his entire political and military identity.
detail: The speech is the dramatic counterweight to Philo's opening. Philo frames Antony's love as a catastrophic failure; Antony's own words make it a conscious, defiant choice. The rhetorical device is hyperbole in service of a renunciation speech: Rome, empire, duty — all are offered as things Antony will cheerfully unmake for Cleopatra's sake. 'Kingdoms are clay' (TLN 38) extends the image: if the great city is worth melting, ordinary kingdoms are only dirt. The irony that this man actually holds one-third of the world's government drives the scene's tension.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 28 (Antony's infatuation with Cleopatra and his neglect of public business), trans. Sir Thomas North (1579).

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'rang'd': 'set in order, arranged in rank' — referring to the ordered, ranked territories of Roman administration.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 36

Plutarch Life of Antony chapter 28 (North 1579) does describe Antony squandering time on pleasures with Cleopatra while neglecting political duties; Schmidt s.v. 'rang'd' as arranged/ordered is a plausible lexicographical reading.

'Rang'd' as 'ordered/ranked' is the standard gloss, the hyperbole identification is correct, and reading the speech as a conscious defiant renunciation rather than mere infatuation is fully supported by the contrast with Philo's framing and Cleopatra's immediate sceptical retort ('Excellent falsehood!').

anchor_text: for the love of Love and her soft hours
summary: 'Love' with a capital letter is Venus, the Roman goddess of love, whom the first-century Romans sometimes called simply 'Love.' Antony invokes her — and the pleasure-filled hours she presides over — as his reason for refusing to hear Rome's messengers. The phrase 'her soft hours' pairs Venus with leisure and sensual ease, the opposite of the dispatch and hard discipline that Roman political life demanded.
detail: Venus (Greek Aphrodite) was also identified with pleasure, idleness, and the dereliction of martial duty that worried Romans attributed to time spent in the east. Antony's casual invocation of Venus here — treated as a familiar patron rather than a reproach — confirms the frame Philo has set: he has surrendered to 'a gipsy's lust.' The phrase echoes Plutarch, who describes Antony's life with Cleopatra as entirely given over to pleasures and the 'society of Isis' (i.e., Cleopatra robed as the goddess).

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 28-29 (Antony's dissolution in pleasures with Cleopatra, 41 BCE), trans. Sir Thomas North (1579).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'Love' n. 10: 'As a personification: the god or goddess of love; Eros or Cupid; also Venus' — the capitalised usage current in Elizabethan poetry.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 50

Plutarch Life of Antony chapters 28-29 (North 1579) describe Antony's dissolution in pleasures with Cleopatra; OED s.v. 'Love' n.10 does record the Elizabethan personification usage covering Venus/Eros, supporting both cited sources.

Identifying the capitalised 'Love' as Venus is the mainstream reading in the context of 'her soft hours' (feminine pronoun, connotations of pleasure and leisure); the OED and standard Elizabethan personification practice support it, even though Cupid/Eros is a possible alternative.

anchor_text: husband, which you say must charge his horns with garlands
summary: To 'charge his horns with garlands' sounds like decorating a beast for a festival, but the joke is bawdy: a cuckolded husband was said to grow invisible horns. Charmian is asking the soothsayer for a husband she can cheat on freely, with the horns he will grow becoming his only crown.
detail: The cuckold's horn was one of the most persistent jokes in Elizabethan comedy: an unfaithful wife supposedly caused her husband to sprout horns like a stag, visible to everyone but him. 'Charge' here means 'load' or 'furnish.' By asking for a husband whose horns she can crown with garlands, Charmian conflates the festival image of a garlanded animal with the sexual insult, making the fortune-telling session an occasion for cheerful obscenity from the first line. The scene's bawdy energy contrasts sharply with the political gravity that follows.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon. 3rd ed. Berlin: Reimer, 1902. s.v. 'horn' (cuckold's horn).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 73
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'horn' covers the cuckold's horn as a stock Elizabethan wordplay, and the claim is well supported.

The cuckold-horn pun on 'charge his horns with garlands' is securely grounded in the Elizabethan cuckoldry convention, and Charmian's wish for a husband she can freely cheat on is entirely consistent with the scene's bawdy register.

anchor_text: In nature's infinite book of secrecy A little I can read
summary: The soothsayer claims only partial access to 'nature's infinite book' — the hidden record of all that exists and will happen. The modesty is conventional for fortune-tellers, but the image establishes the scene's tone: the future can be glimpsed but never fully read.
detail: The 'book of nature' was a Renaissance commonplace: the idea that God inscribed his intentions in the natural world, which could be interpreted by those with learning. Fortune-telling traditions in both classical augury and Elizabethan popular culture rested on reading signs — in the hand, in the stars, in birds. The soothsayer's self-deprecating 'a little' keeps him credible: he does not claim full prophetic power, yet his prophecies in this scene will prove accurate.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1911. s.v. 'secrecy' (hidden or secret things).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 78

Onions s.v. 'secrecy' (hidden or secret things) is a legitimate lexicographic citation for the word-sense invoked, and the 'book of nature' gloss is a standard Renaissance commonplace requiring no further sourcing.

The 'book of nature' as a Renaissance commonplace for divine or natural intelligibility is well-established, and the reading that the soothsayer's modesty ('a little I can read') is a conventional prophetic pose is straightforwardly defensible.

anchor_text: heat my liver with drinking
summary: In Elizabethan medicine the liver was considered the seat of passion and desire. A 'heated' liver meant inflamed emotion, but Charmian prefers the literal meaning: she would rather be inflamed by wine than pine from unrequited love, as the soothsayer has just forecast she will.
detail: Galenic medicine divided the body into three regions, each with a governing organ: the brain (reason), heart (spirit/courage), and liver (appetite and passion, including desire). 'Hot-blooded' and 'liver-burning' were standard ways of saying someone was driven by strong feeling. Charmian's quip inverts the soothsayer's gloomy forecast ('more beloving than beloved') — she would rather drown unsatisfied love in drink than suffer it soberly.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1911. s.v. 'liver' (seat of passion and desire).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 93
Onions s.v. 'liver' for the organ as seat of passion and desire in Galenic medicine is a standard entry in the glossary and supports the claim directly.

Galenic physiology placing the liver as the seat of desire and passion is standard early modern doctrine, and the wordplay whereby Charmian prefers literal wine-induced heat to the figurative emotional heat the soothsayer has just forecast is fully consistent with her comic register here.

anchor_text: Herod of Jewry may do homage
summary: Herod the Great (ruled 37-4 BCE) was the Rome-backed king of Judaea and a client of Antony's. To have a child so magnificent that even Herod must bow down to it is Charmian's way of asking for extraordinary destiny — naming the most powerful local king she can think of as the measure of greatness.

anchor_text: I love long life better than figs
summary: Figs (and the fig gesture, a thumb thrust between two fingers) were a coarse sexual insult and obscenity in both classical antiquity and Elizabethan English. Charmian is saying she prefers a long life to sex — a joke that works because the audience knows she prefers both.
detail: The fig (Latin ficus, Italian fico) had a long obscene tradition: the 'fig of Spain' was a contemptuous gesture, and 'giving the fig' meant an obscene or contemptuous act. In 2 Henry IV (5.3) Pistol uses 'a fig for thee'; Iago's 'Fie, there is no such man; it is impossible' has been read as a fico. In the context of a scene saturated with sexual banter, Charmian's line is almost certainly a bawdy joke: she loves long life more than the alternative. The word will recur — fatally — in 5.2, when the Clown brings Cleopatra the asp hidden in a basket of figs.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon. 3rd ed. Berlin: Reimer, 1902. s.v. 'fig' (obscene gesture and insult).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 100
Schmidt s.v. 'fig' covers the obscene gesture and insult sense (fico / 'fig of Spain'), supporting the bawdy reading at medium confidence as stated.

The bawdy fig-gesture tradition (fico/fig of Spain as an obscene insult) is well-documented in Elizabethan usage, and reading 'I love long life better than figs' as a light sexual joke is reasonable given the scene's sustained bawdy register; the annotation correctly hedges at 'medium' confidence, and the forward-link to 5.2's basket of figs is a legitimate thematic observation, not overreach.

anchor_text: the o'erflowing Nilus presageth famine
summary: Charmian turns Iras's reading of an 'oily palm' (a wet, slippery hand) against her: a flooding Nile was supposed to predict a good harvest, but in fact an excessive flood could destroy the standing crop, bringing famine. The joke applies the same reversal to Iras's sign of 'chastity': an oily palm predicts nothing good.
detail: Egypt's agricultural calendar depended entirely on the annual Nile flood. Too little flooding left the fields unwatered; too much flooded the irrigation works and could wash away crops and villages alike. The classic pattern was that a moderate flood ('the Nile covers it') brought plenty, while extreme levels brought famine. Charmian is being pointed: just as Iras's 'chaste' palm is an ironic sign, so the Nile's flood, meant to be a blessing, can portend the opposite. The detail connects to the play's pervasive use of the Nile as an emblem of Egyptian abundance and extravagance.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 5.58 (the levels of the Nile flood and their significance for harvests).

sources.name: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca historica
sources.citation: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca historica 1.36 (the Nile flood and Egyptian agriculture).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 114

Pliny NH 5.58 does describe Nile flood-level thresholds (18 feet = famine, excess = retarded agriculture) and Diodorus 1.36 discusses Nile flood levels and Egyptian agricultural prediction, both supporting the annotation's claims.

The reading that excessive Nile flood can signify famine (rather than plenty) is historically accurate and the rhetorical reversal — Charmian weaponising the same sign-reading convention against Iras's 'chaste' palm — is clearly supported by the text at lines 113-117.

anchor_text: sweet Isis, I beseech thee
summary: Charmian invokes Isis, the supreme Egyptian goddess, as casually as a Roman might invoke Juno. Isis was the great mother-goddess and protector of women in Egypt, so calling on her for a comically bad fortune for Alexas is entirely in character for one of Cleopatra's Egyptian attendants.
detail: Isis (Egyptian Aset) was the most powerful goddess in the Egyptian pantheon: wife of Osiris, mother of Horus, and the divine model of wifely loyalty and magical power. The Ptolemaic queens, including Cleopatra VII, identified themselves with her. Her cult had also spread through the Mediterranean by the first century BCE, so the invocation is authentic local colour for Cleopatra's court. Charmian will use Isis's name again at 1.2 line 132, and the goddess haunts the play as Cleopatra's divine archetype throughout. The prayer itself is parody — a formal triple invocation (1.127, 1.129, 1.131) applied to the absurd wish that Alexas's future wives be terrible.

sources.name: Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris
sources.citation: Plutarch, Moralia, 'De Iside et Osiride' (On Isis and Osiris): Isis as the supreme Egyptian goddess of life, magic, and protection.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 126
Plutarch's Moralia, 'De Iside et Osiride', is a real work that describes Isis as the supreme Egyptian goddess of life, magic, and protection and is the standard ancient source for this material.

Isis as supreme Egyptian goddess and divine archetype for the Ptolemaic queens (including Cleopatra VII) is sound, and the reading of Charmian's prayer as a parodic triple invocation applied to a comic curse on Alexas is fully consistent with the text at lines 126-131; the claim that the prayer is a 'formal triple invocation' (127, 129, 131) is directly verified by the text.

anchor_text: A Roman thought hath struck him
summary: Cleopatra means that a serious, duty-bound Roman impulse has suddenly seized Antony. 'A Roman thought' means ambition, obligation to the empire, and the Stoic sense of public duty — everything Egypt is not. The phrase crystallises the play's central conflict between Roman discipline and Egyptian pleasure.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579), on Antony's divided life between Roman duty and Eastern/Egyptian pleasure (a theme developed across the Alexandria chapters, esp. chs. 28-29).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 146
Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Chapter 6 does not treat Antony's divided Roman/Egyptian nature; generalized to the Life of Antony (the Alexandria chapters) rather than a single wrong chapter.

The Rome/Egypt binary as the play's central structural opposition is the mainstream scholarly reading, and 'A Roman thought hath struck him' as a concise dramatic statement of Antony's divided loyalties is fully defensible; the detail that this is the set-up for the messenger scenes that follow is confirmed by the scene text.

anchor_text: Speak to me home, mince not the general tongue
summary: 'Speak to me home' means speak bluntly, to the point, without softening. 'Mince not the general tongue' means do not water down or chop up what is commonly said about me in Rome. Antony is commanding the messenger to deliver the worst news plainly, as if Antony were an ordinary person who can bear hard truths.
detail: 'Home' in this sense is common in Shakespeare: to 'come home' or 'speak home' means to hit the mark directly, with no evasion. 'Mince' (as in 'not mince words') means to cut or reduce — to deliver something in small, digestible pieces rather than whole. 'The general tongue' is what Rome generally says, the public opinion. Antony's injunction is deliberately self-abnegating: he wants to hear himself denounced as Rome denies him, with no courtly trimming for his rank.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1911. s.v. 'home' (adv., directly, pointedly) and 'mince' (to soften, extenuate).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 172
Onions s.v. 'home' (adv., directly, pointedly) and 'mince' (to soften or extenuate) are standard entries that directly support both word-sense claims in the annotation.

The gloss on 'home' (pointedly, to the mark) and 'mince' (to cut small, soften) is standard and well-attested, and the reading that Antony is commanding blunt truth-telling, even self-damaging, is clearly supported by lines 172-175 including his explicit instruction to 'Rail thou in Fulvia's phrase; and taunt my faults.'

anchor_text: our ills told us Is as our earing
summary: 'Earing' means ploughing — from the Old English verb 'to ear the ground.' Antony is saying that being told your faults is like ploughing a field: it looks destructive in the moment but is necessary to make anything grow. When minds go idle the result is weeds; criticism is the plough that breaks that up.
detail: The metaphor is agricultural: idle land grows weeds (line 176, 'we bring forth weeds / When our quick minds lie still'); hearing one's faults diagnosed is like being ploughed — painful and disruptive but productive. 'Ear' in the sense of 'to till or plough' survives in the King James Bible (Isaiah 30:24: 'the oxen likewise and the young asses that ear the ground'). The word was already archaic by Shakespeare's day, giving the speech a deliberate rustic solemnity.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ear, v.2': 'to plough, till'; attested from Old English; cf. Isaiah 30:24 (Geneva Bible 1599).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 177

OED s.v. 'ear, v.2' (to plough, till) is the correct lexicographic source, and Isaiah 30:24 ('the oxen that ear the ground') is attested in both the 1611 KJV and the earlier Geneva Bible tradition, supporting the annotation's citation.

The archaic meaning of 'ear' as 'to plough' is securely attested (OED, Geneva Bible Isaiah 30:24), and the agricultural metaphor — idle minds breed weeds; hearing one's faults is like ploughing — is directly supported by lines 176-178 ('we bring forth weeds / When our quick minds lie still; and our ills told us / Is as our earing').

anchor_text: These strong Egyptian fetters I must break, Or lose myself in dotage
summary: Antony pictures his attachment to Cleopatra as iron chains ('fetters') binding him. 'Dotage' is infatuated, foolish devotion that has undermined his judgment. The imagery of enslavement will run throughout the play; here it is the only moment Antony himself states the Roman view of his situation.
detail: Antony's language borrows the Roman vocabulary his critics use: Philo opened the play calling him 'a strumpet's fool' who has given his heart's 'captain's heart' to a 'gypsy.' Here, for one moment, Antony sees himself through Roman eyes — bound by Egypt, unable to act freely. The word 'dotage' (from 'dote,' to be excessively or foolishly fond) is crucial: it is how Roman opinion characterises Antony in 1.1 ('his dotage'), and Antony here concedes the charge, at least in the privacy of his own thought. The self-knowledge is immediately overtaken by further news.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 25 (North 1579): Antony 'besotted' and made unfit for business by Cleopatra.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1911. s.v. 'dotage' (excessive infatuation).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 184

Plutarch, Life of Antony 25 describes Cleopatra's seduction of Antony and his captivation, but does not specifically state he is 'besotted and unfit for business'; that framing runs across chapters 25-29 rather than being localised to ch. 25, making the chapter citation imprecise but not wholly unsupportive.

The reading of 'fetters' as the Roman vocabulary of enslavement applied to Egypt, and 'dotage' as the charge Rome levels at Antony that he here momentarily concedes, is the mainstream interpretation; the link back to Philo's opening speech ('his dotage,' TLN 1-10) is textually sound.

anchor_text: By revolution lowering, does become The opposite of itself
summary: 'By revolution lowering' means 'by turning around, sinking down' — like a wheel that has rotated to its lowest point. Antony is saying that present pleasure, by the simple turning of time, eventually turns into its own opposite: what you desire becomes what you regret. The thought is triggered by the news of Fulvia's death.
detail: 'Revolution' here means rotation or cyclic turning, not political overthrow. The image is related to Fortune's wheel: whatever stands at the top must eventually descend. 'Lowering' (pronounced with three syllables: LOW-er-ing) means declining, sinking. The philosophical content is a version of the stoic observation that desire, once satisfied or lost, transforms into either indifference or regret. Antony's own feeling for Fulvia is the example: he wanted rid of her, now that she is gone he wishes her back.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary

anchor_text: let women die: it were pity to cast them away for nothing
summary: Enobarbus uses 'die' in its common Elizabethan slang sense of achieving sexual climax, alongside the literal sense of death. He is mocking Cleopatra's theatrical swoons and 'deaths' in response to bad news, arguing that if she must die, at least let it be for a real cause — not for nothing, and not just an elaborate performance.
detail: 'To die' as a sexual euphemism (from the idea that orgasm was a brief loss of consciousness) was standard Elizabethan slang — Donne uses it ('The Canonization'), Benedick and Beatrice play with it. Enobarbus's whole speech (lines 207-213) layers the two meanings: Cleopatra 'dies twenty times upon far poorer moment' — she performs death-swoons over trifles, but there is also a compliment hidden in the mockery ('there is mettle in death, which commits some loving act upon her'). The wit is characteristic of Enobarbus: he deflates Antony's crisis with a sexual-comedic reading of Cleopatra's histrionics, and in doing so inadvertently testifies to her magnetism.

anchor_text: Sextus Pompeius Hath given the dare to Caesar, and commands The empire of the sea
summary: Sextus Pompeius (young Pompey) is the son of Pompey the Great, Rome's master-general who was defeated and killed by Julius Caesar. With a powerful fleet he has effectively challenged Octavius Caesar's authority and controls the sea-lanes. This is the third piece of bad news prompting Antony's decision to leave Egypt.
detail: After the defeat of his father's supporters at Munda (45 BCE) and Philippi (42 BCE), Sextus Pompeius built a formidable fleet and operated from Sicily, intercepting Rome's grain supply and sheltering political refugees from the proscriptions. By c. 40 BCE he controlled Sicily, Sardinia, and Corsica and was effectively blockading Italy. The Roman people, hungry and nostalgic, were transferring to him the legendary prestige of his father — 'throw / Pompey the Great, and all his dignities, / Upon his son' (lines 252-254). This process of nostalgia is what Antony specifically describes: the populace is fickle, lionising only when it suits them, now projecting the dead father's image onto the living son.

anchor_text: Pompey the Great, and all his dignities, Upon his son
summary: Pompey the Great was Julius Caesar's former ally turned rival — once Rome's supreme general, he was defeated at Pharsalus (48 BCE) and murdered in Egypt. Here he is only a memory being transferred by a fickle Roman crowd onto his living son Sextus. The two Pompeys — father and son — must not be confused: the dead one is invoked; the young one (Sextus Pompeius) is the real threat.
detail: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (Pompey the Great, 106-48 BCE) was for decades Rome's greatest soldier, conqueror of the eastern Mediterranean, and the man who completed Lucullus's wars in Asia Minor. His three-way alliance with Caesar and Crassus (the First Triumvirate) gave way to civil war; Caesar routed him at Pharsalus in Thessaly in 48 BCE. Fleeing to Egypt, Pompey was murdered by its king's advisers on arrival. His sons continued the war until Caesar crushed them at Munda in Spain in 45 BCE. Sextus, the younger son, then built his fleet. The crowd's nostalgia — projecting Pompey the Great's 'dignities' onto Sextus — is the kind of popular fickleness Antony describes bitterly here.

The disambiguation of Pompey the Great (106-48 BCE, defeated at Pharsalus, killed in Egypt) from Sextus Pompeius his surviving son is accurate, and the reading that the crowd's projection of the father's 'dignities' onto the son is the mechanism Antony is describing is directly supported by lines 252-254.

anchor_text: In time we hate that which we often fear
summary: Charmian offers a sententious maxim — a compressed general truth — to warn Cleopatra: excessive possessiveness creates fear in the beloved, and fear eventually curdles into hatred. The rhyming couplet gives the line the feel of a proverb used to close an argument.
detail: In Shakespeare a rhymed couplet often signals a maxim or a speech-ending 'sentence' (sententia), a brief moral proposition. Charmian is arguing for a different strategy: give way, cross him in nothing (TLN 273). The proverb pattern is common in the period; this particular formulation has no exact classical precedent but echoes Stoic advice on the corrosive effects of dependency. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, notes 'fear' used here in the sense of dread or apprehension of losing.

anchor_text: shake the throned gods, Who have been false to Fulvia
summary: Cleopatra uses hyperbole and a logical trap in the same breath: Antony can swear oaths powerful enough to shake the gods on their thrones, yet even that cannot make his vows credible, since he has already broken his oaths to Fulvia, his first Roman wife. 'Mouth-made vows' are oaths spoken with the lips only, not felt in the heart.

Cleopatra's argument is pointed: the very gods Antony invokes as guarantors of loyalty are themselves 'throned' — seated in power — yet were witnesses to his faithlessness. 'Break themselves in swearing' (TLN 300) means the vows shatter at the very moment of being made, because the swearer's past makes them inherently false. Plutarch stresses that Antony's affair with Cleopatra began while he was still bound to Fulvia (Life of Antony 25, trans. North).

anchor_text: Eternity was in our lips and eyes, Bliss in our brows' bent; none our parts so poor But was a race of heaven
summary: Cleopatra claims that in the height of their love every part of their two bodies, no matter how minor, was a 'race of heaven' — a breed or lineage of the divine, a piece of eternity. 'Brows' bent' means the arch of the brow; 'race' is used in the sense of family stock, implying their love was of divine descent.
detail: The passage is a blazon — a rhetorical praise-catalogue of bodily parts — turned outward to encompass the whole shared moment: not just beauty but eternity was in their physical exchange. The word 'race' (TLN 307) means offspring, species, or lineage (OED, s.v. 'race' n.2, sense 4: 'a breed, stock, or lineage'), so 'race of heaven' implies divine ancestry. Cleopatra uses the image to set an ideal past against an imminent betrayal: if those moments were truly divine, then Antony's departure either destroys that divinity or proves he was always lying. The syntax is compressed: 'none our parts so poor / But was a race of heaven' = 'no part of us, however humble, was not of heavenly stock.'

anchor_text: I would I had thy inches; thou shouldst know There were a heart in Egypt

anchor_text: Sextus Pompeius Makes his approaches to the port of Rome
summary: Sextus Pompeius — the young Pompey — was the son of Pompey the Great, Rome's greatest general before Julius Caesar, who was defeated and killed in 48 BCE. The young Sextus has inherited his father's name and popular support, and commands a powerful fleet that is blockading or threatening Rome's harbours. He is a character in the play; his famous dead father is a separate figure.

The 'condemned Pompey / Rich in his father's honour' (TLN 321-322) is Antony's explanation for why the threat has grown: discontented Romans who have not benefited from the current regime are rallying to a man whose family name carries enormous prestige. This naval threat is Antony's stated political reason for leaving Cleopatra and returning to Rome. Sextus Pompeius's father, Pompey the Great, is a distinct figure; the card pompey-the-great concerns the dead father only.

anchor_text: By the fire That quickens Nilus' slime
summary: Antony swears by the sun's warmth ('fire') that animates the mud ('slime') of the Nile, from which life was believed to spontaneously generate — a famous ancient theory. The ancient Egyptians and Greeks believed that when the Nile flooded and then receded, leaving behind rich black silt, the sun's heat caused living creatures to breed directly from the mud.
detail: The idea of spontaneous generation from Nile mud was a commonplace of classical natural history. Plutarch connects the Nile's creative power to Egypt's fertility, and Pliny the Elder discusses how animals were thought to arise from the silt after the annual inundation (Pliny, Natural History 9.84). Diodorus Siculus, writing specifically on Egypt, gives a detailed account of the Nile's life-giving mud and the creatures it produces (Bibliotheca historica 1.10, 1.36). Shakespeare returns to this image in 2.7 ('Your serpent of Egypt is bred now of your mud by the operation of your sun') and in Antony's own death speech. The oath ties Antony's honor to the earth of Egypt itself, a fitting pledge as he prepares to leave.

anchor_text: Cut my lace, Charmian, come
summary: Cleopatra calls for the lace of her bodice or stays to be cut, a conventional signal of being overcome with emotion — the tightening of laced clothing was thought to restrict breathing and cause faintness. Whether she is genuinely feeling faint or performing distress to regain Antony's attention, the gesture itself is theatrical.
detail: Elizabethan and Jacobean women's dress often featured tightly laced bodices or 'stays'; cutting the lace was the standard first-aid response when a woman appeared to swoon. The gesture on stage reads simultaneously as genuine physical distress and as a calculated performance, consistent with the earlier scene (TLN 278, 'I am sick and sullen'). Editors from Malone onward have noted that the call to cut the lace may begin a fit of weeping or fainting as a new tactical move, since Cleopatra immediately recovers ('But let it be: I am quickly ill and well, / So Antony loves,' TLN 346-347).

anchor_text: this Herculean Roman does become The carriage of his chafe
summary: Cleopatra calls Antony 'Herculean' because he was believed to be a descendant of Hercules, the greatest hero of classical myth — and because his physical power and fierce temper match the god. 'Carriage of his chafe' means the bearing or manner of his anger. She is mocking him to Charmian even as he storms off: look how well this great hero wears his rage.
detail: Plutarch records that the Antonii claimed descent from Anton, a son of Hercules, and that Antony cultivated the image deliberately — dressing and presenting himself to match it (Life of Antony 4). The identification of Antony with Hercules runs throughout the play and becomes tragically important in 4.3, when mysterious music underground signals that the god is deserting his protege on the eve of final defeat. 'Chafe' means anger, irritation, or heat of passion (from Old French chaufer, to warm). Cleopatra's comment is at once affectionate and sardonic — she finds his angry dignity attractive even as she engineers it.

anchor_text: my oblivion is a very Antony, And I am all forgotten
summary: Cleopatra turns Antony's name into a synonym for forgetfulness: 'my oblivion is a very Antony' means her forgetting is as overwhelming as Antony himself — or possibly, Antony is the cause of her losing her train of thought. 'I am all forgotten' is a pun: she is completely forgotten (by him), and she has completely forgotten (what she was about to say).

Cleopatra has been struggling to finish a sentence for several lines — 'something it is I would — ' (TLN 368) — and blames her own distraction on Antony's presence. But 'all forgotten' puns on the passive (I am forgotten, abandoned) and the active (I have forgotten everything). The name 'Antony' becomes an embodiment of oblivion — and for a moment the play names the force that is destroying Antony himself, his failure of Roman memory and duty. The OED records 'oblivion' in the sense of forgetfulness and also of utter inattention to duty (s.v. 'oblivion' senses 1-2).

anchor_text: my becomings kill me, when they do not Eye well to you
summary: 'Becomings' is a rare Shakespearean noun meaning the qualities, graces, or behaviors that suit or become a person. Cleopatra is saying: my own characteristic ways — my moods, my performances, my arts — are destroying me when they fail to please you or look well in your eyes. The word occurs nowhere else in the canon.
detail: The neologism 'becomings' (used only here in Shakespeare) condenses a whole philosophy of Cleopatra's self-presentation: she defines herself through how she appears to Antony, so when her performances misfire she is annihilated. 'Eye well to you' means 'look good to your eyes' or 'appear well in your sight.' The line is Cleopatra's most unguarded moment in the scene — a confession that her theatrical nature is not mere manipulation but the substance of who she is, and that Antony is her essential audience. Schmidt and the Arden editors gloss 'becomings' as 'graces,' 'qualities that become me,' or 'attractive ways.'

anchor_text: upon your sword Sit laurel victory
summary: Cleopatra blesses Antony with a wish that the laurel wreath of Roman victory — the crown awarded to a triumphant general — may perch on his very sword. The laurel wreath was the specific emblem of military triumph in Rome; victorious commanders and emperors were depicted wearing it.
detail: The laurel (Laurus nobilis) was sacred to Apollo and had been the crown of Roman victors and later emperors since at least the Republic. A Roman general granted a full triumph wore a laurel wreath; lesser victories earned the 'ovation,' with a myrtle crown instead. The wish is significant in context: Cleopatra is releasing Antony to fight as Rome's soldier, and the blessing is entirely couched in Roman, not Egyptian, imagery — laurel, not the lotus or the sistrum of Isis. The image also carries irony, since the next time Antony goes to battle at Actium (3.7-3.10) the laurel will belong to Octavius.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony; Plutarch, Life of Caesar; Roman triumphal custom: the laurel wreath as emblem of the victorious Roman commander.

The claim about the laurel wreath is historically sound, but the citation names 'Plutarch, Life of Antony; Plutarch, Life of Caesar' without specifying any chapter, making independent verification of the source support impossible.

The laurel as the specific crown of a Roman triumph (versus myrtle for an ovation) is historically accurate, and the irony of blessing Antony in Roman imagery while sending him away is a mainstream dramatic reading.

anchor_text: Our separation so abides, and flies, That thou, residing here, goes yet with me, And I, hence fleeting, here remain with thee
summary: Antony closes the scene with a paradox: their parting both 'abides' (stays, remains fixed) and 'flies' (moves, is gone). By staying in Egypt, Cleopatra travels with him; by leaving for Rome, he stays with her. The figure is a chiasmus — crossing paired opposites — that makes separation and presence simultaneous. It is the play's first vision of the lovers as mutually constituted: each inhabits the other.
detail: The rhetorical form is chiasmus (X-shaped reversal: A:B :: B:A — she stays/he goes :: he stays/she goes), combined with paradox. 'Abides' and 'flies' are contraries joined by the conjunction 'and': the separation both persists and departs at once. Antony's leave-taking thus circles back toward unity: the two are inseparable even at the moment of separation. The figure recalls the Petrarchan paradoxes of the love-lyric tradition but is more precisely philosophical — it anticipates Cleopatra's much later claim that she contains Antony ('his legs bestrid the ocean,' 5.2). 'Hence fleeting' means 'fleeing hence, moving away from here.'

The chiastic structure is correctly identified and accurately described; the Petrarchan paradox comparison and the forward echo in Cleopatra's 5.2 speech are defensible scholarly connections.

anchor_text: queen of Ptolemy
summary: Cleopatra is 'the queen of Ptolemy' — the last ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty, a Macedonian-Greek royal house founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals that had ruled Egypt since 305 BCE. Octavius Caesar uses the title pointedly, stressing her foreign, dynastic identity rather than her name.
detail: The Ptolemaic rulers presented themselves as pharaohs and divine kings; Cleopatra VII was the dynasty's last and most famous member. To Roman ears the phrase signals everything disreputable about Egypt: a monarchy whose ruler claimed divine status, wielded absolute power, and expected submission Rome associated with 'oriental' despotism. Calling Antony 'less manlike' than this foreign queen is Octavius's way of saying he has been unmanned.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony, trans. North (1579); Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca historica 1 (on Egypt and the Ptolemies).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 393

Plutarch's Life of Antony is a genuine source for the Cleopatra/Ptolemaic framing, and Diodorus Siculus Book 1 does cover Egypt and the Ptolemaic context; the dynasty-founded-305-BCE claim is historically accurate.

The gloss accurately reads the pejorative dynastic title as Octavius stressing Antony's foreign entanglement and emasculation; the claim that 'less manlike than this foreign queen' encodes the unmanning reading is well supported by the immediate text ('is not more manlike / Than Cleopatra; nor the queen of Ptolemy / More womanly than he').

anchor_text: spots of heaven, More fiery by night's blackness
summary: Lepidus defends Antony with a conceit comparing his faults to stars: just as stars appear more brilliant against the darkness of the night sky, so Antony's flaws only throw his greatness into sharper relief. The logic flatters Antony by arguing his vices highlight, rather than hide, his virtues.
detail: The figure is an antithesis built into a simile: darkness (fault/night) makes the light (virtue/star) more visible. 'Spots' could mean blemishes but also the specks of light that are stars, allowing the ambiguity to run both ways. Octavius Caesar flatly refuses this line of reasoning — 'You are too indulgent' — and the debate between the two over whether Antony's past heroism mitigates his present conduct is a structural hinge of the scene.

The pun on 'spots' (blemishes / points of starlight) enabling the antithesis is textually sound, and the note that Octavius flatly rejects Lepidus's reasoning ('You are too indulgent') is accurate to the scene; no over-reading.

anchor_text: keep the turn of tippling with a slave
summary: 'Keep the turn of tippling' means to take one's turn in a round of drinking — to match cup for cup with the others. 'Slave' here means a low-born person, someone beneath a Roman general's dignity. Octavius Caesar is accusing Antony of drinking in rotation with commoners.
detail: 'Turn' in this sense is a place in sequence, the practice of communal drinking rounds. The phrase 'stand the buffet / With knaves that smell of sweat' (TLN 408-409) reinforces the social outrage: not just drinking, but brawling or trading blows ('buffet') with 'knaves' — low, untrustworthy men. For Roman aristocratic ideology, this kind of tavern fellowship was a sign of character disorder, not sociability.

Onions's A Shakespeare Glossary (1911) is a real standard reference and its coverage of 'turn' (rotation/sequence) and 'tippling' (habitual drinking) accurately supports the archaic-vocabulary gloss given.

'Keep the turn' as taking one's round in communal drinking is the established sense and the surrounding lines ('stand the buffet / With knaves that smell of sweat') confirm the social-degradation reading; no over-reading.

anchor_text: taught us from the primal state / That he which is was wish'd until he were
summary: Octavius Caesar is offering a political maxim: from the earliest times ('primal state') it has been observed that every ruler is desired and supported right up to the moment he achieves power, then becomes resented once in place. 'He which is was wish'd until he were' means: the man who now holds power was longed for only until he actually got it.
detail: The line is dense because it compresses a paradox: 'he which is' (the man who now holds power) 'was wish'd' (was desired) 'until he were' (only until he became that man). Once someone holds power, the same people who wanted him there start looking for a replacement. Octavius applies this to Pompey: Pompey is drawing support from everyone who currently fears Caesar, not because Pompey is beloved but because he represents the next hoped-for replacement. The 'ebb'd man' (TLN 433) — the man out of favor — becomes precious precisely because he is absent and powerless. This is a realist reading of popular politics, not a moral observation.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony, trans. North (1579); the general principle reflects the political analysis North's Plutarch attributes to Caesar.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 431

The citation to Plutarch's Life of Antony for the 'primal state' political maxim is too vague — the speech is Shakespeare's composition and Plutarch does not contain this aphorism; the source claim rests on a non-falsifiable 'general principle' assertion rather than a specific passage.

The paraphrase — power is desired until it is achieved, after which the same constituency looks for the next candidate — correctly captures the paradox in the compressed syntax and accurately identifies Pompey as the referent; the attribution to Octavius as a realist rather than moralist is well supported by his cold tone throughout the scene.

anchor_text: vagabond flag upon the stream, Goes to and back, lackeying the varying tide
summary: Octavius Caesar compares the common people ('this common body') to a piece of water-weed or a floating flag drifting back and forth on the tide — blown wherever the current takes it, never fixed on any course. 'Lackeying' means serving slavishly, going wherever a master directs.
detail: A 'vagabond flag' is a water-plant such as a flag-iris, or simply a piece of floating debris, that the tide pulls in and out indifferently. The simile expresses Octavius's contempt for public opinion and popular loyalty: the crowd backs Pompey only because the tide is currently moving that way, not out of any settled judgment. 'To rot itself with motion' — the final phrase — darkens the image: purposeless back-and-forth motion leads not to growth but to decay. The conceit belongs to Octavius's consistently cold, calculating characterization, here expressing the managerial distrust of democratic instability.

Identifying 'vagabond flag' as a floating water-plant (flag-iris or debris) driven by the tide is the standard gloss, 'lackeying' as slavish following is correct, and reading 'rot itself with motion' as purposeless decay rather than growth is consistent with Octavius's contempt for popular opinion expressed throughout the passage.

anchor_text: Menecrates and Menas, famous pirates
summary: Menecrates and Menas were the two chief naval commanders of Sextus Pompeius (the young Pompey), and the word 'pirates' is used accurately: they carried out raids on merchant shipping and Italian coastal towns, disrupting grain supply and threatening Rome. Both appear later in the play, with Menas becoming a significant character at the feast on Pompey's galley.
detail: Sextus Pompeius controlled Sicily and the western sea-lanes and used that control to strangle Rome's grain imports — a form of economic warfare that made him a genuine threat to the triumvirate even without winning pitched battles. Plutarch calls him 'lord of the sea' at this period. Shakespeare keeps the historical names from Plutarch's Life of Antony; Menas, the more prominent of the two, reappears at 2.7 where he offers Pompey a chance to murder the triumvirs by cutting the ship's cable — and the refusal defines Pompey's political character.

anchor_text: lascivious wassails
summary: 'Wassails' are drinking bouts — the word comes from the Old English toast 'waes hael' (be well) and had come to mean any boisterous revelry with heavy drinking. Octavius Caesar turns away from Pompey's threat to address Antony directly and reproach his 'lascivious' (lustful, wanton) drinking parties in Alexandria.
detail: The word carried associations of the old English midwinter feasts and Twelfth Night revels in Shakespeare's day; applying it to Egypt gives Antony's Alexandrian pleasures a note of barbaric, seasonal excess. Octavius Caesar's direct address to the absent Antony — 'Antony, / Leave thy lascivious wassails' (TLN 447-448) — is a rhetorical apostrophe: he is speaking to someone not present. The speech then pivots to recall the heroic endurance Antony showed at the battle of Modena, making the contrast between past virtue and present dissolution as sharp as possible.

anchor_text: beaten from Modena, where thou slew'st / Hirtius and Pansa, consuls
summary: At Mutina (modern Modena) in 43 BCE Antony besieged the conspirator Decimus Brutus; the two consuls Hirtius and Pansa led an army against him. Both consuls died in the fighting, and Antony was driven off. Octavius Caesar is citing this retreat as the moment Antony showed extraordinary endurance — starving, drinking filth, and eating bark — while remembering that even in defeat Antony had defeated two senior Roman officials.

anchor_text: drink / The stale of horses, and the gilded puddle / Which beasts would cough at
summary: 'Stale' means urine — specifically horses' urine. A 'gilded puddle' is a muddy pool with a sheen of slime or pond-scum on the surface ('gilded' from the metallic glitter of stagnant water). Octavius Caesar describes Antony on the retreat after Modena as so desperate for water that he drank filth even animals refused.
detail: The passage is drawn directly from Plutarch's account of Antony's flight across the Alps after Mutina (43 BCE), which North translates in similar terms. 'Gilded' here is a bitter irony: the word usually signals gold, royalty, and luxury, but here the gleam is mere surface scum on foul water. Both images serve Octavius Caesar's argument that the soldier who endured this without complaint — 'thy cheek / So much as lank'd not' (TLN 462-463) — is a different man from the one currently 'tumbling on the bed of Ptolemy.'

anchor_text: Give me to drink mandragora
summary: Mandragora (mandrake) is a real narcotic plant. Its root contains sedative alkaloids and was used in the ancient world as a soporific and painkiller. Cleopatra wants a deep, drug-induced sleep to blot out the slow hours while Antony is away.
detail: The mandrake (Mandragora officinarum) was genuinely used in classical medicine as a sedative; Dioscorides and Pliny both describe its narcotic properties. In Shakespeare's England John Gerard's Herball (1597) reports the same uses alongside the folk legends about the plant's human-shaped root and fatal shriek when uprooted. The mandrake also appears in Othello 3.3 ('not poppy, nor mandragora') and Romeo and Juliet 4.3 in the same context of sleep and oblivion. Cleopatra's request here establishes that for her time without Antony is a kind of death that only unconsciousness can ease.

anchor_text: being unseminar'd, thy freer thoughts
summary: 'Unseminar'd' is Shakespeare's coinage meaning 'having no seed' -- that is, castrated. Cleopatra tells Mardian it is well for him that, being a eunuch, his thoughts are free of the lust that would (as her own longing for Antony does to her) drive them out of Egypt after an absent lover; his 'freer thoughts / May not fly forth of Egypt.' The line also puns on 'seminary,' a seed-bed or place of training.
detail: The word does not appear before this passage in English; Shakespeare forms it from Latin semen (seed) via the adjective 'seminal.' The play on 'seminary' (originally a seed-plot, hence a school) gives the line two registers at once: Mardian lacks both physical seed and its metaphorical equivalent, the training of the passions. Because he is unseeded, he is not carried abroad by desire -- unlike Cleopatra, whose longing keeps flying after Antony. 'Affections' (TLN 496) means 'desires' or 'emotions,' so Cleopatra's next question -- 'Hast thou affections?' -- tests whether a man without seed can still feel.

anchor_text:
The demi-Atlas of this earth, the arm
And burgonet of men
summary: Atlas was a Titan condemned by Zeus to hold up the sky on his shoulders — the archetypal image of one who bears the weight of the world. A 'demi-Atlas' is a half-Atlas: Antony is one of two men (himself and Octavius Caesar) who together carry the burden of the Roman world. A 'burgonet' is a light steel helmet; to call Antony 'the arm and burgonet of men' means he is both the sword-arm and the protecting head of mankind.
detail: The compound 'demi-Atlas' is Shakespeare's own coinage (not in the classical sources), but its meaning is unmistakable: Antony bears half the world as Atlas bore the whole sky. The reference pairs with Philo's opening lines (1.1) calling Antony 'the triple pillar of the world' — see the-second-triumvirate card. A burgonet (also spelled 'burganet') was a close-fitting soldier's helmet; OED traces it to the mid-sixteenth century from French bourguignotte. Together 'arm' and 'burgonet' give Antony both offensive and defensive glory.

anchor_text:
that great medicine hath
With his tinct gilded thee
summary: Both 'great medicine' and 'tinct' are alchemical terms. In alchemy the 'great medicine' (or Philosopher's Stone) was the ultimate transmuting agent, believed capable of turning base metals into gold. 'Tinct' is its tincture — the colouring or transmuting essence it imparted. Cleopatra says that Alexas, a mere messenger, has been 'gilded' (turned to gold) simply by carrying Antony's touch, because Antony is the great medicine who transforms everything around him.
detail: Renaissance alchemy imagined the Philosopher's Stone as a red or golden powder or 'tincture' that could transmute lead to gold; by extension the 'great medicine' was any supreme perfecting agent. Shakespeare returns to the same alchemical vocabulary at 1.4 ('great medicine') and elsewhere in the canon (All's Well That Ends Well, where Helena's cure is the 'great medicine'). Cleopatra's compliment is extravagant but precisely chosen: it does not say Alexas is worthy, only that proximity to a perfect thing confers some of its lustre. The alchemical metaphor fits the play's wider interest in transformation and in Antony's supernatural charisma.

anchor_text:
By Isis, I will give thee bloody teeth
If thou with Caesar paragon again
My man of men
summary: Cleopatra swears 'by Isis,' the supreme Egyptian goddess. This oath is not decorative: the Ptolemaic queens presented themselves as the living image of Isis, so for Cleopatra to swear by Isis is to swear by her own divine identity as queen. 'Paragon' here means 'compare as an equal' — she threatens Charmian for ranking Julius Caesar ('that brave Caesar') alongside Antony.
detail: Isis was the great mother-goddess of Egypt — giver of the Nile's abundance, protector of the dead, and divine queen. Plutarch (Life of Antony 54) records that Cleopatra gave audience 'in the habiliments of the goddess Isis,' and Shakespeare returns to this identification explicitly at 3.6. To swear by Isis is therefore, for Cleopatra, both a religious oath and a claim of sovereign identity. The verb 'paragon' (to compare as equal, to match) is obsolete in modern English; OED traces it as a verb meaning 'to compare' to the mid-sixteenth century. The 'Caesar' Charmian praises is Julius Caesar (Cleopatra's former lover), not Octavius Caesar — the same Julius Caesar named at TLN 514.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 54, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Cleopatra presenting herself as the goddess Isis.

anchor_text:
My salad days,
When I was green in judgment
summary: 'Salad days' is Shakespeare's coinage meaning the days of inexperience and immaturity — the 'green' time of life, when judgment is unripe like uncooked vegetables. Cleopatra admits that admiring Julius Caesar was a young woman's mistake, implying that her love for Antony is the mature, considered passion of a grown queen.
detail: The phrase appears to originate here in English; no earlier use has been traced. summary: Pompey delivers a shrewd one-line portrait of each triumvir: Octavius Caesar is a cold fiscal operator who wins revenue but alienates loyalty; Lepidus (the weakest of the three) merely flatters both his stronger partners and is not genuinely valued by either. anchor_text: Epicurean cooks / Sharpen with cloyless sauce his appetite
summary: 'Epicurean' here means devoted to sensual luxury — rich food, pleasure, and indulgence. The word comes from Epicurus, the Greek philosopher, whose followers in Rome were popularly (if unfairly) associated with feasting and pleasure. 'Cloyless' means never cloying, never satiating: the sauce is so perfectly made it keeps sharpening rather than dulling Antony's appetite. Pompey is picturing Antony held captive by endlessly pleasurable dining.
detail: The historical Epicurus (341-270 BCE) actually advocated a simple life and the absence of pain rather than active hedonism; but 'Epicurean' had long been misused in popular Latin and English writing to mean purely pleasure-seeking and self-indulgent — Cicero and Horace both play with the oversimplification. The phrase 'Epicurean cooks' distills the slur: Antony's household is not just comfortable but governed by a philosophy of appetite. Two lines later Pompey adds 'Lethe'd dullness' — the river of forgetfulness in the classical underworld — as the final destination of this cycle of feasting and sleep: Antony will forget his honor entirely, reduced to an animal round of eating and sleeping.

anchor_text: 'Twere pregnant they should square between themselves
summary: 'Pregnant' here means obvious, full of likelihood — not physical pregnancy, but a sense of something weighty and evident. 'Square' means to quarrel or fight. As figures of inexorable doom they were appropriate messengers of terrible news in classical rhetoric. The contrast with 'a formal man' (a man in ordinary social dress, going through proper forms) sharpens the point: the news is too terrible for human normalcy.

anchor_text: I do not like 'but yet', it does allay The good precedence
summary: Cleopatra objects to the phrase 'but yet' because it qualifies (or 'allays,' meaning weakens and cancels) the good news that came before it. anchor_text: Hadst thou Narcissus in thy face, to me Thou wouldst appear most ugly

anchor_text: Though he be painted one way like a Gorgon, T'other way he's a Mars

The double image captures Cleopatra's conflict: Antony has done something monstrous (married Octavia), yet he remains the embodiment of heroic manhood to her. 'Perspective' or anamorphic paintings, which showed different images depending on the viewing angle, were fashionable in late 16th-century Europe; Cleopatra's image may glance at this technique (compare Richard II 2.2.18).

anchor_text: Wherefore my father should revengers want

anchor_text: Rid all the sea of pirates; then to send / Measures of wheat to Rome
summary: The peace terms Pompey describes are the actual conditions of the historical Treaty of Misenum (39 BCE). Sextus was to clear the Mediterranean of pirates in exchange for control of Sicily, Sardinia, and Achaea; Rome in turn depended on Sicily for its wheat supply, so reliable grain shipments were a central demand. 'Targes undinted' means shields with no dents — i.e., swords sheathed and shields untouched, the idiom for making peace without fighting.

Sextus himself commanded a network that controlled much of Rome's grain supply, which gave him enormous leverage. 'Unhacked edges' means unblunted sword-blades; 'targes undinted' means undented shields. Together the two images form a legal formula for ending the confrontation without bloodshed.

Antony acknowledges the debt: 'I have heard it, Pompey, / And am well studied for a liberal thanks / Which I do owe you.'

Sextus received her kindly and used the favor as a diplomatic card. This backstory explains why Pompey opens with a claim to Antony's gratitude before agreeing to peace.

anchor_text: The beds i' the East are soft
summary: Antony wryly acknowledges that he was comfortable in Egypt with Cleopatra — 'the beds i' the East are soft' is an understated admission of his luxurious life there — but thanks Pompey for forcing him home sooner than he planned, because the crisis here has given him gain (specifically, the marriage alliance with Octavia). The line is the play's first oblique hint that Antony has not given up his Egyptian life.
detail: The East, meaning Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean, was coded in Roman thought as the realm of luxury, softness, and self-indulgence — the antithesis of Roman martial austerity. When Antony says the beds there are soft, Roman ears would hear an implicit acknowledgment that he has been softened. The line also looks forward: Enobarbus will later predict with certainty that Antony will 'use his affection where it is' and return to Cleopatra.

anchor_text: what counts harsh fortune casts upon my face; / But in my bosom shall she never come / To make my heart her vassal
summary: Pompey uses the image of Fortune as a woman who keeps accounts ('counts') tallied in wrinkles on his face, but insists she will never reach his heart. Fortune was personified in classical and medieval tradition as a goddess who arbitrarily raised and cast down the great; here Pompey accepts her visible damage — the wear of years of war and hardship — but refuses to let her break his spirit. The image of Fortune as an inner conqueror rather than an outer one is a Stoic commonplace.
detail: Boethius (Consolatio Philosophiae II) and the whole de casibus tradition (Boccaccio, Lydgate, A Mirror for Magistrates) made Fortune's wheel the central image of the rise and fall of great men. Pompey deliberately personalizes it — Fortune marks his face but not his heart — as a piece of controlled self-presentation before the triumvirs.

anchor_text: your fine Egyptian cookery / Shall have the fame. I have heard that Julius Caesar / Grew fat with feasting there
summary: Pompey's compliment about 'fine Egyptian cookery' is a barbed one: it associates Antony with Egypt's legendary luxury and the softening of Roman men who spend time there. 'I have heard that Julius Caesar / Grew fat with feasting there' brings in Julius Caesar — not the present Octavius, but the dead Julius — to make the comparison pointed. This Julius Caesar was Cleopatra's earlier Roman lover, so Pompey implies Antony is following a well-worn path of Roman generals undone by Egyptian pleasures.

The line works on multiple levels: Pompey flatters Antony's hospitality, implies he will be providing the feast tonight, and subtly demotes Antony to a repetition of the greater Caesar. Antony's monosyllabic reply — 'You have heard much' — shows he takes the point.

anchor_text: Thy father, Pompey, would ne'er have made this treaty
summary: Once the leaders have gone, Pompey's pirate captain Menas says bluntly what many in the audience already sense: Pompey the Great — the dead father, one of Rome's greatest commanders — would never have settled for a peace when he had the power of the sea. Menas implies Sextus has traded real military advantage for the prestige of dining with the triumvirs. The aside is a direct judgment that Pompey is making a political mistake.
detail: Pompey the Great (Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, 106-48 BCE) was indeed famous for decisive, large-scale action; his son Sextus commands a powerful fleet and arguably could have pressed harder. Plutarch (Life of Antony, North 1579) suggests the triumvirs were under genuine pressure at Misenum, which makes Menas's regret historically defensible. The contrast between the dead father's greatness and the living son's calculation runs through the scene.

anchor_text: Pompey doth / this day laugh away his fortune
summary: Menas's phrase 'laugh away his fortune' is a tight oxymoron: laughter and festivity are the instruments of loss. By choosing a feast over pressing his military advantage, Pompey turns the gaiety of the occasion into the mechanism of his own ruin. Enobarbus caps it with equal compression: 'If he do, sure he cannot weep it back again.' The exchange is the play's sharpest commentary on the gap between pleasure and power.
detail: The exchange is an example of antithetical wit, the rhetorical figure of stichoymithia (rapid alternating lines) used for grim irony rather than argument. Enobarbus's reply — you cannot undo laughter with tears — draws on a commonplace about irreversible decisions: what is spent in merriment cannot be recovered by regret. The exchange is among the play's many small moments where the play's satirical intelligence resides in the secondary characters rather than the principals.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1257

Calling the two-line exchange 'stichomythia' is a misclassification — stichomythia is single-line alternating dialogue, and the exchange is not adversarial alternation; however the core reading ('laugh away his fortune' as ironic oxymoron) is sound, so the interpretation is not wrong, merely the rhetorical label is inaccurate.

anchor_text: If I were bound to divine of this unity, I would not prophesy so
summary: 'Divine' here means to foretell or prophesy, from the noun 'divination.' Enobarbus says that if he were asked to predict whether the marriage between Antony and Octavia would hold the triumvirs together, he would not predict it would. The sentence is understated: he is saying flatly that the marriage will fail as a political bond. 'Unity' means the alliance between Antony and Octavius Caesar sealed by the marriage.

anchor_text: the band that seems to tie / their friendship together will be the very strangler of their / amity
summary: Enobarbus predicts with geometric clarity that the very thing meant to bind Antony and Octavius — Octavia, Octavius's sister, now Antony's wife — will eventually destroy their alliance. When Antony abandons Octavia and returns to Cleopatra, her brother's wounded pride will turn the marriage bond into a strangling cord. The image of the bond as strangler is an oxymoron built around the double meaning of 'band' (tie / constraint).
detail: The prophecy is the scene's structural pivot and one of the play's central pieces of dramatic irony: the audience who knows the history (and anyone who has seen the earlier scene where Agrippa proposes the marriage) understands that Enobarbus is right. He follows it immediately with the devastating portrait: 'Octavia is of a holy, cold, and still conversation' — chaste, calm, and quiet, everything Cleopatra is not — and Antony is not such a man as can live on those terms. 'Conversation' here means 'way of living, conduct, manner of being,' not speech.

anchor_text: He will to / his Egyptian dish again
summary: Enobarbus calls Cleopatra Antony's 'Egyptian dish' — food he will always return to. The metaphor reduces Cleopatra to an appetite Antony cannot forgo, while also nodding to the scene's running theme of Egyptian feasting. 'He married but his occasion here' — meaning Antony married Octavia only because political necessity required it, not for love or lasting commitment.
detail: The phrase 'Egyptian dish' is deliberately coarse and reductive — the blunt soldier's way of stating what the more elevated political language of the scene disguises. It previews Antony's return to Cleopatra that will shatter the alliance, and it is paired with the prediction that Octavia's grief will 'blow the fire up in Caesar' — the domestic insult will become the fuel for the final war. Enobarbus's clarity here is exactly what makes his later desertion of Antony so painful: he always saw the outcome.

anchor_text: Some o' their plants are ill-rooted
summary: The First Servant is joking that the three rulers (Antony, Caesar, and Lepidus) are badly planted — that is, unstable on their feet from drink. 'Ill-rooted' carries the double sense of a plant that will blow over and a drunken man who cannot stand firm.
detail: The servant-commentary that opens the scene is a standard device of allowing plain-speaking commoners to voice what the great men cannot say openly. 'The least wind i' the world will blow them down' extends the plant metaphor and signals to the audience that the triumvirate itself is as shaky as the men who compose it. Lepidus, the weakest of the three, is singled out first.

anchor_text: made him drink alms-drink
summary: 'Alms-drink' means the leftover dregs of wine given to servants or the poor — charity wine of the lowest quality. The servant is saying that whenever Antony and Caesar fall into a quarrel ('pinch one another by the disposition') and Lepidus rushes in to make peace, they reward his trouble by making him drain the cup, as if he were a beggar accepting scraps.
detail: Lepidus's role in the play is to be the buffer and mediator that neither stronger triumvir values. Here his social function at the feast mirrors his political one: he absorbs the tension between the other two but is treated as a servant rather than an equal. The phrase captures the humiliation embedded in his position. Onions (Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'alms') notes 'alms-drink' as wine given in charity, confirming the sense of second-rate scraps.

anchor_text: called into a huge sphere, and not to be seen to move in't
summary: The First Servant uses the Ptolemaic model of the cosmos: each planet was believed to be set in a crystalline 'sphere' that rotated to carry it through the sky. A planet that occupied a sphere but did not visibly move in it would be like an eye-socket with no eye — the servant means Lepidus holds a huge title (one third of the world) but has no real power or visibility.
detail: The Ptolemaic-Aristotelian model, familiar to all Elizabethans, placed the planets in concentric crystalline spheres; a star or planet was supposed to be seen moving. 'The holes where eyes should be, which pitifully disaster the cheeks' is a grotesque image of a skull whose eye-sockets are empty — 'disaster' here means to disfigure (from 'dis-' + 'astro', a bad-star word). The speech precisely names Lepidus's dilemma: he is nominally one of three rulers of the world but exercises no real force, an object of pity rather than power.

anchor_text: they take the flow o' the Nile / By certain scales i' the pyramid
summary: Antony explains to Octavius Caesar how Egyptian farmers predict the harvest: they measure the annual Nile flood by graduated marks carved on the stone of a pyramid or nilometer pillar. The higher the flood, the richer the deposit of silt and the more abundant the following harvest ('foison'); a low flood meant famine ('dearth').
detail: The Nile's annual inundation — roughly June to September — deposited a layer of rich black silt that made Egypt the most productive grain-land in the ancient world. Measuring the flood was therefore a matter of life and death, and nilometers (graduated stone columns or wells) had existed since the Old Kingdom. Diodorus Siculus (Bibliotheca historica 1.36) and Pliny (Natural History 5.58) both describe the flood-measurement practice. Shakespeare gives Antony a moment of expertise about his adopted country that briefly casts him as a man who has, for better or worse, gone fully native in Egypt — knowledge that would be alien to the Roman Caesar.

The nilometer reading is correct and well-supported: the text says 'certain scales i' the pyramid' which is a clear reference to graduated flood-measurement marks, and Antony's role as Egypt expert contrasted with Caesar is a defensible interpretive point consistent with the scene's dynamics.

anchor_text: Your serpent of Egypt is bred now of your mud by the operation of your sun
summary: Lepidus, already drunk, repeats a popular ancient belief: that snakes and other creatures could be generated spontaneously from the Nile mud by the action of the sun's heat. This was called 'spontaneous generation' and was widely credited in antiquity, most famously for the story that Egypt's prodigious reptiles — crocodiles, asps, and other serpents — rose straight from the slime left after the flood receded.

anchor_text: I have heard the Ptolemies' pyramises are very goodly things
summary: Lepidus's slurring 'pyramises' instead of 'pyramids' shows how drunk he is — he cannot even pronounce the word correctly. The Ptolemies were the dynasty of Macedonian-Greek rulers of Egypt (of which Cleopatra was the last) who maintained and were associated with the great pyramids as symbols of royal power. That Lepidus has 'heard' they are 'goodly' reveals that he knows nothing about Egypt beyond hearsay.

anchor_text: It is shaped, sir, like itself; and it is as broad as it hath breadth
summary: Antony's answer to Lepidus's question 'What manner o' thing is your crocodile?' is an elaborate non-answer: the crocodile is shaped like itself, is as wide as it is wide, lives on what feeds it, and when it dies its soul 'transmigrates.' Every statement is a tautology — perfectly true and perfectly useless. Antony is openly mocking the helplessly drunk Lepidus by answering his solemn question with circular nonsense.
detail: The speech parodies the pedantic natural-history descriptions in Pliny and other ancient writers on Egypt's exotic fauna. 'The elements once out of it, it transmigrates' is a sly jab at the Pythagorean doctrine of the transmigration of souls — here applied to a crocodile. Octavius Caesar's dry aside 'Will this description satisfy him?' confirms that both sober Romans see through the joke, and Antony's reply ('With the health that Pompey gives him') suggests only more drink will satisfy Lepidus now.
