anchor_text: Thou art, if thou dar'st be, the earthly Jove: Whate'er the ocean pales or sky inclips / Is thine
summary: Menas tells Pompey that he could be 'the earthly Jove' — Jupiter, the supreme ruler of the gods — because he has all three rulers of the world on his ship. 'Whate'er the ocean pales or sky inclips' means everything fenced in by the sea and vaulted by the sky, that is, the entire world. If Menas cuts the cable and kills the three, the whole world becomes Pompey's.
detail: Jupiter (Jove) was the king of the gods and ruler of the universe in Roman religion; to be called his earthly counterpart was the highest claim to world-domination. The phrase 'ocean pales' means 'the ocean fences in' (from 'pale,' a fence or enclosure); 'sky inclips' means 'the sky embraces' (from 'clip,' to clasp or encircle). The flattery deliberately invokes the Ptolemaic image of a bounded cosmos — everything beneath the sky and above the sea — and it is exactly this picture of world-rule that the play's triumvirs have divided among themselves. Plutarch (Life of Antony, North's translation) supplies the scene's historical basis: the pirate Menas did indeed suggest murdering the leaders.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 32, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Menas proposes to Pompey that he cut the cable and kill the triumvirs.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1354

Calling Pompey the 'earthly Jove' as supreme ruler-claim is the obvious force of the speech; 'pale' (fence/enclosure) and 'inclip' (embrace/encircle) are standard glosses, and the Plutarch source for Menas's offer is well-established.

anchor_text: These three world-sharers, these competitors
summary: Menas names the three men at the feast — Antony, Octavius Caesar, and Lepidus — as the 'world-sharers,' the joint rulers of the Roman world after Julius Caesar's assassination. 'Competitors' here does not mean rivals fighting each other; it means partners, co-claimants sharing the same office. Together they formed the Second Triumvirate, an officially constituted three-man commission to govern the state.
detail: The Second Triumvirate (Antony, Octavius, and Lepidus) was formally established in 43 BCE by the Lex Titia, giving the three men sweeping powers to reorganize the state. 'World' here means the Roman world, and their division of it — Antony the East, Octavius the West, Lepidus Africa — is the 'three-nook'd world' referred to elsewhere in the play. The scene makes darkly visible what 'sharing the world' actually means: three drunken men on a pirate's galley, one being carried out insensible.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)

anchor_text: this thou shouldst have done, / And not have spoke on't! In me 'tis villainy: / In thee't had been good service
summary: Pompey (Sextus Pompeius) refuses to sanction Menas's plan to murder his guests — but he also admits he wishes it had been done without his knowledge. 'In me 'tis villainy: / In thee't had been good service' means: had Menas done it without telling him, Pompey could have kept clean hands and inherited the benefit; by asking, Menas has forced Pompey to either condemn the act or brand himself dishonoured. Pompey chooses honor over profit.
detail: The speech is one of Shakespeare's most concentrated explorations of the distinction between personal honor and political advantage. Pompey is not saying the murder would have been morally fine; he is saying that plausible deniability would have let him maintain his public reputation while reaping a private gain — a deeply cynical position, yet one the play presents with some sympathy, since Pompey is the only figure at the feast who upholds a code, even a compromised one. Plutarch (Life of Antony 32) preserves the same anecdote: Pompey said Menas ought to have done it without telling him.

Plutarch Life of Antony 32 (North 1579) is confirmed: Pompey rebukes Menas for telling him and says he ought to have done it unasked, matching the annotation's claim precisely.

Pompey's 'plausible deniability' reading is the standard interpretation of this speech and is strongly supported by the text — 'being done unknown, / I should have found it afterwards well done' makes the logic of deniability explicit, and Plutarch's parallel is exact.

anchor_text: 'A bears the third part of the world, man
summary: Enobarbus points to the servant carrying out the unconscious Lepidus and jokes that he is physically bearing 'the third part of the world' — meaning one of the three rulers of the Roman world. The joke works because Lepidus's portion of world-power has been reduced, in this scene, to a dead weight draped over a servant's shoulder.
detail: The Second Triumvirate divided the Roman world into three parts; Lepidus received Africa. Calling him 'the third part of the world' is both accurate (his formal title) and savagely comic (he is a limp body being carried off the ship). Menas's answering joke — 'The third part, then, is drunk; would it were all, / That it might go on wheels!' — extends it: if the whole world were as drunk as its 'third part,' the globe itself would roll uncontrollably. The scene is the play's clearest dramatization of the trimuivirate's instability.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 32, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the scene at Misenum; Lepidus carried drunk from the table.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1381

Plutarch Life of Antony 32 covers the Misenum feast generally, but the specific detail of Lepidus being carried drunk from the table is not confirmed in the Perseus text of that chapter; the citation may be accurate but could not be directly verified.

The joke on Lepidus as both a political 'third part of the world' and a literal dead weight being physically carried is well-grounded in the scene's staging direction and in Menas's follow-up joke about the globe going 'on wheels'; the triumvirate's instability reading is sound.

anchor_text: This is not yet an Alexandrian feast
summary: Pompey (Sextus Pompeius) tells Antony that the party on the galley is not yet as extravagant as the legendary feasts of Alexandria — Cleopatra's court was famous throughout the ancient world for banquets of extraordinary luxury and excess. Antony replies that it is 'ripening towards it,' confirming that his time in Egypt has made him a connoisseur of that world.
detail: Plutarch's Life of Antony describes Cleopatra's Alexandrian banquets in detail, including the famous story that she dissolved a pearl in vinegar and drank it to win a wager over who could give the most extravagant dinner. The 'Alexandrian feast' was a Roman topos for eastern excess and prodigal luxury, the opposite of Roman austerity. Antony's easy familiarity with the comparison — and his wish to 'ripen' the evening toward it — marks him as already more Egyptian than Roman in his appetites. Octavius Caesar's discomfort at this scene contrasts directly.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 28-29, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): descriptions of Cleopatra's extravagant banquets at Alexandria.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1386
Plutarch Life of Antony 28-29 (North 1579) is confirmed to describe the extravagant Alexandrian feasting of the 'Inimitable Livers' period, supporting the 'Alexandrian feast' gloss.

The Alexandrian feast as a Roman topos for eastern luxury is mainstream and well-sourced in Plutarch; Antony's easy familiarity with it as a marker of his 'going native' is a defensible interpretive point consistent with the play's broader characterization of him.

anchor_text: the Egyptian Bacchanals / And celebrate our drink
summary: Enobarbus calls for an 'Egyptian Bacchanal' — a wild, drunken celebration in the manner of the Egyptian worship of Bacchus, the god of wine. In the play Antony was associated with the god Bacchus (Dionysus) in Egypt, just as Cleopatra was with Isis. The Bacchanal was a ritual of ecstatic wine-worship, famously disorderly — here it merges the Egyptian feast tradition with Roman religious abandon.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 24 (North 1579): Antony welcomed in the East as the new Dionysus/Bacchus (his entry into Ephesus).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1397

Antony's identification with Bacchus/Dionysus in Egypt is well-attested in Plutarch and is a recurring motif of the play; calling the feast a 'Bacchanal' in that context is the expected allusion, and the staging detail of the song immediately following confirms the theatrical embodiment.

anchor_text: conquering wine hath steep'd our sense / In soft and delicate Lethe
summary: Antony calls the wine a 'soft and delicate Lethe' — naming it after Lethe, the river of forgetfulness in the classical underworld. Souls of the dead drank from Lethe to forget their earthly lives before rebirth. Here Antony means the wine will soak ('steep') their minds in a kind of pleasurable oblivion, washing away care and political tension for the night.
detail: Virgil (Aeneid 6.703-715) describes the souls of the dead drinking from Lethe to forget before they can be reborn; Ovid places Lethe by the cave of Sleep (Metamorphoses 11.602-604). The image of wine as a 'delicate Lethe' perfectly captures Antony's appeal to pleasure over duty: surrender reason and memory temporarily to the pleasure of the feast. The irony is that Lethe, the river of forgetting, is exactly what Octavius Caesar refuses to enter — he wants to keep his brain clear, not 'fouled' by drink.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 6.703-715: the souls drink from Lethe, the river of forgetfulness, before rebirth in the underworld.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1401
Virgil Aeneid 6.703-715 is confirmed to include the Lethe-drinking passage (souls quaff 'care-quelling floods and long oblivion' at lines 709-711), directly supporting the annotation.

Wine as a 'delicate Lethe' invoking the river of forgetfulness is the obvious classical allusion and a mainstream gloss; the contrast with Caesar's refusal to let drink 'foul' his brain is textually supported and interpretively sound.

anchor_text: the wild disguise hath almost / Antick'd us all
summary: Octavius Caesar says the wild behavior of the feast — the drinking, dancing, and singing — has almost 'antiked' them all, meaning it has made them perform like theatrical clowns or grotesque jesters ('anticks'). An 'antick' was a grimacing clown or fool; the word gives us 'antics' in the modern sense. Caesar is embarrassed and wants to leave: the evening has reduced even him to undignified foolery.

sources.name: OED s.v. antick
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'antick' (also antic), n. and adj.: a grotesque buffoon; a clown or jester; hence, to cause to behave grotesquely. From Italian 'antico' applied to grotesque ancient Roman decorative figures.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1419
OED s.v. 'antick' (antic) is a real entry with the Italian 'antico' etymology for grotesque figures, accurately supporting the gloss.

'Anticked' meaning made to behave like grotesque clowns is the standard gloss; the Italian 'antico' derivation applied to grotesque figures is the accepted etymology, and Caesar's embarrassment at being reduced to foolery is fully supported by TLN 1414-1420.

anchor_text: You have my father's house
summary: As the feast ends, Pompey (Sextus Pompeius) lets slip a grievance to Antony: 'You have my father's house.' He is referring to Pompey the Great's mansion in Rome, which Antony had seized after the elder Pompey's death and the subsequent proscriptions following Julius Caesar's assassination. The line breaks through the feast's forced conviviality to reveal the real tension beneath the surface peace.
detail: After Pompey the Great was murdered in Egypt (48 BCE), his properties in Rome were confiscated. Antony acquired the elder Pompey's Roman house — the same house that figures in the historical record as one of Antony's more brazen acts of appropriation. The young Pompey (Sextus) knows it and resents it; his 'but, what? we are friends' is a deliberate suppression of the grievance, an attempt to swallow the insult in the spirit of the Misenum treaty. The unfinished sentence marks the price of political accommodation.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 21, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Antony's purchase and occupation of Pompey the Great's house in Rome after the latter's death.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1425
Plutarch Life of Antony 21 (North 1579) is confirmed: Antony acquired and occupied Pompey the Great's house in Rome, consistent with the annotation's historical claim.

Sextus Pompey's reference to Antony holding his father's Roman house is historically grounded in Plutarch and is the standard interpretation; the reading of the unfinished sentence as a suppressed grievance beneath forced conviviality is well-supported by the text's own 'but, what? we are friends.'

anchor_text: Let Neptune hear we bid a loud farewell / To these great fellows
summary: Menas invokes Neptune — the Roman god of the sea — to bear witness to the noisy farewell the galley gives the departing leaders. The call is fitting: the entire scene takes place on a warship in Pompey's naval domain, and Neptune was the presiding deity of the maritime power that made Pompey a threat to Rome.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses; Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Neptune (Greek Poseidon), god of the sea: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.283-300; Virgil, Aeneid 1.124-156 (Neptune calming the storm).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1431
Ovid Metamorphoses 1.283-300 and Virgil Aeneid 1.124-156 are real passages establishing Neptune/Poseidon as the sea deity; the sources adequately support the basic identification invoked.

Menas invoking Neptune to witness the farewell from a galley in Pompey's naval domain is a natural and defensible classical allusion; the connection between Neptune, sea-power, and Pompey's strength is appropriate to the scene's setting and Pompey's character.

anchor_text: Marcus Crassus' death
summary: Marcus Crassus was a Roman general who led an army into Parthia (modern Iran and Iraq) and was catastrophically defeated and killed at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE. The Parthians then captured and displayed the Roman legionary standards, a national humiliation. Ventidius has now killed Pacorus, the Parthian king Orodes's son, as payback for Carrhae. Shakespeare here links Ventidius's victory to a Roman grievance more than two decades old.
detail: At Carrhae, Crassus lost roughly 20,000 Romans dead and 10,000 captured, and the Parthians paraded his severed head at their court. The lost standards were not recovered until Octavius Augustus negotiated their return diplomatically in 20 BCE. Plutarch's Life of Crassus narrates the disaster in detail; Plutarch's Life of Antony (the play's principal source, in North's 1579 translation) provides both this scene and the context of Ventidius's campaign. By killing Pacorus, son of the Parthian king Orodes who ordered Crassus's defeat, Ventidius closes the circle of vengeance that Rome had waited a generation to complete.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 33-34, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579); cf. Plutarch, Life of Crassus 17-31 (Carrhae, 53 BCE, and the death of Crassus).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1436

Plutarch Life of Antony 33-34 and Life of Crassus are real and supportive; the chapter range 'Crassus 17-31' is slightly short (the narrative runs through ch. 33), but the core claims about casualties (20,000 dead, 10,000 captured), Pacorus's death, and the Augustus standards-recovery in 20 BCE are all accurate and well-sourced.

The historical link between Ventidius's revenge killing of Pacorus and the Carrhae humiliation (53 BCE) is directly cued by the text ('Pays this for Marcus Crassus') and is mainstream Plutarchan scholarship with no overreach.

anchor_text: a lower place, note well, / May make too great an act
summary: Ventidius explains that a subordinate officer who wins too much glory in the absence of his commander risks losing favor rather than gaining it. 'A lower place' means a lower rank; 'make too great an act' means perform a deed too brilliant for someone of that rank. Roman military careers ran on a patron's credit: if an officer's success eclipsed the general's reputation, the general resented it and the officer's career stalled.
detail: Plutarch records this calculation explicitly in the Life of Antony: Ventidius, one of the shrewdest men in Antony's service, chose not to press deeper into Parthia precisely because a further triumph would overshadow Antony himself. Shakespeare makes the passage into a general maxim about power. The logic anticipates Iago's 'I am not what I am' and the whole problem of service under great lords in the play: Enobarbus, who serves Antony too honestly, is also undone by the logic of how much truth a patron can hear. 'His offence' (TLN 1462) means Antony's displeasure — the offense taken, not given.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 34, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Ventidius's deliberate restraint after the Parthian victory.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1448

Plutarch Life of Antony 34 explicitly states Ventidius chose not to pursue the Parthians further because he feared Antony's jealousy, and Antony later intervened to claim credit — the source is real and directly supports the summary.

The core reading of the patron-credit dynamic is sound and Plutarch-grounded, but the detail note's comparison to Iago's self-concealment and the claim that Enobarbus is 'undone by the logic of how much truth a patron can hear' are thematic over-readings that go well beyond what this short scene supports.

anchor_text: Sossius, / One of my place in Syria
summary: Sossius was a historical Roman officer who served as Antony's governor of Syria and lost Antony's favor by winning too much success too quickly. Ventidius names him as a cautionary example to explain his own decision to stop the Parthian campaign before it goes far enough to threaten Antony's prestige.
detail: Gaius Sosius (Sossius) was Antony's governor of Syria and legate in Judaea c. 38-37 BCE; he won Antony genuine victories but was later suspect in the factional politics around Antony and Octavius. Plutarch does not tell this precise anecdote in the same form as Shakespeare uses it, but North's Life of Antony 34 supplies the general context of Ventidius's restraint. The point Ventidius draws is systemic, not personal: 'quick accumulation of renown' (acquiring fame too fast) is the officer's career trap under a Roman warlord. The verb 'achiev'd by the minute' means 'won in rapid, minute-by-minute succession,' not that the renown was minor.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 34, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579); cf. Josephus, Jewish War 1.17.2 on Sossius's campaigns in Judaea.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1453

Plutarch Antony 34 mentions Sossius effecting much in Syria but does not present him as a cautionary example of punishment for outshining Antony; the Josephus citation 'Jewish War 1.17.2' is imprecise — section 2 of BJ 1.17 concerns Herod's campaign against Antigonus, not Sosius specifically, whose main narrative appears in BJ 1.18; the annotation itself concedes Plutarch does not tell this anecdote in Shakespeare's form, reducing confidence.

The identification of Sossius as a cautionary example of an officer who accumulated fame too fast and lost Antony's favour is consistent with the text and with the Plutarchan context, and the annotation honestly flags that Plutarch does not supply this anecdote in precisely Shakespeare's form.

anchor_text: ne'er-yet-beaten horse of Parthia / We have jaded out o' the field
summary: 'Horse' here means cavalry, not a single animal — the Parthian cavalry arm was famous across the ancient world for its mounted archers, who won at Carrhae by riding and shooting. 'Jaded out' means driven off exhausted, worn down, used up — a 'jade' was a broken-down, worthless horse. Ventidius is saying that Rome has now run the fabled unbeaten Parthian cavalry off the field until it was spent.
detail: Parthian cavalry tactics — feigned retreats followed by the 'Parthian shot' loosed backward over the saddle — were legendary in the ancient world and had destroyed Crassus at Carrhae. 'Jaded' (OED s.v. 'jade', v.) carries the double sense of 'driven like a jade' and 'worn out'; the compound image is of the proud, never-defeated horses finally run to exhaustion. The phrase 'ne'er-yet-beaten' points back to Carrhae and the decades of Roman humiliation the scene opens by invoking. Onions's Shakespeare Glossary notes 'jade' as a common Shakespearean term of contempt for an inferior or worn-out horse.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. R. D. Eagleson (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1986), s.v. 'jade,' 'horse.'

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Crassus
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Crassus 18-25 (Parthian cavalry tactics at Carrhae, 53 BCE).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1470

The Onions Shakespeare Glossary entry for 'jade' (noun) confirming the contemptuous horse meaning is genuine and available on Perseus; the 1986 Eagleson-revised Oxford edition exists; the Plutarch Crassus 18-25 citation for Parthian cavalry tactics is reasonable, with the cavalry archery engagement appearing in chapters 23-25; the verbal sense 'jaded out' is well-attested in Shakespearean usage even though Onions's entry is nominal only.

The gloss of 'horse' as cavalry arm and 'jaded out' as driven off exhausted is accurate Elizabethan usage, the OED double sense of 'jade' is standard, and the tie to Carrhae and the Parthian shot is properly contextualised.

anchor_text: Lepidus, / Since Pompey's feast, as Menas says, is troubled / With the green sickness
summary: The 'green sickness' was an Elizabethan medical term for chlorosis, a form of anemia thought to afflict pale, listless young women. Enobarbus applies it mockingly to Lepidus: since the drunken feast on Pompey's galley (2.7), the weakest triumvir has been sick with worry and excess, as wan and feeble as a lovesick girl.
detail: Chlorosis (the 'green sickness' or 'greensickness') was understood as a wasting condition marked by a pale or greenish complexion, thought to result from too much sitting still and from unfulfilled desire, and diagnosed almost exclusively in young women. Applying the term to Lepidus — a Roman general and triumvir — is a deliberate insult to his virility and strength of nerve. Enobarbus and Agrippa use it as shorthand for political and physical feebleness. Lepidus will later be deposed and imprisoned by Octavius (3.5), so the diagnosis of debility proves accurate.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'green-sickness' (also 'greensickness'): 'A form of anaemia causing a pale or greenish complexion, affecting esp. young women; chlorosis.' First cited usage 1582.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1479

OED 'green-sickness' and Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon are real reference works whose entries support the claim about chlorosis as a pallid wasting condition diagnosed in young women, applied satirically to Lepidus.

The application of 'green sickness' (chlorosis, an illness coded as feminine) as a deliberate insult to Lepidus's virility is standard Elizabethan usage and defensibly mocking in context; the gloss is accurate and mainstream.

anchor_text: Caesar? Why he's the Jupiter of men
summary: Enobarbus and Agrippa are mocking Lepidus's fawning praise of both Octavius Caesar and Antony, exaggerating it until it collapses into absurdity. When Enobarbus calls Caesar 'the Jupiter of men' — king of the gods — and Agrippa one-ups him by calling Antony 'the god of Jupiter' (i.e., greater than the greatest god), the competition of compliments becomes self-defeating nonsense. The joke is on Lepidus, who really does flatter both men this extravagantly.
detail: Jupiter (Greek Zeus) was the supreme Roman deity, king of heaven and ruler of the other gods. To call a man 'the Jupiter of men' is already superlative; Agrippa's parody answer — 'the god of Jupiter' — reaches beyond the summit by positing a god above the top god. The rhetorical device here is a mock-competition in hyperbole (incrementum or auxesis taken to self-parody), ending in Enobarbus's 'Kneel down, kneel down, and wonder' (TLN 1495). The comedy cuts at Lepidus as an empty sycophant, but it also quietly establishes that no mortal praise can settle who is the greater of the two triumvirs — a rivalry that will end the play in civil war.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'Jupiter': the supreme Roman deity, king of the gods; in Shakespeare invoked as the highest standard of divine power and authority.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the Life records the competitive honours and tensions between Antony and Octavius in the years before their final rupture.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1485

Onions on Jupiter as supreme Roman deity is sound, and Plutarch Life of Antony (North 1579) does record the competitive tensions between Antony and Octavius; both citations adequately support the annotation's claims.
The escalating mock-hyperbole (Jupiter → god of Jupiter) is correctly identified as a parody of Lepidus's sycophancy; the reading is supported by the text and is standard editorial consensus.

anchor_text: thou Arabian bird
summary: The 'Arabian bird' is the phoenix, a mythical creature said to live for five hundred years in the deserts of Arabia, then burn itself on a spice-scented pyre and rise reborn from its own ashes. It was unique — there was only one at a time in the world. Agrippa calls Antony 'the Arabian bird' to match Enobarbus's absurd comparison of Caesar to Jupiter: Antony is as one-of-a-kind as the phoenix itself.

anchor_text: hearts, tongues, figures, scribes, bards, poets, cannot / Think, speak, cast, write, sing, number
summary: Enobarbus uses a formal rhetorical device called 'asyndeton' (a rapid list with commas but no conjunctions) to enumerate every human faculty and medium of expression — then declares all of them insufficient to express Lepidus's love for Antony. The six faculties (hearts, tongues, figures/arithmeticians, scribes, bards, poets) are exactly matched to six verbs (think, speak, cast, write, sing, number), a figure called 'parison' (matched parallel members). The mid-list exclamation 'Hoo!' bursts the formal structure open, performing the very inadequacy of language that Enobarbus is describing.
detail: The passage is a virtuoso parody of the classical 'inexpressibility topos' (occupatio or adynaton: the claim that words cannot express something). Each noun pairs with its corresponding verb in strict sequence — heart:think, tongue:speak, figures:cast (i.e., calculate), scribes:write, bards:sing, poets:number (i.e., versify). The doubled 'Hoo!' — once at the start and once mid-line — is a performance of mock-ecstasy or theatrical exasperation, a clown's interjection breaking the rhetorical elaboration. The joke is that all this apparatus of eloquence is devoted to describing a sycophant's empty flattery. Shakespeare uses similar enumerations seriously at moments of genuine overload (Antony's grief for Caesar, Lear's accumulating losses), making this comic deployment especially noticeable.

sources.name: Peacham, Garden of Eloquence
sources.citation: Henry Peacham, The Garden of Eloquence (1577, rev. 1593), on asyndeton and parison as rhetorical figures of amplification and parallel construction.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'cast': 'to reckon, calculate' (as an arithmetician does); s.v. 'number': 'to compose verse, to versify.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1492

Peacham's Garden of Eloquence (1577, rev. 1593) is a real Renaissance rhetoric handbook covering asyndeton and parison, and Schmidt's entries for 'cast' (to reckon) and 'number' (to versify) are genuine lexicographic citations.

The noun-verb pairing analysis (heart:think, tongue:speak, figures:cast, etc.) is plausible but the annotation overstates the structural tidiness: 'figures' more likely means 'figures of speech' or 'numerals' rather than 'arithmeticians', and treating 'Hoo!' as a deliberate formal interruption of asyndeton is interpretive speculation not established editorial consensus — the reading is defensible but not mainstream-certain.

anchor_text: They are his shards, and he their beetle
summary: A 'shard' is the hard wing-case (elytron) of a beetle; the beetle raises its shards to fly. Enobarbus means that Antony and Caesar are Lepidus's 'shards' — the strong pair on whom he relies to get anywhere — while Lepidus is the dung-beetle being carried between them. The image is contemptuous: Lepidus is an insect that cannot fly without his betters.
detail: In Elizabethan English 'shard' or 'sherd' could mean a fragment of pottery, but in the context of beetles it meant specifically the hard outer wing-covers (later called elytra). The dung-beetle (Geotrupes or similar) was a familiar English insect, associated with dung and low material. Shakespeare uses 'shardborne beetle' similarly in Macbeth (3.2), where it means the beetle borne on its shards as it flies. The joke here applies to Lepidus's political situation: he is the weakest triumvir, dependent on the other two for any forward motion, a passenger rather than a power. His subsequent fate — drunk at the feast, then deposed — fulfils the image.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'shard' (also 'sherd'), sense 4: 'The wing-case or elytron of a beetle.' Cf. Shakespeare, Macbeth 3.2.42, 'the shard-borne beetle.'

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'shard': the wing-case of a beetle; thus 'shard-borne' = carried on its wing-cases.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1497
OED s.v. 'shard' sense 4 (wing-case of a beetle) and the Macbeth 3.2 cross-reference are accurate, and Onions is a real reference that supports the gloss.

The beetle/shard reading (shards = wing-cases, Lepidus as a dung-beetle carried by his betters) is confirmed by OED and the Macbeth parallel, and fits the contemptuous tone of Enobarbus's remark perfectly.

anchor_text: piece of virtue which is set / Betwixt us as the cement of our love
summary: Octavius Caesar addresses Antony: Octavia is the 'piece of virtue' — a measure of good faith — placed between the two men as the cement of their alliance. But the metaphor then turns dangerous: Caesar warns that the same woman who holds the building together could become the battering-ram that knocks it down if either man fails to cherish her. The extended building metaphor (cement / fortress / ram to batter) makes Octavia the structural guarantee of an alliance both men know is fragile.
detail: 'Cement' here is used in its Latin sense (caementum: binding mortar between stones). The image of a political marriage as the mortar in a joint structure was a common Elizabethan analogy for diplomatic alliance. Caesar's warning is pointed: the metaphor converts from building imagery to siege warfare — 'the ram to batter / The fortress of it' — turning Octavia from a bond into a weapon. Dramatically, the speech is ironic: the audience knows (from the Soothsayer's warning in 2.3 and Enobarbus's certainty throughout) that Antony will abandon Octavia for Cleopatra, and Caesar's warning about the woman becoming a battering-ram foreshadows exactly the war that Octavia's abandonment will trigger.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the marriage of Antony to Octavia as the political bond between the triumvirs; its dissolution triggers the final war.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cement' (noun): 'A bonding substance; the mortar used to bind stones in building'; also figuratively 'that which binds together.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1506

Plutarch Life of Antony (North 1579) does record Antony's marriage to Octavia as the political bond between the triumvirs, and OED s.v. 'cement' supports the bonding-mortar sense used in the annotation.

The building-metaphor reading (cement → ram to batter the fortress) is directly in the text and the gloss accurately tracks the shift from constructive to destructive imagery; the Plutarchan backstory of Octavia as political bond is correct.

anchor_text: the swan's down feather, / That stands upon the swell at the full of tide, / And neither way inclines
summary: Antony describes Octavia's internal conflict — torn between her brother and her new husband — by comparing her to a swan's-down feather floating on the surface of the tide at its absolute full, perfectly balanced, not moving toward the shore nor out to sea. It is one of the play's finest similes: complete stillness at the point of maximum pressure, neither side winning.
detail: The image is precise and visual. At the 'full of tide' — high water — the tide is neither coming in nor going out; there is a brief moment of stasis. A feather (the lightest possible object) resting on that still swell is in perfect, motionless suspension. Antony's simile translates an emotional state — Octavia cannot speak her mind to Caesar nor stop trying to — into a natural phenomenon of balance. The simile also carries a quiet threat: tides turn, and the feather will eventually be swept one way. Dramatically, the speech comes as Antony watches his own wife in distress, and his calm, observational tone raises the question of how much he cares about which way she falls.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the pathos of Octavia's position between the two rivals is recorded in Plutarch, though the swan's-down image is Shakespeare's own invention.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'swell': the undulation of a body of water, especially at high tide.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1531

The annotation honestly acknowledges the swan's-down image is Shakespeare's own invention while citing Plutarch only for Octavia's difficult position between the rivals; Schmidt on 'swell' is a real entry — the sources do not overclaim.

The simile of the swan's-down feather at the exact turning of the tide is precise natural observation rendered as emotional stasis; the reading is textually grounded, not over-interpreted, and the gloss accurately captures Octavia's irresolution between brother and husband.

anchor_text: When Antony found Julius Caesar dead, / He cried almost to roaring; and he wept / When at Philippi he found Brutus slain
summary: Agrippa recalls two episodes from Antony's earlier career: his grief at finding the assassinated Julius Caesar's body in 44 BCE, and his weeping over the dead Brutus after the Battle of Philippi in 42 BCE. Julius Caesar here is the dead dictator — not Octavius — and Brutus is the chief conspirator who killed him. Both incidents establish that Antony is capable of deep, demonstrative feeling; Enobarbus then cynically dismisses the weeping as mere 'rheum' (a cold).

sources.name: Plutarch, Lives (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 14 (North 1579): Antony at Julius Caesar's body and the funeral oration; Life of Brutus 53: Antony's honouring of the dead Brutus after Philippi. (The 'weeping' is Shakespeare's dramatic amplification of these episodes.)

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'rheum': 'a watery secretion from the mucous membranes; a cold in the head; any morbid flux of humours.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1539

Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Kept the correct event-loci (Life of Antony 14; Life of Brutus 53) but noted explicitly that the literal weeping/roaring is Shakespeare's amplification, not stated by Plutarch; kept OED for 'rheum'.

Both historical events (Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE, Battle of Philippi in 42 BCE) and the Plutarchan sourcing are accurate; the 'rheum' deflation is correctly glossed and Enobarbus's dismissal of Antony's tears as a cold is the standard reading.

anchor_text: Herod of Jewry dare not look upon you
summary: Herod of Jewry is Herod the Great (reigned 37-4 BCE), the Roman-backed king of Judaea notorious in Shakespeare's England as a byword for terrifying, explosive rage — derived from his portrayal in the medieval mystery plays, where he ranted and fumed to the point of absurdity. Alexas flatters Cleopatra by claiming even this fearsome king would not dare meet her gaze when she is displeased.
detail: The phrase 'Herod of Jewry' carries two layers. Historically Herod was a real, powerful client-king of Rome who rebuilt the Jerusalem Temple and massacred potential rivals, including members of his own family (Josephus, Antiquities 15-17). On the English popular stage, however, he was the raving tyrant of the mystery cycles, a byword for theatrical extravagance; Hamlet derides bad acting as 'out-heroding Herod' (Hamlet 3.2). Both senses reinforce the flattery: even the stage's greatest fury would be cowed by Cleopatra's anger. Cleopatra's next lines reveal the flattery is not quite enough to calm her: she imagines having Herod executed, but only through Antony's power — immediately establishing the anxiety driving the whole scene.

sources.name: Josephus, Antiquities
sources.citation: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 15-17 (Herod the Great's reign, 37-4 BCE).

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'Herod' — the stage tyrant of the mystery plays; compare Hamlet 3.2.14, 'it out-herods Herod.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1563

Josephus Antiquities 15-17 genuinely covers Herod the Great's reign, building projects, and family massacres; Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real source for Herod as the ranting stage tyrant, and the Hamlet 3.2.14 parallel ('it out-Herods Herod') is accurately cited.

Both layers of the gloss — the historical client-king and the raving mystery-play tyrant — are well-attested and the Hamlet parallel is explicit; the reading that Alexas flatters Cleopatra by claiming even this figure would be cowed is squarely supported by the text ('dare not look upon you / But when you are well pleas'd').

anchor_text: That Herod's head / I'll have: but how?
summary: Cleopatra's wish to have 'Herod's head' glances at the beheading of John the Baptist, whose head was delivered to Salome on a platter at Herod Antipas's command in the Gospels. The allusion is sardonic: Cleopatra imagines herself as the one who commands such executions, but immediately undercuts the boast by acknowledging she can only act through Antony.
detail: The Baptist's beheading is in Matthew 14:1-11 and Mark 6:14-29 (Geneva 1599). The figure responsible in the biblical account is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great — Shakespeare and his audience elided the two Herods freely in this kind of allusive shorthand. The joke lands because Cleopatra claims the power to order the execution of even the most feared king in the biblical imagination, then confesses the punch-line: 'when Antony is gone, / Through whom I might command it.' Her political impotence without Antony is the anxiety the whole scene papers over with Octavia's unflattering portrait.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 14:3-11 (Geneva 1599): Herod Antipas has John the Baptist beheaded; the head brought to Salome on a platter.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1565

Matthew 14:3-11 in the Geneva Bible 1599 does describe Herod Antipas ordering John the Baptist beheaded and the head brought on a charger; the annotation's elision of Herod the Great and Herod Antipas is acknowledged and defensible as Elizabethan conflation.

The wish for 'Herod's head' most naturally continues the Herod-of-Jewry figure just introduced (Cleopatra would execute even this fearsome king), and need not invoke the Baptist's beheading at all; the biblical echo is possible but is a reach given no other signal in the text, and the elision of Herod the Great with Herod Antipas is a genuine complication the annotation acknowledges but does not fully resolve.

anchor_text: O Isis! 'tis impossible
summary: Charmian swears by Isis, the great Egyptian mother-goddess — wife of Osiris, giver of the Nile's life, and the divine form in which Cleopatra herself chose to be presented at public ceremonies. For an Egyptian attendant this is not mere exclamation but an invocation of the goddess whose earthly image stands before her; the oath intensifies the absurdity of comparing Octavia to Cleopatra.
detail: Plutarch records in the Life of Antony (54) that Cleopatra gave audience 'in the habiliments of the goddess Isis' — a deliberate claim to divine queenship. To swear by Isis in Cleopatra's palace, before the woman who embodied the goddess, is theatrically pointed: the attendants routinely invoke the deity who is, in a real ritual sense, their own mistress. Shakespeare returns to the identification explicitly at 3.6, where Octavius Caesar reports in disgust that Cleopatra sat 'in the habiliments of the goddess Isis' at the Donations of Alexandria. The oath here thus reinforces the Egypt-vs-Rome contrast running through the play.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 54, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Cleopatra presenting herself robed as the goddess Isis.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1580

Plutarch Life of Antony chapter 54 (confirmed via Perseus) states Cleopatra 'assumed a robe sacred to Isis and was addressed as the New Isis'; North's 1579 translation is the established Shakespearean source for the play.

Charmian's oath by Isis in the presence of Cleopatra, who publicly presented herself as the goddess's embodiment (attested in Plutarch Life of Antony 54 and dramatised explicitly at 3.6), is a well-supported and dramatically pointed reading with no overreach.

anchor_text: Her motion and her station are as one; She shows a body rather than a life, A statue than a breather
summary: 'Motion' here means movement while walking; 'station' means how a person holds themselves when standing still. The Messenger reports that Octavia moves so stiffly and slowly that there is no difference between walking and standing — she looks more like a statue than a living person. This is the opposite of the vitality the play consistently attributes to Cleopatra.
detail: The contrast with Cleopatra is pointed. Earlier in the play Enobarbus describes Cleopatra at the Cydnus: 'she did lie / In her pavilion, cloth-of-gold of tissue, / O'erpicturing that Venus where we see / The fancy outwork nature' (2.2) — all animated beauty, effortlessly surpassing art. Octavia is here reduced to what art without life produces: a statue. 'Station' in the sense of posture or standing deportment is glossed at Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'station'; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'station.' The image of a living woman compared unfavourably to her own statue anticipates, with bitter irony, the play's final scenes, when the living Cleopatra will refuse to grace Caesar's triumph by transforming herself — deliberately, sovereignly — into her own effigy.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'motion' (bodily movement), 'station' (manner of standing, posture).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1585

Onions Shakespeare Glossary s.v. 'station' is confirmed via Perseus Digital Library with the definition 'manner of standing,' explicitly citing Antony and Cleopatra 3.3.19; the gloss on 'motion' as bodily movement is standard Shakespearean lexicography consistent with Onions.

The gloss of 'motion' as walking-movement and 'station' as standing-posture is standard and supported by Onions; the statue-versus-breather contrast is directly in the text, and the thematic link to Cleopatra's final self-transformation is a legitimate interpretive observation that does not overstate its claim.

anchor_text: Round even to faultiness
summary: The Messenger judges Octavia's face 'round even to faultiness' — so round as to be a flaw. In Elizabethan physiognomy and beauty standards, a long oval face was the ideal for women; a notably round face was considered coarse or unremarkable. Cleopatra's response ('For the most part, too, they are foolish that are so') extends the insult into a judgment of character, as Elizabethan face-reading ('physiognomy') held that facial features revealed inner traits.

sources.name: Pseudo-Aristotle, Physiognomica
sources.citation: Pseudo-Aristotle, Physiognomica (the Greek face-reading tradition, widely known in Renaissance Europe), which associates a long, well-proportioned face with nobility and wit and reads character from facial form.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1602

Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Dropped the misattributed Elyot's Castel of Helth (a humoral/dietary handbook, not a physiognomy treatise); kept Pseudo-Aristotle's Physiognomica, the genuine source for character-reading from facial form.

The Elizabethan preference for a long oval face over a round one is well-documented in the physiognomical tradition, and Cleopatra's follow-on line ('they are foolish that are so') explicitly invokes character-reading from facial features, confirming the annotation's framing without overreach.

note_internal: Review-queue rescue 2026-06-02. Dropped the misattributed Elyot's Castel of Helth (a humoral/dietary handbook, not a physiognomy treatise); kept Pseudo-Aristotle's Physiognomica, the genuine source for character-reading from facial form. [orig: source=refuted, interp=verified]

anchor_text: her forehead / As low as she would wish it
summary: The Messenger damns Octavia with a last detail: her forehead is as low as a woman could want — meaning it is, in fact, low and unfashionable. In Elizabethan fashion, a high, broad forehead was prized as a sign of intelligence and aristocratic beauty; women sometimes plucked their hairline to raise it. A low forehead suggested coarseness. The Messenger's phrasing is double-edged politeness — 'as low as she would wish it' — that damns rather than praises.

sources.name: Tudor beauty convention (portraiture)
sources.citation: The Tudor fashion for a high, broad forehead as a mark of beauty and intelligence -- women plucked the hairline to raise it -- is well attested in Elizabethan portraiture (e.g. portraits of Elizabeth I and court ladies).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'forehead': the high forehead as an admired feature; cf. the period idiom contrasting a 'low' (unfashionable) with a 'high' brow.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1605

Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Replaced the unsupported Linthicum (costume only) and the non-existent Onions 'forehead' gloss with the well-attested portraiture evidence for the Tudor high-forehead ideal and OED for the word.

The Tudor fashion for a high forehead is well-attested in portraiture and contemporary record, and the Messenger's phrasing 'as low as she would wish it' transparently damns by faint praise in exactly the way the annotation describes; the reading is restrained and text-grounded.

anchor_text: I harried him
summary: 'Harried' means harassed, tormented, or roughly used — from Old English 'hergian,' to ravage or plunder. Cleopatra regrets that she physically and verbally abused the Messenger when he first brought the news of Antony's marriage to Octavia (in Act 2, she struck him). Now that the same man has delivered the reassuring portrait of Octavia, she feels remorse for her earlier violence.
detail: The verb carries military weight — to harry an enemy is to raid and ravage them repeatedly — which gives Cleopatra's self-reproach a slight irony: she treated a mere messenger as if he were an enemy combatant. The earlier scene (2.5) where she threatened and struck the Messenger is a celebrated character moment: her rage at the news is ungovernable and she orders him whipped, then relents. Here the same word-choice reveals her self-awareness about her own violence, and the Messenger's professional pliability — telling the queen what she rewards him for saying — gets rewarded with gold.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'harry' v., sense 2: 'To disturb, trouble, harass, worry; to urge, press.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1614

The etymology of 'harry' from Old English 'hergian' (to ravage, plunder) is confirmed, and the weakened sense of 'harass, disturb' from c.1400 is well-documented; the OED does carry a sense for harry meaning to disturb/harass, though the exact sense-number wording quoted cannot be independently verified without OED subscription access.

The OED gloss and the back-reference to the Act 2 Scene 5 striking are both accurate and supported by the text; the observation that 'harry' carries a military weight that adds slight irony to Cleopatra's self-reproach is a modest, defensible interpretive note rather than an overreach.

anchor_text: Spoke scandy of me
summary: 'Scandy' is a contracted form of 'scantily' — meaning sparingly, grudgingly, or with deliberate meanness. Antony is saying Octavius Caesar spoke of him as little and as slightingly as possible, only when forced to, and even then in the coldest terms.
detail: The word belongs to a cluster of complaints in this speech about Caesar withholding due honour: he paid Antony only the barest minimum of praise ('cold and sickly'), gave him the narrowest possible recognition ('most narrow measure'), and even when praise was due, delivered it insincerely ('from his teeth'). 'Scandy' is not a standard dictionary entry; it appears to be a contracted adverbial form, effectively synonymous with 'scantly' or 'scarcely.' Onions's Shakespeare Glossary notes 'scant' as meaning 'sparingly, barely' across several plays.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Robert D. Eagleson (Oxford UP, 1986), s.v. 'scant,' 'scantly.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1629

Onions does carry 'scantly' (glossed 'grudgingly', citing A&C III.iv.6 — the exact passage) and 'scant' as an adjective meaning 'chary/restrained'; both entries are real and support the annotation's summary of 'sparingly, grudgingly.'

Glossing 'scandy' as a contracted adverbial form of 'scantly/scantily' meaning sparingly or grudgingly is linguistically defensible and fits the speech's sustained catalogue of Caesar withholding due honour.

anchor_text: did it from his teeth
summary: To do or say something 'from the teeth' (or 'from his teeth') means to say it insincerely — through clenched teeth, as a bare lip-service with no genuine feeling behind it. When Antony's praise was finally given, Caesar grudged it even then.
detail: The idiom appears elsewhere in Shakespeare for hollow or coerced speech: compare 'I will speak daggers to her, but use none' in Hamlet, and more directly 'praise from the teeth outward' in Othello (2.1). The teeth are the barrier that barely let the words out — the image catches an expression forced through reluctance rather than freely given. Antony is building a catalogue of slights: Caesar praised him only when 'perforce he could not' do otherwise, and even then the tribute was half-withheld. Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon records 'from the teeth' as a fixed phrase for insincere utterance.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, 3rd ed. (Berlin: Georg Reimer, 1902), s.v. 'tooth, teeth' (collocations for insincere speech).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1633

Schmidt's Lexicon s.v. 'Tooth' explicitly includes 'did it from his teeth' glossed as 'not from his heart, only for form's sake and with reluctance', citing Antony and Cleopatra III.4.10 — the precise passage annotated.

The idiom 'from the teeth' for insincere or coerced utterance is well-attested; the Othello parallel ('praise from the teeth outward') is apt, and the core gloss is mainstream, even if the Hamlet comparison is imprecise.

anchor_text: Stomach not all
summary: Here 'stomach' is a verb meaning to resent, take offense at, or digest with anger. Octavia is telling Antony: even if you must believe the worst of your rival, do not let all of it poison you with rage — do not take every grievance to heart.
detail: In Elizabethan usage the stomach was thought of as the seat of anger and pride as well as digestion — to 'stomach' something was to swallow it bitterly, to bridle with resentment. Shakespeare uses the verb elsewhere in this sense: 'He cannot but with measure fit the honours / Which we devise him' (Coriolanus 2.2) — and 'stomach' as noun = resentful pride appears throughout the plays (e.g. Henry VIII 1.1). Octavia's counsel is one of tactical emotional restraint: accept the fact of Caesar's provocations but do not let them inflame Antony into immediate war. Onions glosses 'stomach' as vb. = 'to resent, take offence at.'

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Robert D. Eagleson (Oxford UP, 1986), s.v. 'stomach' vb.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1636
Onions s.v. 'stomach' vb. (stomach2) is confirmed as a real entry glossed 'to resent', with citations from Antony and Cleopatra, directly supporting the annotation's claim.

Using 'stomach' as a verb meaning to resent or take offense at is standard Elizabethan usage and correctly glossed; the Coriolanus example cited does not actually illustrate the verb but does not undermine the sound core interpretation.

anchor_text: yours so branchless
summary: Antony calls himself 'branchless' — stripped of his branches like a tree that has been severely lopped. He means stripped of honour and reputation: a man without dignity or public standing, as bare and useless as a trunk with no growth on it.
detail: The tree/branch metaphor for honour and family lineage runs throughout Shakespeare; to be 'branchless' is to be dishonoured, disinherited of reputation, cut off from any claim to greatness. The word occurs nowhere else in the canon and may be a Shakespearean coinage. Antony's point is: it would be better for Octavia to be without him altogether than to be married to a man publicly dishonoured and degraded. The rhetorical structure — 'better I were not yours / Than yours so branchless' — makes 'branchless' the climactic insult, the nadir of what Caesar's conduct has threatened to reduce him to. The OED records 'branchless' in exactly this figurative sense, citing this passage.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED Online, s.v. 'branchless' adj., sense 2 (figurative: deprived of dignity or honour); citing Antony and Cleopatra 3.4.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1649

The OED does have a 'branchless' entry and the word is first-recorded in this A&C passage, but the annotation specifies 'sense 2 (figurative: deprived of dignity or honour)' with that exact sub-gloss text — the OED is paywalled and the precise sense-numbering and gloss wording cannot be verified, making the citation specificity unconfirmable.

Reading 'branchless' as stripped of honour and public standing is strongly supported by the surrounding lines about losing honour and losing oneself; the tree-as-reputation metaphor is standard Shakespearean usage.

anchor_text: The Jove of power make me, most weak, most weak
summary: Octavia prays to Jove — Jupiter, the supreme Roman god of sky, thunder, and sovereign power — to make her effective as a peacemaker despite her own weakness. The phrase 'Jove of power' singles out Jupiter's aspect as ruler and enforcer, the only force capable of reconciling two men who are tearing the world apart.
detail: Jove (Latin Jupiter) was the king of the Olympian gods, whose thunderbolt enforced divine authority over gods and mortals alike. Invoking him as 'the Jove of power' — Jupiter in his capacity as sovereign — is precise: Octavia is not asking for a domestic favour but for an almost impossible act of political and cosmic mediation. Her following image, that war between Antony and Octavius Caesar would be like the world itself cleaving in two and needing the bodies of slain men to solder up the crack, gives the invocation its full weight: she is praying for a miracle from the only deity whose writ runs at that cosmic scale. The Roman framing (Jove rather than 'God') is consistent with the play's self-conscious Roman world; Shakespeare invokes Jupiter by name throughout the Roman plays to signal divine authority.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 1.254-296 (Jupiter as supreme arbiter of fate, speaking Rome's destiny); the standard classical epitome of Jove as the 'power' that orders the universe.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the general context of Octavia's role as peacemaker between Antony and Octavius.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1655

Jupiter's prophecy to Venus is real (Aeneid 1.257-296; the cited range 254-296 is off by three lines at the start but not fabricated), and Plutarch's Life of Antony in North's 1579 translation genuinely depicts Octavia as peacemaker between Antony and Octavian — both sources are real and directionally support the claims.

Invoking Jove specifically in his sovereign/power aspect as the only force capable of reconciling two men tearing the world apart is defensible and well-supported by the world-cleaving image that immediately follows (TLN 1657-1658).

anchor_text: what is the success
summary: 'Success' here means outcome or result, not a favorable one — Enobarbus is asking what happened next, not whether anyone succeeded. The word kept this neutral sense ('the success of the venture') well into the eighteenth century.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'success,' sense 1a: 'The action or an act of succeeding or coming after; sequence, succession... Also: outcome, result, consequence' — the older, neutral sense current in Shakespeare's time.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1669
OED s.v. 'success' does record an early neutral sense ('outcome, result') as sense 1a, confirmed obsolete from the 18th century, accurately supporting the annotation's claim.

Enobarbus's line 'This is old: what is the success?' clearly uses 'success' as a neutral term for outcome — the 'this is old' framing shows he already knows the news and wants the result, confirming the archaic sense is correct.

anchor_text: denied him rivality; would not let him partake in the glory
summary: 'Rivality' means partnership or equal share — Octavius Caesar, having used Lepidus to fight Sextus Pompeius, then refused him any credit and arrested him on charges of treasonous letters to Pompey. 'The poor third is up' means imprisoned ('up' = locked up, confined). This is the historical end of the Second Triumvirate: with Lepidus deposed around 36 BCE, only Antony and Octavius remained to fight for sole mastery of Rome.
detail: Plutarch records that after the defeat of Sextus Pompey, Octavius stripped Lepidus of his armies and exiled him to Circei under guard — the 'up, till death enlarge his confine' of this scene. Lepidus lived out his days under house arrest, stripped of every office except the honorary priesthood of Pontifex Maximus, which Octavius coveted and took when Lepidus died in about 13 BCE. Shakespeare's 'seizes him: upon his own appeal' means Octavius used Lepidus's own submission (his appeal for mercy) as the legal pretext to arrest him. The triumvirate's card-the-second-triumvirate is the infrastructure for the whole play's three-way world, and this scene marks the moment it collapses to two.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 54-55, in Sir Thomas North's translation, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579): Octavius deposes Lepidus after the Sicilian war and takes his legions.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1671

Plutarch Life of Antony 55 (North 1579) genuinely records Octavius's deposition of Lepidus after the Sicilian war and his seizure of Lepidus's armies and territory; historical details about Circei house-arrest, retention of Pontifex Maximus, and death c. 13 BCE are all accurate — chapter 54 in the citation range covers different material but ch.55 squarely supports the core claim.

The gloss accurately tracks the scene's dialogue — 'denied him rivality,' 'would not let him partake in the glory,' 'seizes him,' and 'the poor third is up, till death enlarge his confine' are all directly on the page, and the interpretation of 'up' as imprisoned and 'his own appeal' as submission-turned-pretext is standard and defensible.

anchor_text: world, thou hast a pair of chaps, no more; And throw between them all the food thou hast, They'll grind the one the other
summary: 'Chaps' (also spelled 'chops') are jaws — specifically the jaw-bones of an animal. Enobarbus pictures the world as a mouth with only two jaws left, Antony and Octavius Caesar; whatever the world feeds them, those jaws will end by grinding each other to pieces. It is a metaphor for a zero-sum struggle in which the former triumvirate's collapse leaves only two rivals, and compromise is impossible.
detail: The image belongs to a cluster of feeding and devouring metaphors throughout the play — Antony's 'dotage' 'o'erflows the measure,' Cleopatra is 'a morsel for a monarch.' 'Chaps' appears again at 1 Henry IV 2.4 ('you fat-kidneyed rascal... you... chops') and throughout the corpus for animal jaw-power. Enobarbus's terse two-line prophecy here proves accurate: the scene is set shortly before Actium, after which there will indeed be only one jaw left.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'chaps': 'the jaws, the jaw-bones'; the spelling 'chaps' and 'chops' are interchangeable in the early texts.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1675

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'Chaps' defines the word as 'the jaws, the jaw-bones' and notes the interchangeability of 'chaps'/'chops' in the early texts, precisely matching the annotation's citation.

The 'pair of chaps / jaws' metaphor for Antony and Caesar grinding against each other is straightforward from the text and the gloss correctly identifies it as a zero-sum-rivalry image without over-reading; the supporting note on the play's devouring-metaphor cluster is accurate but appropriately qualified.

anchor_text: spurns The rush that lies before him
summary: 'Spurns' means kicks — Antony is furiously pacing the garden, kicking aside the rushes strewn on the path. Rushes (dried hollow grass stems) were routinely scattered on the floors of houses and garden paths in the period; they were cheap, easily swept out, and served as a soft, fragrant surface. Eros is painting a picture of Antony in barely-contained rage, kicking at something utterly beneath him.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'spurn': 'to kick, to strike with the foot'; and s.v. 'rush': 'the plant used for strewing on floors.'

Onions' Shakespeare Glossary is a real and standard reference; 'spurn' meaning 'to kick' and 'rush' as the plant used for strewing floors are both well-attested entries consistent with the glossary's scope and style.

The text reads 'spurns / The rush that lies before him' and the scene is set in 'the garden,' so 'spurns = kicks' and 'rush = strewn plant material' are both straightforwardly correct, and the claim that rushes were scattered on paths is historically sound rather than anachronistic.

anchor_text: More, Domitius
summary: Eros addresses Enobarbus by his Roman family name, Domitius — his full historical name was Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus ('Ahenobarbus' means 'bronze-beard'). The use of the personal name rather than the more familiar 'Enobarbus' signals the scene's urgency and the intimacy between these two men who serve Antony.
detail: Plutarch names him Domitius Ahenobarbus and records his defection to Octavius late in the play — the desertion that Antony responds to with unexpected generosity, sending Enobarbus's treasure after him, an act that breaks Enobarbus's heart and kills him. The cognomen 'Ahenobarbus' (Latin for 'bronze beard') was a hereditary mark of the family; Suetonius mentions the legend that explained the name. 'Enobarbus' is simply a Latinised Greek spelling of the same word. Shakespeare's choice to use 'Domitius' here is faithful to his Plutarchan source.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 63-64 (North 1579): Domitius Ahenobarbus deserts to Caesar; Antony sends his baggage and servants after him.

sources.name: Suetonius
sources.citation: Suetonius, Nero 1 (on the cognomen Ahenobarbus, 'bronze-beard,' and its origin in the family's legends).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1683

Plutarch Life of Antony 63 (North 1579) confirms Domitius Ahenobarbus's desertion and Antony's sending of his baggage after him; Suetonius Nero 1 confirms the Ahenobarbus cognomen and its legendary origin with the divine transformation of the beard.

The identification of Domitius as Enobarbus's family name and the Plutarchan source-fidelity claim are sound, but the annotation says Eros addresses Enobarbus to signal 'urgency and intimacy' — that interpretive claim is not clearly supported by the line, which is simply Eros urging him along ('More, Domitius; / My lord desires you presently'), so the functional reading is fine but the intimacy-signal gloss overreaches slightly.

anchor_text: Contemning Rome, he has done all this
summary: 'Contemning' means showing open contempt for or scorning. Octavius Caesar opens by declaring that Antony has publicly defied Rome's authority and expectations through his conduct in Alexandria.
detail: The word combines social and legal weight: to 'contemn' an institution or custom was not merely to disregard it but to show deliberate disrespect. Octavius is building a political case — Antony has not just drifted away from Rome, he has acted in open defiance of it.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1689

The gloss is accurate — 'contemning' as deliberate, open scorn is OED-supported and correctly captures Octavius's political framing of Antony's acts as wilful defiance rather than mere neglect.

anchor_text: I' the market-place, on a tribunal silver'd, / Cleopatra and himself in chairs of gold / Were publicly enthron'd
summary: Antony and Cleopatra staged a massive public ceremony in Alexandria in which they sat on golden thrones on a silver platform — the 'donations of Alexandria' — and publicly parcelled out the eastern Roman world to their children. Octavius recounts this as scandalous evidence of Antony's contempt for Roman governance: a Roman commander had no right to give away conquered territory without the Senate's consent.
detail: Plutarch reports the event in the Life of Antony (54): 'Antony...made Cleopatra sit beside him in great state, and Caesarion also, who was said to be the son of Julius Caesar. Then Antony himself sat aloft on a tribunal of silver.' The detail is followed closely here. In Roman custom a 'tribunal' was the raised platform from which a magistrate pronounced judgment; 'silvering' it was an act of kingly pomp wholly foreign to Republican norms. Shakespeare treats the scene as the piece of propaganda Octavius used to justify war: by staging himself as a divine king with his queen-goddess, Antony handed Rome a ready excuse.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 54, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the 'donations of Alexandria,' Antony and Cleopatra enthroned on silver and gold.

anchor_text: Caesarion, whom they call my father's son
summary: Caesarion ('little Caesar') was Cleopatra's son by Julius Caesar — making him, if the claim held, the blood heir of Julius Caesar and therefore a direct rival to Octavius, who was Caesar's adopted heir only. Octavius resented the claim bitterly: he based his entire power on being Caesar's heir, and a living biological son would undercut that.

anchor_text: His sons he there proclaim'd the kings of kings
summary: 'Kings of kings' was a Near-Eastern royal title — used by the Persian Great Kings and later by rulers of Parthia and Armenia — asserting supremacy over all other monarchs. By giving the title to his own sons and distributing Media, Parthia, Armenia, Syria, Cilicia, and Phoenicia among them, Antony was not just rewarding family but publicly reorganizing the Roman East as a client empire of his own, entirely outside Roman constitutional law.
detail: The title 'king of kings' (in Aramaic and Persian, 'shahanshah') was the official title of the Achaemenid Persian emperors and was adopted by the Parthian Arsacids, Rome's great eastern rivals. Applying it to his sons at a public ceremony declared Antony's eastern empire coequal with Parthia and superior to any Roman mandate. This was the propaganda gift Octavius needed: he could now portray Antony not as a rogue Roman general but as a foreign-style monarch setting himself above Rome itself. Plutarch records the same titles (Life of Antony 54) and notes that Octavius used the report to inflame opinion in Rome.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 54, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the titles and territorial grants at the donations of Alexandria.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1702
Plutarch, Life of Antony 54 explicitly uses the phrase 'Kings of Kings' for Antony's sons and lists the territorial grants, fully supporting the annotation.

The gloss correctly identifies 'kings of kings' as a Near-Eastern royal title (Achaemenid / Arsacid) and its propagandistic force in a Roman context; the Plutarch citation is precise and the political-propaganda reading is mainstream, not an overreach.

anchor_text: In the habiliments of the goddess Isis / That day appear'd
summary: 'Habiliments' means clothing, dress, or regalia. Cleopatra appeared at the ceremony robed as Isis, the great Egyptian mother-goddess — an act of political theatre claiming divine queenship. Plutarch records this explicitly: the Ptolemaic queens regularly identified themselves with Isis, and for Roman observers like Octavius it confirmed that Antony had surrendered to a foreign deity.
detail: Isis was the preeminent goddess of Egypt — wife of Osiris, mother of Horus, mistress of life and death, and the patron of the Nile's harvest. The Ptolemaic dynasty, Macedonian-Greek rulers who had governed Egypt since 305 BCE, adopted Egyptian divine kingship and presented their queens as the earthly Isis. Cleopatra VII intensified this: Plutarch notes (Life of Antony 54) that she gave audience in the 'habiliment and apparell of the goddess Isis' (North's phrasing), and that Antony was styled as Dionysus/Osiris, her divine consort. For Rome the image was deeply unsettling: Isis was a popular but periodically persecuted 'oriental' cult that the Senate repeatedly tried to suppress. Octavius's account here drips with the disgust of a Roman administrator for god-king theatrics he regards as non-Roman corruption.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 54, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Cleopatra appearing 'in the habit and fashion of the goddess Isis.'

sources.name: Plutarch, Moralia
sources.citation: Plutarch, Moralia, 'On Isis and Osiris' (De Iside et Osiride), trans. J. G. Griffiths (1970).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1706

Plutarch, Life of Antony 54.6 confirms Cleopatra wore robes sacred to Isis and was called 'New Isis'; the Griffiths 1970 edition of Plutarch's Moralia 'De Iside et Osiride' is a real and standard scholarly work that supports the Isis background.

All claims are defensible: 'habiliments' as dress/regalia is standard; the Isis identification draws directly from North's phrasing ('habit and fashion of the goddess Isis'); the Ptolemaic dynasty's Isis-identification and Rome's periodic suppression of the cult are uncontroversial historical context — nothing here overreaches.

anchor_text: having in Sicily / Sextus Pompeius spoil'd, we had not rated him / His part o' the isle
summary: This is Antony's accusation: after Octavius defeated Sextus Pompeius (the young Pompey, son of Pompey the Great) and took Sicily, he did not give Antony his agreed share of the island. Sextus Pompeius was not Pompey the Great — he was the young naval commander whose fleet had threatened Rome until Octavius's admiral Agrippa crushed him at Naulochus in 36 BCE.
detail: The name 'Sextus Pompeius' is the young Pompey's formal name: Sextus Julius Caesar Pompeius, son of Pompey the Great. He held Sicily and dominated the western Mediterranean with his fleet after his father's death, controlling Rome's grain supply and giving the triumvirs serious trouble until he was defeated at Naulochus (36 BCE). Octavius then removed Lepidus from the triumvirate at the same time. Antony's grievance — that Sicily was conquered in part thanks to his support (ships he lent) but the spoils were not shared — was a real political dispute Plutarch records (Life of Antony 54-55). When Octavius says Caesar 'did not rate him his part,' the word 'rate' means to allot or assess a fair portion, not to scold.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 54-55, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Antony's accusations against Octavius, including the Sicily share.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1716

Accurate on all points: Sextus Pompeius as Pompey the Great's son, the naval war ending at Naulochus (36 BCE), and 'rate' meaning to allot/assess rather than to scold are all correct; Antony's grievance over the Sicily share is attested in Plutarch.

anchor_text: Lepidus of the triumvirate / Should be depos'd; and, being, that we detain / All his revenue
summary: Antony's third accusation: that Octavius deposed Lepidus — the third member of the ruling triumvirate — and then kept all his estates and income rather than sharing them. Lepidus was the weakest of the three world-rulers; Octavius stripped him of his military command after the Sicily campaign (36 BCE), imprisoned him, and seized his wealth. Antony protests that Lepidus's deposition was illegal and that the revenue should have been divided.
detail: The deposition of Lepidus is a fait accompli reported earlier in the play (3.5) and confirmed here as one of Antony's formal accusations. Marcus Aemilius Lepidus had once been powerful enough to be the third equal in the triumvirate, but Octavius engineered his removal to consolidate his own position in the West before turning against Antony. The word 'detain' means wrongfully to hold back what should be paid — Antony is framing this as theft of a share that was his by treaty right. Plutarch (Life of Antony 55) records Antony raising exactly this complaint as a pretext for war, though both sides were by this stage maneuvering toward an inevitable final conflict.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 55, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Antony's grievances against Octavius, including the deposing of Lepidus.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1720
Plutarch, Life of Antony 55 explicitly records Antony's accusation that Octavius ejected Lepidus from office and kept his revenues, matching the annotation exactly.

The reading is accurate — 'detain' as wrongful withholding of due payment is the correct Elizabethan sense, and Antony's grievance over Lepidus's deposition and seized revenues is confirmed in Plutarch (Life of Antony 55) and by the play's own 3.5.

anchor_text: Hail, Caesar, and my lord! hail, most dear Caesar!
summary: Octavia's double greeting — saluting her brother Octavius Caesar both as 'Caesar' (his political title and name) and as 'my lord' (her family superior) — captures her impossible position: she is simultaneously Caesar's sister and Antony's wife, two loyalties that are now at war with each other. The formal 'Hail' echoes Roman salutation and immediately sets a public, ceremonious tone that contrasts sharply with her private grief.

The reading is sound — the doubled greeting does register Octavia's split allegiance, and the formal 'Hail' echoing Roman salutation contrasting with private distress is a defensible, text-grounded interpretation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: A market-maid to Rome; and have prevented / The ostentation of our love
summary: Octavius rebukes Octavia for arriving in Rome like a market-girl — quietly, privately, unannounced — instead of with the full military escort and public ceremony a triumvir's wife deserved. 'Prevented' means forestalled or anticipated, not blocked. 'Ostentation' is not boasting but the proper outward display of honour — the official show of welcome and love that Octavius wanted to stage but could not because Octavia gave no warning of her arrival.
