anchor_text: Cleopatra / Hath nodded him to her. He hath given his empire / Up to a whore
summary: 'Nodded him to her' means beckoned him with a nod — Cleopatra has merely gestured and Antony has abandoned Rome to follow. The image reduces the world's greatest general to a dog called by its owner with a nod of the head. Octavius immediately follows this with 'He hath given his empire / Up to a whore' — deliberately inflammatory language designed to provoke Octavia's sympathy and present the coming war as a personal injury to family honour.
detail: The verb 'nod' carries the force of effortless, contemptuous command — a nod costs nothing and compels completely. That a woman's nod can undo an empire is Octavius's point: Antony's capitulation was total and caused by something trivial. The word 'whore' (applying to Cleopatra) is Octavius's political language throughout the play; it frames the war as a morality campaign and projects Antony's choice as degradation rather than love or policy. The sequence of 'Hath nodded' followed immediately by 'He hath given his empire / Up to a whore; who now are levying / The kings o' the earth for war' maps the personal corruption onto its military consequence.

sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'nod,' v.: to beckon with a nod.

The reading of 'nodded him to her' as effortless, contemptuous beckoning is linguistically sound and the political framing of 'whore' as Octavius's calculated propaganda language (not a neutral descriptor) is a mainstream scholarly reading, well supported by Octavius's consistent rhetoric throughout the play.

anchor_text: Bocchus, the king of Libya; Archelaus / Of Cappadocia; Philadelphos, king / Of Paphlagonia; the Thracian king, Adallas
summary: Octavius lists the client kings from across the eastern Mediterranean whom Antony has assembled as his allies — Libya, Cappadocia, Paphlagonia, Thrace, Arabia, Pontus, Judaea (Herod of Jewry), Comagene, Media, and Lycaonia. The list demonstrates the enormous scale of the coalition Antony and Cleopatra have built, while also showing (from Octavius's perspective) that Antony has allied Rome's eastern dependencies with a foreign queen against Rome itself.
detail: Shakespeare takes this list almost verbatim from Plutarch (Life of Antony 61), who enumerates the kings on Antony's side at Actium. The identifiable figures include: Bocchus of Mauretania (loosely, Libya); Archelaus of Cappadocia (central Anatolia); Mithridates of Comagene (a small kingdom in present-day southern Turkey). 'Herod of Jewry' is Herod the Great, who was a client king under Roman protection — his presence on Antony's side explains why after Actium he quickly transferred allegiance to Octavius. These are not Antony's enemies but his client-kings and allies, and their number — 'More larger list of sceptres' — signals the eastern empire Antony has built and is about to stake at Actium.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 61, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the catalogue of kings on Antony's side before Actium.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1767

Plutarch, Life of Antony 61 (confirmed via Perseus) lists client kings including Bocchus of Libya/Mauretania, Archelaus of Cappadocia, Philadelphus of Paphlagonia, and a Thracian king (named Sadalas in the Greek text, rendered as Adallas in Shakespeare's text), supporting the annotation's claims about the Actium coalition.

The catalogue itself is handled correctly and the Plutarch source is apt, but the annotation misidentifies 'Bocchus' as king of Mauretania and then parenthetically equates Mauretania with 'Libya' — the play's text says 'Libya,' Plutarch has a different list, and the equation is imprecise enough to risk confusing students; the core point about the eastern coalition is sound, but the geographic identification should be marked uncertain pending closer source check.

anchor_text: let determin'd things to destiny / Hold unbewail'd their way
summary: 'Determined things' are events that have already been decided or set in motion — what destiny has fixed. 'Hold unbewail'd their way' means let them proceed without being mourned or lamented. Octavius is telling Octavia: do not grieve over what is already in motion, let fate run its course without weeping.
detail: The construction is compressed: 'let [those things that have been] determined [by fate/events] hold their way unbewailed' — that is, let destiny's already-fixed course go forward without grief. 'Determined' carries its Elizabethan sense of 'settled, resolved, fixed' (not merely decided by a person, but settled by fate or circumstance). The counsel is characteristic of Octavius: cold, forward-looking, and contemptuous of emotional display. He is essentially telling his sister to stop feeling and start enduring — which is what Caesar himself exemplifies throughout the play. The phrase has a Stoic cast: the wise person does not mourn the inevitable.

anchor_text: gives his potent regiment to a trull / That noises it against us
summary: 'Regiment' here means authority, rule, or power — not a military unit. Maecenas says Antony has handed his great power to a 'trull' (a prostitute or low woman), who is now using it to make war against Rome. The word 'noises' means to spread news loudly, to declare publicly.

anchor_text: from Tarentum and Brundusium / He could so quickly cut the Ionian sea
summary: Antony is astonished that Octavius Caesar has already sailed from two heel-of-Italy ports — Tarentum (modern Taranto) and Brundisium (modern Brindisi), both major Roman naval bases — across the Ionian Sea, the stretch of the Mediterranean between Italy and western Greece, to seize the Greek port of Toryne. The speed of the crossing is what stuns him.
detail: These were the standard Roman embarkation points for the eastern Mediterranean: the Adriatic and Ionian seas were the route to Greece and beyond. Brundisium in particular was where Antony and Octavius had made peace by the Treaty of Brundisium in 40 BCE (dramatized in Act 2). The crossing represents Octavius closing the strategic distance with uncharacteristic aggression, wrong-footing Antony, who had expected more preparation time. Plutarch (Life of Antony 62) confirms the speed of Octavius's advance to the promontory of Actium as a shock to Antony's commanders.

sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 62, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Octavius moved swiftly to the Actium promontory, surprising Antony's forces.

anchor_text: wage this battle at Pharsalia, / Where Caesar fought with Pompey
summary: Canidius suggests meeting Octavius Caesar at Pharsalia (in Thessaly, northern Greece), where Julius Caesar defeated Pompey the Great in 48 BCE — the decisive battle that ended the Republic's last great resistance and made Caesar master of the Roman world. The suggestion is that a land battle on that famous field would be on Antony's terms, not Caesar's.
detail: The 'Caesar' who 'fought with Pompey' here is the dead Julius Caesar, not Octavius. Octavius merely has the name; the field belongs to his great-uncle. Canidius is implying that Antony, like the first Caesar, should fight where a great Roman general fights best — on land in a pitched infantry battle. Pharsalus (the more usual ancient spelling) was fought on 9 August 48 BCE; Pompey the Great fled to Egypt, where he was murdered. The allusion also quietly reminds Antony of what he is risking: the last general to refuse a good land position and fight by sea (Pompey's admiral Bibulus) was ineffective.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Caesar
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 42-45, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the battle of Pharsalus, 48 BCE, defeat and flight of Pompey the Great.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1840

anchor_text: Away, my Thetis
summary: Antony calls Cleopatra 'my Thetis,' addressing her as the sea-goddess Thetis from Greek myth — one of the Nereids, the fifty daughters of the sea-god Nereus, and the divine mother of Achilles. On the eve of a sea-battle, calling Cleopatra a sea-goddess is pointed flattery and also a hint that he associates her with command of the waves.

The name-choice carries an edge the scene does not fully develop: Thetis could not protect her son from his destined death no matter how she tried. Since Antony is about to fight a sea-battle over everyone's objections and with an inferior fleet, calling his queen 'Thetis' associates her both with the sea she has chosen as the medium of battle and with a goddess who loves a great warrior whom she cannot save. For Shakespeare's audience Thetis was known chiefly from Virgil's Aeneid and from Ovid's Metamorphoses.

anchor_text: By Hercules, I think I am i' the right
summary: The anonymous soldier swears by Hercules — the same hero-god that Antony claimed as his divine ancestor and patron. The oath resonates: it is a soldier of Antony's army invoking Antony's own tutelary deity to affirm that Antony is wrong. The irony grows darker because later in the play (4.3) music underground signals the god Hercules silently deserting Antony on the eve of his last battle.

For a soldier to swear 'By Hercules' that his own general is on the wrong course is to use the general's patron against him. The phrase also functions as a conventional mild oath for Elizabethans, but its specific resonance in this play — where Antony is repeatedly aligned with and then abandoned by Hercules — gives it a weight far beyond convention. The later scene of Hercules's departure (4.3) is the culmination of this motif.

anchor_text: the time's with labour; and throes forth / Each minute some
summary: Canidius closes the scene with a compressed metaphor: time itself is in labour, convulsed with birth-pangs ('throes'), and delivers some new event every minute. 'Throes' is the word for the agonizing contractions of childbirth. The image captures the accelerating pace of events at Actium — dispatches, troop movements, Caesar's arrival — all pressing in at once.

The line formally closes the scene as an exit couplet, its urgency contrasting with the extended, careful arguments of the preceding debate. The same sense of events outrunning deliberation is the scene's dramatic point: by the time Antony's officers have laid out every reason not to fight by sea, the moment has already passed for any different choice.

anchor_text: Strike not by land; keep whole; provoke not battle
summary: Octavius Caesar orders Taurus, his land-force commander, to hold back and not engage Antony on the ground — the sea-battle alone will decide the campaign. By keeping his land forces intact ('keep whole') Octavius ensured that if the sea-battle went against him, he would not lose his army too; in the event, Cleopatra's squadron fled and Antony's sea-power collapsed. Shakespeare signals this strategy neatly in four words, letting the audience grasp that the two sides have mirror-image plans — Antony insisted on fighting at sea (3.7), Octavius on keeping the land quiet.

anchor_text: the number of the ships behold, / And so proceed accordingly
summary: Antony is ordering a reconnaissance: count how many ships Octavius Caesar has deployed, then decide what to do. This brief scene frames the catastrophic sea battle of Actium (2 September 31 BCE) — the decisive engagement of the Roman civil war in which Antony, persuaded against his generals' advice to fight at sea rather than on land, was defeated by Octavius's admiral Agrippa.

The scene is deliberately short: Shakespeare uses it as one of a rapid series of brief interlocked scenes (3.7-3.10) that dramatize the chaotic collapse at Actium from multiple perspectives.

anchor_text: Naught, naught, all naught
summary: 'Naught' means nothing, worthless, or ruined. Enobarbus is saying that everything is lost: he has just watched Cleopatra's flagship and her sixty supporting vessels turn and flee the naval battle at Actium.
detail: The triple repetition ('Naught, naught, all naught') is a rhetorical figure called anaphora used to convey shock and despair. 'Naught' carries the full weight of military catastrophe: not merely nothing, but ruin. The same word appears in the Elizabethan phrase 'set at naught' (to treat as worthless). Enobarbus, who argued against fighting by sea, now watches the disaster he predicted unfold.

anchor_text: greater cantle of the world is lost
summary: A 'cantle' is a segment or slice — Scarus means the larger portion of the known world is now lost to Antony's cause. The phrase echoes the play's repeated idea that Antony and Cleopatra hold dominion over vast territories that are now being squandered.

The word 'cantle' appears in Henry IV Part 1 (3.1) where Hotspur describes Glendower's map-dividing as cutting a 'cantle out' of England; here it carries the same sense of a physical chunk carved from a territory. anchor_text: like the token'd pestilence
summary: A 'token'd pestilence' is a plague outbreak whose victims already show the tell-tale spots or 'tokens' — dark blotches on the skin that appeared in the final, fatal stage of bubonic plague, meaning death was certain. Scarus is saying their military situation is as hopeless as a man already marked with those spots: no recovery is possible.

The 'tokens' (Latin: signa) were the subcutaneous hemorrhages that signaled the body was beyond saving. Scarus extends the metaphor to the battle: Antony's fleet is not merely losing but already past the point of rescue, visibly doomed. The image of the 'token'd pestilence' would have struck an Elizabethan audience with visceral immediacy; several major outbreaks, including the 1592-1593 epidemic that closed the London theatres, were within living memory.

anchor_text: She once being loof'd, The noble ruin of her magic, Antony, Claps on his sea-wing, and, like a doting mallard

The comparison strips Antony of every military dignity: Rome's greatest general reduced to a lovesick bird.

The image of the 'doting mallard' — the drake mindlessly following the duck — recalls the play's animal imagery for Antony's surrender of reason to passion. Plutarch (North's translation, Life of Antony 66) records that Antony followed Cleopatra's retreating ship and left sixty fighting vessels behind; Shakespeare adds the degrading farmyard simile.

anchor_text: he at Philippi kept / His sword e'en like a dancer
summary: Antony is raging that Octavius Caesar — 'the young man' — won the battle of Philippi (42 BCE) without doing any real fighting, keeping his sword in its scabbard 'like a dancer' (a dancer wore a decorative sword, not a weapon for actual use). Antony himself killed Cassius and defeated Brutus in the same battle. Now this ceremonial soldier has beaten him.
detail: Antony and Octavius together defeated the assassins Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in 42 BCE, avenging Julius Caesar. Octavius, however, was ill and reportedly took no active part; his general Agrippa handled the fighting. anchor_text: My heart was to thy rudder tied by the strings, / And thou shouldst tow me after

anchor_text: Fortune knows / We scorn her most when most she offers blows

anchor_text: 'tis his schoolmaster

anchor_text: Think, and die.

The pairing also foreshadows his own fate: he will think through his position too clearly, desert, and die of a broken heart.

Enobarbus uses it here to assign sole blame to Antony — exonerating Cleopatra by noting that even if she fled the battle, Antony had no obligation to follow. anchor_text: Against the blown rose may they stop their nose / That kneel'd unto the buds

anchor_text: thou most renown'd: Caesar entreats / Not to consider in what case thou stand'st / Further than he is Caesar

anchor_text: He is a god, and knows / What is most right: mine honour was not yielded, / But conquer'd merely
summary: Cleopatra tells Thyreus that she submits not out of willingness but because she was 'merely' (purely, entirely) conquered — her honor was taken by force, not given. She simultaneously flatters Octavius Caesar as godlike and builds a legal-diplomatic defense: she is a victim, not a traitor.
detail: The distinction between 'yielded' and 'conquer'd' is a political maneuver. If her honor was yielded (surrendered willingly), she is a collaborator; if conquered, she is a captive, with the moral standing of a victim and potential diplomatic leverage. Cleopatra has been conducting negotiations with Caesar throughout this scene, playing a subtle game that Enobarbus reads as treachery to Antony but which can also be read as her attempt to preserve herself and Egypt. The comment that Caesar 'is a god' ironically foreshadows his future deification as Augustus.

anchor_text: Your Caesar's father / Oft, when he hath mus'd of taking kingdoms in, / Bestow'd his lips on that unworthy place, / As it rain'd kisses
summary: Cleopatra tells Caesar's messenger Thyreus that Julius Caesar — Octavius Caesar's adoptive father — often kissed her hand when he was dreaming of conquest. She is not referring to Octavius (the man in the scene) but to the dead Julius Caesar, her former lover. The scene marks Thyreus's attempt to kiss her hand as something she endured from a far greater man.
detail: This is a crucial disambiguation. 'Your Caesar' means Octavius Caesar, who is Thyreus's master; 'your Caesar's father' is Julius Caesar — who was not Octavius's biological father but his great-uncle and adoptive father in his will, making Octavius legally his heir. Julius Caesar was Cleopatra's earlier lover and the father of her son Caesarion. By invoking Julius Caesar, Cleopatra simultaneously honors Octavius's lineage, implies she is not a stranger to the Julian family, and condescends to Thyreus: she endured kisses from the man Octavius only inherited his name from.

The disambiguation between Julius Caesar (Octavius's adoptive father, Cleopatra's former lover) and Octavius is essential and correct; the social condescension toward Thyreus is clearly the rhetorical purpose of the speech.

anchor_text: Favours, by Jove that thunders!
summary: Antony bursts in swearing by Jove (Jupiter), king of the Roman gods and the god of thunder and lightning. The oath is fittingly Roman and violent: Jove's thunderbolt was how he punished the presumptuous. Antony invokes the highest Roman deity at the moment he discovers Thyreus about to kiss Cleopatra's hand.

anchor_text: Ah, you kite!
summary: A 'kite' was a common scavenger bird (the red kite), associated with theft and feeding on carrion. Antony hurls it at Thyreus as a term of contempt — a low creature that steals what it can from others' carcasses. The insult fits: Thyreus has come to pick off Cleopatra from the ruins of Antony's cause.
detail: The kite was proverbially associated with cowardice and filching in Elizabethan English; it stole food from smaller birds and hovered around slaughterhouses. The word appears several times in Shakespeare as an abuse for a low, mercenary, scavenging person. Antony also calls Thyreus a 'Jack' (TLN 2194, 2206), another contempt-term for a low-born man. The pair of insults is Antony at his least regal — furiously belittling a messenger because the situation itself has become unbearable.

anchor_text: Like boys unto a muss
summary: A 'muss' was a children's game in which coins or small objects were thrown down in a scatter for players to scramble and grab. Antony recalls how kings would come running at his call like boys diving for scattered coins — now no one answers. The image captures his lost authority through a childhood game.
detail: The 'muss' was also called 'scramble' and was played at holiday celebrations, including when spectators would throw coins from a window for crowds to fight over. Antony's memory of kings scrambling to obey him contrasts savagely with his present predicament: he is giving orders that go unanswered, reduced to confronting a single messenger from his enemy. The detail is characteristic of how the play measures Antony's fall through the withdrawal of others' deference.

anchor_text: Upon the hill of Basan, to outroar / The horned herd! for I have savage cause
summary: Bashan (spelled 'Basan' in the Geneva Bible) was a fertile plateau east of the Jordan famous for its strong, well-fed bulls. Psalm 22 uses 'many bulls of Basan' as an image of enemies surrounding the sufferer. Antony wishes he could bellow louder than this whole herd of horned beasts — partly because 'horned' carries the double meaning of a cuckolded husband.
detail: The Psalm reads 'Many bulls have compassed me: mighty bulls of Basan have closed me on every side' (Psalm 22:12, Geneva 1599). The image of Bashan's bulls as overwhelming enemies was well known from its use in the Psalms and in the Passion narrative (the Psalm is the one that begins 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me,' quoted by Christ on the cross). Antony's use of it is both boastful and self-pitying. Crucially, 'horned herd' also plays on the Elizabethan cuckold's horn — a man whose wife is unfaithful was imagined to sprout horns — so Antony is declaring that even if he is a cuckold, he has cause to roar louder than all the world's cuckolded men together.

anchor_text: our terrene moon / Is now eclips'd, and it portends alone / The fall of Antony
summary: Antony addresses Cleopatra as 'our terrene moon' — the earthly moon, as opposed to the celestial one. A lunar eclipse was held to be a dire omen foretelling catastrophe for kings. By casting himself as the moon's subject, he acknowledges that his fate is tied to Cleopatra, and an eclipse of her favor portends his own ruin.
detail: The moon had complex symbolic weight: as a planetary body it governed lower nature, the tides, and women; it also linked Cleopatra to the goddess Isis (who was associated with the moon) and to the lunar deity whose waning threatened earthly order. Elizabethan and Jacobean audiences took lunar eclipses seriously as portents — Gloucester in King Lear (1.2) speaks of recent eclipses as omens of disaster. For Antony to say the eclipse 'portends alone / The fall of Antony' is both an astrological statement and a striking admission: the source of his downfall is the 'moon' he chose to follow.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the general association of Cleopatra with Isis and lunar symbolism; cf. Plutarch, 'On Isis and Osiris.'

Plutarch's 'On Isis and Osiris' does treat Isis in a lunar aspect, and the Life of Antony records Cleopatra's association with Isis; the citations support the cultural-context claim about lunar symbolism.

'Terrene moon' as the earthly moon (Cleopatra) and the eclipse as omen are well supported; the Isis/lunar association is standard in the scholarship and Antony explicitly frames the eclipse as portending his own fall.

anchor_text: one that ties his points
summary: 'Points' were the laced ties that fastened a man's doublet (jacket) to his hose (trousers) in Elizabethan dress. Someone who 'ties his points' is a menial body-servant — a dresser or lackey. Antony accuses Cleopatra of flirting with one of Caesar's most trivial attendants.
detail: The insult works by social contempt: Thyreus is not a general or a senator but the equivalent of a valet. To 'mingle eyes' (flirt) with such a person would be the most degrading possible betrayal of Antony's status. The points themselves were often ornate, expensive, and associated with a man's personal servant managing his clothing; it was a famously intimate domestic role. Antony reduces Caesar's envoy to the most servile level his aristocratic imagination can find.

Points as the laced fastenings of Elizabethan dress and the one who ties them as a menial body-servant is the standard gloss; the social contempt reading is directly supported by the scene's pattern of Antony reducing Thyreus to the lowest possible status.

anchor_text: let heaven engender hail, / And poison it in the source; and the first stone / Drop in my neck
summary: Cleopatra calls down a curse on herself as proof of her loyalty: if her heart is cold toward Antony, let heaven breed hailstones from it, poison them at their source in her heart, and let the first stone fall on her own neck. The oath escalates into a self-destruction prayer that extends to her children and her people.
detail: The speech (TLN 2270-2279) is an extended conditional self-curse — 'if I am false, let these things happen to me.' Such oaths were a recognized rhetorical form (the 'imprecation'). What makes it striking is the specificity and the escalation: from her own neck, to 'The next Caesarion' (her son by Julius Caesar), through 'the memory of my womb' (all her children), to all Egyptians, lying unburied and eaten by flies and gnats. The oath is simultaneously a passionate declaration of love and a speech that acknowledges the worst possibility — that Antony's suspicion might be warranted.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2271

The conditional self-curse (imprecation) form is correctly identified; the escalation through her own neck, Caesarion, all her children, and all Egyptians is accurately described and the text at TLN 2270-2279 supports it.

anchor_text: The next Caesarion smite!
summary: Caesarion ('little Caesar') was the name of Cleopatra's son by Julius Caesar — not Octavius Caesar. He was about thirteen years old at this point in the play's action. Cleopatra invokes him as the ultimate measure of her sincerity: she would rather have hail destroy her own son than be false to Antony.
detail: Caesarion (Ptolemy XV Caesar, born c. 47 BCE) was the product of Cleopatra's liaison with Julius Caesar and was co-ruler of Egypt with his mother. After Actium, Cleopatra sent him away for safety; he was eventually caught and executed on Octavius's orders after Cleopatra's death in 30 BCE — Octavius had no interest in letting a legitimate heir of Julius Caesar live. The name in this oath thus carries heavy irony: Cleopatra calls down destruction on this child to prove her love, and history will bring that destruction anyway.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)

Caesarion's identity as Cleopatra's son by Julius Caesar and his eventual fate at Octavius's order are historically accurate; the irony that the oath invoking his destruction is historically fulfilled is a legitimate and non-sentimental observation.

anchor_text: I'll make death love me; for I will contend / Even with his pestilent scythe
summary: Antony personifies Death as a figure armed with a scythe — the medieval and Renaissance image of Death the Reaper who cuts down all lives. He resolves to fight so ferociously that even Death will admire him. 'Pestilent' means plague-bearing; Death's scythe was imagined as carrying pestilence as well as cutting men down.
detail: The personification of Death as a scythe-wielding harvester ('the Grim Reaper') was ubiquitous in medieval art and emblem literature, appearing in paintings, woodcuts, and the danse macabre tradition. Antony's defiant boast — that he will fight so well Death itself will 'love' him — transforms Roman military bravado into something almost theatrical. The speech marks his shift from jealous fury at Cleopatra back to the exhilarated soldier he was; it sets up, with great irony, his actual death in Act 4, which is botched and prolonged.

Death personified with a scythe as the Grim Reaper is a genuine Renaissance tradition (danse macabre, Holbein); 'pestilent' meaning plague-bearing is correct; the ironic foreshadowing of his botched actual death is a sound literary observation.

anchor_text: The dove will peck the estridge
summary: An 'estridge' is an ostrich (sometimes also used for a goshawk in this period). Enobarbus uses a proverb: when a person is 'frighted out of fear' — transported into a beyond-fear recklessness by rage — even the gentlest creature (the dove) will attack the fiercest (the ostrich or hawk). He is describing Antony's newly manic bravery as the courage of a creature that has passed through terror into something beyond normal calculation.
detail: The word 'estridge' appears in Shakespeare for both ostrich and goshawk; editors debate which is meant here, but the proverbial sense is clear in either case: when rage and despair override the instinct for self-preservation, natural hierarchies of predator and prey collapse. Enobarbus's reading is diagnostic, not admiring: Antony's boldness is not sound courage but the frenzy of despair, 'frighted out of fear' — a psychological paradox that perfectly describes the over-the-top defiance of the scene's last speeches.

anchor_text: when valour preys on reason, / It eats the sword it fights with. I will seek / Some way to leave him.
summary: Enobarbus closes the scene with a vivid paradox: when courage feeds on (destroys) reason, it devours the very instrument — rational judgment — that makes courage effective. A fearless man without judgment is self-destructive. This is his final verdict on Antony, and his decision to desert follows immediately.
detail: The metaphor is precise and brutal. A soldier's sword needs a wielding hand guided by reason; without judgment, the sword is turned on its user. Enobarbus has spent the whole scene watching Antony vacillate between fury (whipping Thyreus), jealousy, grief, and manic bravado, each outburst further from the clear-headed generalship that once made Antony great. 'I will seek / Some way to leave him' is a complete reversal of the loyal-follower position he defended in his earlier aside (TLN 2127-2131), marking the completion of his moral journey from loyalty to desertion.

anchor_text: He calls me boy
summary: Antony addresses Octavius Caesar as 'boy' in his challenge, a calculated insult targeting Caesar's relative youth -- he was about 33 at this point, against Antony's roughly 52. The taunt denies Caesar the status of a legitimate military equal, since Octavius had never personally won glory in pitched battle the way Antony had.
detail: Octavius had never personally commanded in pitched battle the way Antony had; his victories depended heavily on his admiral Agrippa. For Antony, a hardened soldier shaped by decades of Roman warfare, 'boy' was not merely an insult but a substantive argument: Octavius was unproven, a politician and schemer, not a warrior. Plutarch (Life of Antony 75) records Antony's challenge to single combat and Caesar's cold reply that Antony 'had many other ways to die.' Caesar's response in this scene is the pragmatist's answer to the warrior's challenge: he does not need to fight Antony personally when time and superior resources are on his side.

anchor_text: dares me to personal combat
summary: Antony challenges Octavius Caesar to single combat — one general against the other, winner takes the war. This was an ancient Roman gesture of honor, but by the late republic it was already archaic; Caesar's dismissal ('I have many other ways to die; meantime / Laugh at his challenge') is the political realist's response to a soldier playing by codes his opponent simply does not share.
detail: Plutarch (Life of Antony 75) records Antony's actual challenge letter, in which he proposed personal combat to decide the war. Caesar's reported reply was that Antony had other ways of dying — a deflating non-answer that refuses to engage on Antony's terms. The exchange captures a central dramatic contrast of the play: Antony frames himself as a heroic individual, a man of direct physical courage; Caesar operates through armies, resources, and attrition. For Shakespeare's audience, accustomed to the chivalric-honor language of the history plays, Antony's challenge reads as a rearguard action of an older heroic world against a calculating modern statecraft that finds it merely amusing.

anchor_text: Make boot of his distraction
summary: 'Make boot of' means to profit from, to take advantage of. 'Distraction' here means mental frenzy or breakdown — the state of a man losing control. Maecenas is telling Caesar not to give Antony time to recover, but to press the attack while Antony is falling apart mentally and militarily.
detail: 'Boot' in this sense (advantage, profit, gain) was standard Elizabethan usage; Onions gives 'that which is given into the bargain' and more broadly 'advantage, benefit, use' (Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'boot'). 'Distraction' could mean simply a pulling apart or confusion, but in Shakespearean usage it shades consistently toward mental disorder or frenzy — the loss of self-command. Maecenas's preceding lines make the argument: a great man in a rage is 'hunted / Even to falling,' because rage destroys its own defenses. The compressed advice is a piece of cool strategic psychology: Antony's emotional volatility after the loss of Actium and Enobarbus's defection is itself a weapon Caesar can exploit by keeping up the pressure.

'Boot' as profit/advantage and 'distraction' as mental disorder are both well-attested Elizabethan senses fully consistent with the immediate context of Maecenas urging Caesar to exploit Antony's volatility, with no interpretive stretching.

anchor_text: feast the army; we have store to do't, / And they have earn'd the waste
summary: Caesar orders a feast for his army, pointedly noting that within his ranks ('our files') are soldiers who served Antony until very recently. The feast is both reward and propaganda: binding Antony's former troops to the winning side with loyalty purchased through generosity. 'Waste' here means lavish expenditure, prodigal spending — what soldiers have earned by their service.
detail: Plutarch records that after Actium and the collapse of Antony's cause, soldiers and commanders deserted to Caesar in steady numbers. Caesar's strategy of absorbing Antony's forces was deliberate; Enobarbus's defection (3.13) is the play's most prominent example of this hemorrhage. By feasting the army — including men newly crossed over — Caesar cements the loyalty of those he needs to capture Alexandria. 'Store' means an ample supply of provisions, and 'waste' carries its Elizabethan sense of extravagant outlay or prodigality (OED s.v. 'waste' n. 1b, 'lavish expenditure'). The final 'Poor Antony!' is ambiguous: it could be contemptuous, pitying, or even slightly uneasy — a man who knows the war is nearly won and allows himself one moment of reflection on the enemy he is destroying.

sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 68-73, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the steady desertion of Antony's forces to Caesar after Actium.

anchor_text: I'll strike, and cry 'Take all.'
summary: 'Take all' was a gambling cry meaning 'I stake everything on one throw — winner takes everything.' Enobarbus is saying he will fight with no thought of escape or survival: he puts all on Antony's last battle, win or lose.
detail: The phrase belongs to dice and card play; a gambler who cried 'take all' pushed his whole stake into a single desperate wager. The idiom is cited in contemporary English sources and was familiar to Elizabethan audiences from game-playing. Coming from Enobarbus — a character defined by his clear-eyed realism — the phrase is charged: he knows the odds, and still stakes all on his general. The irony is that Enobarbus will not in fact keep this pledge; he deserts Antony before the battle.

anchor_text: the period of your duty
summary: 'Period' here means 'end' or 'conclusion,' not a unit of time. Antony is telling his servants that tonight may be the last night they owe him service — the end-point, the full stop, of their obligation to him.

anchor_text: I, an ass, am onion-ey'd: for shame, / Transform us not to women
summary: 'Onion-eyed' means eyes streaming with tears — the same effect a raw onion produces. Enobarbus is embarrassed to find himself weeping, and protests that Antony is 'transforming' the soldiers into women by making them cry. Roman military culture regarded public weeping as unmanly; Enobarbus calling himself an 'ass' is a self-correction for giving way to emotion.
detail: The onion-as-cause-of-tears was a standard Elizabethan simile; 'onion-eyed' is Shakespeare's compressed coinage from it (the word appears only here in his works). The Roman prohibition on soldiers weeping in public is tied to the Stoic ideal of self-mastery: grief is permissible privately, but to weep before your general before a battle is to infect the whole company with despair. Enobarbus's 'transform us not to women' reflects the gendered Roman hierarchy in which emotional display was associated with the feminine — compare 4.14 when Antony himself, faced with apparent defeat, says his valor has 'melted into... a woman's way.' The scene is thus a pointed study in the Roman emotional code cracking under strain.

sources.name: OED

anchor_text: Peace, what noise
summary: The stage direction calls for 'music as of hautboys under the stage' — hautboys (pronounced 'oh-boys') are an early form of oboe, with a reedy, penetrating tone. Elizabethan theatres had a trapdoor space beneath the stage, and musicians placed there could produce eerie, sourceless sound that seemed to rise from underground. The soldiers cannot agree whether the music is coming from the air or the earth: the ambiguity is the point.
detail: The subterranean music signals a supernatural event. Placed on the night before Antony's final battle, it functions as an omen or portent — the kind of prodigy that Roman thought associated with divine displeasure or the withdrawal of divine protection. A second soldier immediately gives the sound a name: the departing god Hercules. The word 'hautboys' (from French 'haut bois,' literally 'high wood') entered English in the sixteenth century; the instrument is the predecessor of the modern oboe. Cf. Plutarch, Life of Antony 75 (North 1579) for the source of the episode.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 75, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): on the night before the final battle 'there was heard a marvellous sweet harmony of sundry sorts of instruments... going through the midst of the city towards the gate that opened to the enemies.'

The instrument description, 'haut bois' etymology, staging mechanics, and Plutarch parallel are all accurate; the soldiers' air/earth disagreement is faithfully drawn from the scene.

anchor_text: It signs well, does it not
summary: 'Signs' here means 'augurs' or 'bodes' — it carries the technical force of a Roman omen. Romans officially read the gods' will in prodigies: strange sounds, monstrous births, unusual animal behaviour. The Fourth Soldier hopes the unexplained music is a favourable sign; the Third Soldier flatly says no.
detail: The brief exchange dramatizes Roman omen-reading: interpreting unsolicited portents was a recognized, state-sanctioned practice in Rome, conducted by augur-priests and reported to commanders before battle. The disagreement between the soldiers ('It signs well' / 'No') mirrors how augury worked in practice — the same phenomenon could be read in opposite ways. The bitter irony is that the music will immediately be glossed by a fellow soldier as the god Hercules abandoning Antony, which is the most unfavourable omen possible on the eve of battle.

sources.name: Cicero, De Divinatione

Reading 'signs' as 'augurs/bodes' is lexically sound, and the note that Roman omen-reading underlies the exchange is defensible, though the soldiers are reacting instinctively rather than conducting formal augury — the annotation does not overclaim this distinction.

anchor_text: No, my chuck
summary: 'Chuck' is an Elizabethan term of endearment, roughly equivalent to 'sweetheart' or 'darling,' used between intimate companions. Antony brushes off Cleopatra's plea for him to sleep a little with affectionate but firm impatience.

anchor_text: Rarely, rarely; He that unbuckles this, till we do please To daff't
summary: 'Rarely' here means 'excellently' or 'splendidly' — Antony is complimenting Cleopatra on buckling his armour well. 'Daff' (or 'doff') means to put off or remove; 'daff't' = 'daff it' = take it off. He is promising that anyone who tries to unbuckle the armour before he himself chooses to remove it will face his fury.

'Rarely' in the sense of 'admirably, excellently' was the ordinary superlative of 'rare' (= fine, choice); Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'rarely') cites this line as a clear instance. 'Daff' (from Old English daf-, to put aside) is the same root as 'doff' (do off); by the early modern period 'doff' was becoming standard, and 'daff' was already slightly old-fashioned, giving a clipped military ring here. The combined effect is Antony's characteristic swagger: the armour fits perfectly and will not come off until he wins.

anchor_text: my queen's a squire More tight at this than thou
summary: A 'squire' was a knight's attendant who helped him arm before battle — Antony is teasing Eros by saying Cleopatra performs this military service more skillfully than he does. 'Tight' means 'expert, capable, or handy at' a task, not the modern sense of a snug fit.
detail: 'Squire' (from Old French escuyer, shield-carrier) originally named the young nobleman who bore a knight's armour and weapons; by Shakespeare's day 'to squire' someone could mean simply to attend or serve them. Using the word for Cleopatra is playfully incongruous — the Queen of Egypt as a military page-boy — and the joke flatters her while needling Eros. 'Tight' in the sense of 'skilled, ready, capable' (OED s.v. 'tight' adj. 4) is obsolete in standard English but was common in the period; Onions cites it as 'competent, proficient.' Antony's teasing also underlines how domestically intimate the arming scene is despite its martial subject.

'Tight' = capable/dexterous (OED sense 4) and 'squire' as arming-attendant are both sound; the playful incongruity of Cleopatra-as-page is a standard editorial observation.

anchor_text: worthy shameful check it were, to stand On more mechanic compliment
summary: 'Mechanic' here means belonging to tradespeople or common laborers, and by extension 'base, ordinary, beneath a gentleman's dignity.' A 'mechanic compliment' is a long, fussy ceremonial farewell of the kind a common person might perform — Antony says a soldier's brief kiss is the right leave-taking, and that lingering over elaborate goodbyes would be embarrassing and unworthy.
detail: In Elizabethan usage 'mechanic' (from Greek mekhanikos, one who works with his hands) denoted manual laborers and artisans, the social rank below gentleman; anything 'mechanic' was therefore low, commonplace, or ungentlemanlike. Antony is drawing a sharp distinction between the decorum of a soldier going to battle and the drawn-out ceremony of a civilian or courtier. The speech (TLN 2464-2469) crystallizes the play's Rome-versus-Egypt tension at the level of body language: a quick martial kiss versus elaborate Eastern court protocol. Plutarch's Life of Antony, in North's translation, repeatedly marks Antony's identity as primarily that of a Roman soldier, and this speech is Shakespeare's distillation of that self-image at the moment of departure.

anchor_text: he and Caesar might Determine this great war in single fight
summary: Cleopatra wishes the war could be settled by personal combat between Antony and Caesar — here meaning Octavius Caesar, Antony's rival and the future emperor Augustus, not the dead Julius Caesar. The wish invokes the ancient heroic ideal, common in Homer and in Roman tradition, that two champions might spare whole armies by fighting it out themselves.
detail: The idea of two commanders resolving a war in personal single combat (monomachia) was celebrated in Homer's Iliad, where Hector and Achilles, and Paris and Menelaus, fight as champions; the custom was also part of the Roman military tradition. Antony himself later challenges Octavius directly in 3.13: 'Tell him he wears the rose / Of youth upon him; from which the world should note / Something particular: I'll fight with him by single fight.' Caesar refuses — pointedly, in keeping with his cold-blooded character. Cleopatra's wish here, spoken as Antony marches out gallantly, is undercut by her trailing off: 'Then, Antony, — but now — Well, on.' She cannot finish the thought, instinctively aware that the wish is futile. North's Plutarch records that Antony did send this challenge, and that Caesar declined.

anchor_text: kings that have revolted, and the soldier
summary: After the defeat at Actium (31 BCE), many of the eastern client kings who had fought under Antony switched allegiance to Octavius Caesar. The soldier is telling Antony that if he had heeded warnings to fight on land, those defections — and Enobarbus's desertion — would never have happened.

The phrase 'kings that have revolted' condenses weeks of cascading defections into a single line, and the soldier links them directly to Antony's catastrophic choice to fight by sea rather than use his army's superior land strength. This scene sits in the aftermath of those losses.

The historical context of post-Actium client-king defections is accurate, and the soldier's speech explicitly ties them to the sea-battle decision, so the interpretive claim is grounded directly in the text.

anchor_text: The time of universal peace is near
summary: Octavius Caesar is predicting the Pax Romana, the era of empire-wide peace he will inaugurate after defeating Antony. 'The three-nook'd world' is the known world divided into three continents — Europe, Asia, and Africa; 'bear the olive freely' means produce peace (the olive branch was the classical symbol of peace). By defeating the last rival, Octavius will become the first Roman emperor and close a century of civil war.
detail: Suetonius records that Augustus (the name Octavius took in 27 BCE) closed the temple of Janus — kept open in wartime — only three times, advertising a world at peace. Shakespeare's audience also heard a providential note: the 'time of universal peace' was the reign in which, according to Luke 2:1, 'there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus' and Christ was born. The cold efficiency of Octavius throughout the play takes on a chilly, world-historical weight from this line: the man who destroys Antony and Cleopatra is also, in Renaissance reckoning, the unwitting instrument of a larger design.

The Pax Romana gloss is mainstream; the providential Luke 2:1 overlay was a Renaissance commonplace (Virgil's Fourth Eclogue / Nativity typology), and the annotation correctly frames it as ironic world-historical weight rather than a simple compliment to Caesar.

anchor_text: Plant those that have revolted in the van
summary: Octavius Caesar orders his commanders to place soldiers who have defected from Antony at the front of the battle line (the 'van,' short for vanguard). The tactic is coldly calculated: if Antony sees his own former men in the forefront, he will either be forced to kill them or hesitate — and Octavius can then claim that Antony 'seem to spend his fury / Upon himself,' as if tearing his own army apart.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)

anchor_text: Your emperor / Continues still a Jove
summary: Caesar's soldier calls Antony a 'Jove' — Jove being the Roman name for Jupiter, king of the gods, whose defining trait was sovereign munificence and the dispensing of gifts. Antony has just sent Enobarbus, who betrayed him, not punishment but all of his treasure back plus a 'bounty overplus' (an extra gift on top). Comparing him to Jove says he is so far above ordinary men that betrayal cannot diminish him.

sources.name: Roman religion
sources.citation: Jove/Jupiter Optimus Maximus, the sovereign sky-god and dispenser of fortune and bounty -- the highest Roman deity, conventional figure for supreme munificence.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)

anchor_text: This blows my heart: / If swift thought break it not, a swifter mean / Shall outstrike thought
summary: Enobarbus is saying that Antony's act of forgiving him has broken his heart with grief and shame. 'Blows my heart' means swells it to bursting, as if inflating a vessel until it splits. He then weighs two ways to die: 'swift thought' means grief so intense it kills by itself (the Elizabethan belief that extreme sorrow could stop the heart); 'a swifter mean shall outstrike thought' means he may choose a faster, deliberate method before grief can do the job. Enobarbus's phrasing deliberately leaves his intended 'swifter mean' unnamed, which heightens the self-disgust: he cannot even bring himself to say the word for it. The passage is the emotional turning-point of his arc — the moment he stops hoping to survive his treachery.

anchor_text: Nobler than my revolt is infamous
summary: Enobarbus says Antony's nobility is greater than his own desertion is infamous — and then calls himself 'a master-leaver and a fugitive,' the Roman military terms for a soldier who abandons his general. To desert a Roman commander was not merely a personal betrayal but a legal crime punishable by death.
detail: In Roman military law, desertion (desertio) was a capital offence. 'Master-leaver' has no classical Latin equivalent, but it translates the precise legal status: a soldier or officer who leaves before discharge. Plutarch (Life of Antony, North's translation) records that Domitius Ahenobarbus — the historical Enobarbus — deserted to Caesar just before Actium, 'as one sorry for that he had done,' and died of fever shortly afterward; Shakespeare transforms that bare report into this scene of guilt and collapse. By asking that 'the world rank me in register' as a traitor, Enobarbus invokes the Roman tradition of public record: infamy was formally inscribed, not merely remembered.

anchor_text: man his galleys
summary: To 'man' a ship or galley means to supply it with enough oarsmen and fighting men to operate it. A galley was a warship propelled mainly by rows of oars (not sails), and required large crews. Antony has drawn soldiers from his land army to fill those rowing benches.
detail: Roman war galleys of this period were typically triremes or quinqueremes, propelled by banks of oars and carrying marines for boarding actions. Manning them required far more personnel than sailing ships, which is precisely why pulling troops from a land army to crew a fleet was a serious military trade-off — a fact Caesar is coldly calculating here.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'man' v. 8a: 'To furnish (a vessel) with a sufficient number of men; to provide (a fleet, ship, boat) with a crew.'

The verbal sense 'to furnish a vessel with crew' is standard and directly supported by the text; the detail on galley-crewing requirements is historically accurate and proportionate.

anchor_text: Swallows have built / In Cleopatra's sails their nests: the augurers
summary: Augurers were Roman state priests whose job was to read omens in the natural world — especially the behaviour of birds — and determine whether the gods favoured a course of action. Swallows nesting in the warship's sails are an evil sign: birds normally flee before a battle fleet, not breed in it, and the augurers' visible dismay ('look grimly') means they can read the omen but dare not speak its meaning to Antony.
detail: Cicero's De Divinatione describes the professional practice: augurs observed the flight and song of birds, lightning, and the entrails of sacrifices to pronounce whether a public action was 'auspicious' (literally 'bird-favoured'). Plutarch notes that before Actium Antony's camp was thick with omens of disaster, which his officers refused to report to him. Shakespeare here transfers that atmosphere to this second sea-battle. The irony is that the sign is legible to everyone except the man it most concerns: the whole army can see the swallows, and the augurers' speechless grimness communicates the verdict more forcefully than words could.

The augury gloss is accurate — Roman augurers reading bird behaviour is standard practice, the swallows-in-sails omen is clearly a bad sign per the text ('look grimly'), and the Plutarch pre-Actium parallel is a defensible contextual inference, not an overreach.

anchor_text: Triple-turn'd whore
summary: 'Triple-turn'd' means turned or changed three times. Antony accuses Cleopatra of having transferred her loyalty three times over: she was formerly Julius Caesar's lover, then aligned herself with Pompey the Great's party, and finally became Antony's consort — and now, he believes, she has gone over to Octavius Caesar. The insult collapses her whole political career into a charge of serial betrayal.
detail: Plutarch notes Cleopatra's calculated alliances with Rome's successive strong men: she had been Julius Caesar's mistress and bore him a son, Caesarion; after Caesar's murder she navigated among the factions before committing to Antony after their meeting on the Cydnus. Antony's rage here fuses political betrayal with sexual insult — 'whore' converts diplomatic flexibility into prostitution. 'Novice' in the next line is Antony's contemptuous word for Octavius Caesar, the cold young nephew who has outmanoeuvred him. Some editors count only two prior turns and read 'triple' as an intensifier for 'thrice-faithless,' but the three identifiable alliances make the literal reading fully defensible.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 25-28 (Cleopatra's alliance with Julius Caesar) and 26 (her meeting with Antony on the Cydnus), trans. Sir Thomas North (1579).

The three-turn reading (Julius Caesar → Pompey's faction → Antony → Octavius) is the mainstream editorial position, the annotation honestly flags the alternative 'intensifier' reading, and the fusion of political betrayal with sexual insult is exactly what the line performs.

anchor_text: Like a right gypsy, hath, at fast and loose, / Beguil'd me
summary: 'Fast and loose' was a well-known Elizabethan street con game: a swindler would fold a belt or rope into a loop and challenge a bystander to pin the loop 'fast' with a skewer; the con-man could always work the belt free ('loose'), no matter how firmly the victim thought he had it fixed. Antony says Cleopatra has played the cheat on him all along, making him believe he held something secure when in fact he never did. 'Right gypsy' means a thoroughbred cheat — Elizabethans stereotyped Romani people as the usual operators of the swindle.
detail: The game is documented in Samuel Rid's The Art of Juggling (1612) and was already proverbial by the 1590s. Ben Jonson also has a character use the phrase in this sense. The racial slur is Antony's — and the play's — not the audience's endorsement; Cleopatra herself deploys such labels against herself ('I am no more but e'en a woman, and commanded / By such poor passion as the maid that milks', 4.15). Antony's invective here — 'spell,' 'witch,' 'false soul of Egypt,' 'right gypsy' — is the language of a man who has recast love as enchantment to externalize his own collapse.

The rope-trick game description is correct, 'right gypsy' as ethnic slur meaning thoroughbred cheat is the standard reading, and the annotation appropriately contextualises the slur as Antony's rage-language rather than authorial endorsement.

anchor_text: The shirt of Nessus is upon me: teach me, / Alcides, thou mine ancestor, thy rage: / Let me lodge Lichas on the horns o' the moon
summary: Antony invokes the myth of Hercules's death. Nessus was a centaur shot by Hercules (also called 'Alcides', his Greek name from the family line) for trying to abduct his wife Deianira. As he died Nessus tricked Deianira into keeping his poisoned blood, telling her it was a love-charm; when she later smeared it on a shirt and sent it to Hercules, the burning garment could not be removed and drove him into an agonised frenzy. In his madness Hercules seized his servant Lichas — who had innocently delivered the shirt — and hurled him so hard into the sea that Lichas was turned to stone.

anchor_text: more mad Than Telamon for his shield
summary: Telamon was the father of Ajax, the Greek champion at Troy. When Achilles died, Ajax and Odysseus both claimed his armour; the Greek army awarded it to Odysseus, and Ajax went mad with rage and humiliation, massacring a flock of sheep under the delusion they were his enemies. The armour is the 'shield.' Cleopatra compares Antony's fury to this proverbial classical madness.

anchor_text: the boar of Thessaly Was never so emboss'd
summary: The 'boar of Thessaly' is the Calydonian boar — a monstrous beast sent by the goddess Diana to ravage Calydon (in what is now northern Greece, near Thessaly) as punishment for a neglected sacrifice. The heroes of Greece hunted it together in one of classical myth's great collective quests. 'Emboss'd' here means foaming at the mouth from exhaustion and fury, said of a hard-pressed hunted animal. Cleopatra is saying even that legendary beast was never as dangerously enraged as Antony is now.
detail: The Calydonian boar hunt is told in Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.260-444. Calydon is in Aetolia, not Thessaly proper, but ancient and Renaissance writers often blur the regional geography, and 'Thessaly' was a general byword for wild, heroic Greece. The hunt assembled the greatest heroes of the pre-Trojan generation (Atalanta, Meleager, Theseus), and the boar was nearly unstoppable. 'Emboss'd' derives from the hunting vocabulary meaning an animal driven to the point of foaming at the mouth and collapse (OED s.v. 'emboss'); it paints a picture of berserk, exhausted rage. The double classical comparison -- Ajax's human madness, the boar's animal fury -- stacks one image on top of another to convey that Antony has gone beyond ordinary anger.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.260-444 (the Calydonian boar hunt, in Golding's 1567 English translation).

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2719

'emboss, v.2' correctly captures the hunting-vocabulary sense of a foaming, exhausted animal; both sources are real and support the claims made.

The geographic note (Calydon is in Aetolia, not Thessaly proper) is honestly disclosed and the Renaissance blurring explanation is standard; 'emboss'd' as hunting vocabulary for a foaming, hard-pressed beast is well-attested, and the overall reading of Cleopatra's stacked classical comparisons is mainstream.

anchor_text: send him word you are dead
summary: Charmian's advice to send Antony a false report of Cleopatra's death is the hinge on which the play's catastrophe turns. Cleopatra takes it: she orders the eunuch Mardian to deliver the lie. In Plutarch's account, Cleopatra retreats to her monument and sends word she has killed herself, which drives Antony to fall on his sword. Shakespeare follows this sequence almost exactly.
detail: Plutarch, Life of Antony 76-77 (North's 1579 translation), describes Cleopatra withdrawing to her monument and sending a messenger with the false news of her death; Antony, believing it, asks Eros to kill him, and when Eros kills himself instead, Antony falls on his own sword. The decision here is Cleopatra's attempt to deflect Antony's rage (he has just had her messenger Thyreus whipped and turned violently on her), but it becomes catastrophically miscalculated. The scene is one of the starkest examples of Shakespeare compressing Plutarch: the entire fatal sequence is set in motion in three lines.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 76-77, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Cleopatra locks herself in her monument and sends the false report of her death to Antony.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2722

The identification of this moment as the catastrophic hinge that triggers Antony's suicide, following Plutarch Life of Antony 76-77, is entirely correct; the minor inaccuracy that Thyreus's whipping is in the preceding scene (not this one) does not affect the soundness of the interpretive claim.

anchor_text: The soul and body rive not more in parting Than greatness going off
summary: 'Rive' means to split or tear apart violently -- it is used of splitting wood or cleaving rock. Charmian's aphorism compares the violence of a great person's fall from power to the ultimate violent separation: the soul tearing free from the body at death. Nothing tears more brutally than a soul leaving its body -- except, she says, a great man losing his greatness. The remark frames Antony's collapse in cosmic, almost metaphysical terms before the scene exits.
detail: The comparison uses 'not more... than' as a rhetorical figure of emphasis (auxesis): the body-soul separation at death is the most extreme tearing apart imaginable, and Charmian elevates Antony's fall to that level. 'Rive' (OED s.v. 'rive, v.': to split, cleave, tear apart) is deliberately physical and violent, not a polite parting but a rending. The observation also functions as a kind of consolation or perspective: what Cleopatra and her women are witnessing has the scale of death itself. The line is Charmian's only contribution in this scene beyond urging immediate action.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2723

Labelling the figure 'auxesis' is a mild over-precision — it is more straightforwardly a simile or comparatio — but the core interpretation of 'rive' as violent tearing and the framing of Antony's fall in cosmic terms parallel to death is sound and mainstream.

anchor_text: black vesper's pageants
summary: A 'pageant' was a theatrical spectacle or display; 'black vesper' is the darkening hour of evening. Antony means: the shifting, illusory cloud-shapes he has just described are evening's own theatrical show — gorgeous, convincing, and gone in an instant. He is comparing his own dissolving identity to these transient images.
detail: The metaphor links theatre to mortality with deliberate precision: 'vesper' is Vespers, the canonical hour of evening prayer, and by the time the sky is fully dark the cloud-dragon has vanished just as the office ends. 'Pageant' carried the resonance of a wagon-stage processing through the streets, here applied to clouds — spectacles put on for the eye and then withdrawn. Antony is saying his shape, his soldierly identity, is equally a temporary performance that the moment is dissolving.

'Black vesper's pageants' is correctly glossed: 'pageant' as theatrical spectacle and 'vesper' as evening are both mainstream, and the cloud-dissolution as figure for Antony's dissolving identity is the standard modern consensus reading.

anchor_text: The rack dislimns; and makes it indistinct
summary: 'Rack' here means a mass of drifting clouds (not a torture device). 'Dislimns' means to erase or unportray — to remove the limning (painting or drawing) of a shape. Antony is saying that the cloud-horse is dissolved by the shifting cloud-mass until it is as formless as water mixed with water.
detail: 'Dislimn' is a rare coinage, from 'limn' (to paint or portray), negated: to un-draw. The word appears almost nowhere else in the period, which suggests Shakespeare coined it for the specific effect of watching a shape unmake itself without a sharp moment of erasure. The cloud-dissolving image is Antony's sustained metaphor for his own loss of identity after what he believes is Cleopatra's betrayal and death: he is the shape, Octavius Caesar's victory is the rack.

'Rack' as drifting cloud-mass and 'dislimn' as to erase a painted image are well-attested glosses, and the identification of this as Antony's metaphor for identity-loss is the received scholarly interpretation.

anchor_text: Pack'd cards with Caesar, and false-play'd my glory
summary: Antony accuses Cleopatra of cheating at cards with his rival Octavius Caesar (his fellow triumvir, later the emperor Augustus): to 'pack cards' meant to arrange a deck dishonestly before play. 'False-play'd' extends the gambling metaphor — she has wagered away Antony's glory by playing a rigged game. 'Triumph' in the next line doubles as the name of a card game (an ancestor of modern Trumps) and as the Roman triumphal procession Antony fears.
detail: The card-game cluster is exact Elizabethan slang. 'Pack' (to pack cards) = to stack the deck in collusion with a confederate. 'Triumph' was a card game popular in sixteenth-century England, making the pun on Roman 'triumph' (the victory parade) available to any Elizabethan theatre-goer. The accusation is that Cleopatra and Octavius Caesar conspired together and lost Antony's military honour as if it were a stake at the table. The charge is false — Cleopatra has merely sent Mardian with a fabricated report of her death — but Antony does not yet know that.

anchor_text: Ourselves to end ourselves
summary: Antony means that suicide is left to them as the only honourable exit. The Roman Stoic ideal held that a great man defeated in war should die by his own hand rather than be led in chains through his enemy's city. This is the 'high Roman fashion' of suicide that recurs across the play.
detail: The phrase echoes the Stoic self-possession that the play repeatedly codes as Roman virtue. The exemplary models were Cato the Younger (who killed himself at Utica in 46 BCE rather than submit to Caesar) and, shortly before, Brutus and Cassius at Philippi (42 BCE). Plutarch's Life of Antony records that Antony had prepared himself mentally for exactly this ending after Actium. Shakespeare uses the phrase 'the high Roman fashion' later in the play (4.15) to name the same idea explicitly.

sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Antony's resolve to die rather than be displayed in Octavius's triumph.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2755

Framing this as the Roman Stoic suicide ideal, with Cato and the Plutarchan precedent, is sound and mainstream; the play itself names the 'high Roman fashion' explicitly at 4.15, confirming the interpretive frame.

anchor_text: sevenfold shield of Ajax cannot keep / The battery from my heart
summary: Ajax was the mightiest defensive warrior of the Trojan War, famous for his enormous shield made of seven layers of ox-hide topped with bronze — the sturdiest in the Greek army. Antony says that even Ajax's seven-ply shield could not protect his heart against grief: the emotional blow is greater than any weapon.
detail: Homer describes Ajax's shield as made of seven layers of bull's-hide with a bronze facing (Iliad 7.219-223), and its sheer size and weight made Ajax the unmovable fortress of the Greek forces when all others retreated. 'Battery' means a bombardment of blows (military term). The allusion measures the absolute extremity of Antony's pain: the unbreakable becomes insufficient. Calling Cleopatra's supposed betrayal a force that surpasses Ajax's shield also, with bitter irony, echoes the opening of the play, where Philo mourned that Antony had abandoned 'the office and devotion of their view' for a strumpet's fool.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad

Ajax's seven-layered ox-hide shield from Iliad 7.219-223 is the direct source, 'battery' as bombardment is correct, and the hyperbolic measure of grief is the straightforward dramatic point; the closing comparison to Philo's opening speech is an editorial observation rather than a claim about the text and does no harm.

anchor_text: the torch is out, / Lie down, and stray no further
summary: Antony addresses himself in the second person, ordering his own body to stop moving: without Cleopatra, the torch that lit his way is extinguished. The torch was the standard classical image for the soul or guiding spirit of a person; its going out means death. Antony is telling himself to die.

anchor_text: Where souls do couch on flowers, we'll hand in hand, / And with our sprightly port make the ghosts gaze: / Dido and her Aeneas shall want troops
summary: Antony imagines Elysium — the blessed fields of the classical afterlife where the virtuous dead rest — as a place of flowered meadows. He imagines himself and Cleopatra walking there with such energy ('sprightly port' = lively bearing) that the ordinary shades will stop and stare. Dido and Aeneas, the most famous tragic lovers of the classical world, will lose their audience to Antony and Cleopatra.
detail: Virgil's Aeneid (Book 6) describes the Elysian Fields: the souls of the blessed rest in grassy meadows and groves, where Aeneas finds his father Anchises. Dido and Aeneas appear again in this same underworld: Aeneas encounters Dido's shade, and she turns silently away (Aeneid 6.450-476). Antony imagines himself and Cleopatra supplanting even this most celebrated pair as the presiding lovers of the underworld — an extraordinary act of competitive self-glorification even in the moment of defeat. The allusion also quietly marks Antony's resemblance to Aeneas: both abandoned a great queen for larger political purposes, both will be mourned for it.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 6.440-476 (Dido in the underworld turning from Aeneas) and 6.637-659 (the Elysian fields of the blessed dead).

The Virgilian Elysium (Aeneid 6) and the Dido-Aeneas encounter in the underworld (6.450-476) are the correct references, and the reading of Antony as competitively displacing even Dido and Aeneas as presiding lovers is the standard modern interpretation; the Aeneas-Antony parallel is a legitimate scholarly observation.

anchor_text: I, that with my sword / Quarter'd the world, and o'er green Neptune's back / With ships made cities
summary: Antony looks back on his military career with a pair of hyperboles: his sword 'quartered' (divided, dominated) the world, and his fleets were so vast that his warships moving on the sea ('green Neptune's back') looked like a floating city. Neptune is the Roman god of the sea. Both images measure how far he has fallen.

anchor_text: she which by her death our Caesar tells / 'I am conqueror of myself'
summary: Antony means that Cleopatra's supposed suicide has sent a message to Octavius Caesar — his rival and fellow triumvir (the future emperor Augustus) — that she conquered herself, dying by her own choice rather than surrendering. This is the Stoic ideal: defeating the enemy that truly matters (one's own fear of death) even when defeated on the battlefield. Antony feels she has shown more nobility than he has.
detail: The phrase 'our Caesar' is Antony's bitter possessive — Octavius Caesar, whom both Antony and Cleopatra have been fighting. The argument about who 'conquers' whom runs through the scene: Antony argues that by dying before him Cleopatra won the moral victory, making him feel cowardly for outliving her. The logic is classically Stoic (familiar from Plutarch's accounts of Cato the Younger and Brutus). Antony is shamed into his own suicide as much by her (supposed) example as by defeat in the field.

anchor_text: when the exigent should come,--which now / Is come indeed
summary: 'Exigent' means an extreme emergency, a pressing crisis — specifically here: the moment when there is no way out and death becomes the only option. Antony had earlier bound Eros by an oath to kill him if this moment ever arrived.
detail: From Latin exigere (to demand, drive out); an 'exigency' or 'exigent' was a crisis so extreme it required an immediate, decisive response. The word was used in military and legal contexts for a situation of ultimate necessity — a 'last necessity.' Antony's use of it frames this not as despair but as a fulfillment of a pre-meditated arrangement — the Roman way of choosing death at the moment of one's own judgment, not at the enemy's.

anchor_text: thus do I escape the / sorrow / Of Antony's death
summary: Eros, ordered to kill his master, kills himself instead — escaping the grief of watching Antony die while also fulfilling his own Roman duty: he will not be the one to strike down a man he loves. Antony immediately recognizes this as the nobler act ('Thrice nobler than myself!'). The suicide of a devoted freedman to spare his master is drawn from Plutarch.
detail: Plutarch's Life of Antony (76) records that Eros was a freedman who had been freed by Antony and had sworn to kill him if ever asked; when the moment came, Eros told Antony to turn away, then stabbed himself, falling dead at Antony's feet. Shakespeare follows this closely. The episode belongs to the Roman ideal of 'good death' — the slave-turned-freedman dying free, by his own choice, rather than doing what custom and his oath required. Antony's response ('Thou teachest me') shows he reads it as moral instruction: if his servant can die this way, so can he.

anchor_text: The star is fallen. / And time is at his period
summary: Two guards respond to the sight of the dying Antony with brief, cosmic elegies. 'The star is fallen' casts Antony as a heavenly body whose fall marks a new, diminished age. 'Time is at his period' means 'time has reached its full stop' — 'period' meant end or full stop, as in punctuation. The two lines together are the soldiers' way of saying an era has ended.
detail: The falling-star topos for the death of a great man was common in classical funeral rhetoric (compare Horace, Odes 1.24, on the death of Quintilius). 'Period' (from Greek periodos, a circuit or completion) had both the rhetorical meaning of a rounded sentence and the general meaning of an end or conclusion — so 'time is at his period' means time has rounded to its full stop. The brevity of the soldiers' lines — two short declarations and a shared 'Alas, and woe!' — is itself a kind of theatrical economy: ordinary men cannot find more words for what they are witnessing.

anchor_text: Lock'd in her monument. She had a prophesying fear / Of what hath come to pass
summary: Diomedes explains that Cleopatra retreated to her royal mausoleum — the monument she had built for herself — and barricaded herself inside. The Ptolemaic queens of Egypt built elaborate tombs during their own lifetimes. Fearing Antony's rage if he thought she had defected to Octavius Caesar, she sent a false report of her death, which is what drove Antony to his suicide attempt.
detail: Plutarch (Life of Antony 76-77) describes Cleopatra withdrawing into her mausoleum after the second defeat, sending word that she was dead. The monument was real: a two-storey stone building in the palace precinct where she had stored her treasure. It becomes the setting for the play's final scenes, and Antony will be hauled up to it by ropes while dying. The political logic behind Cleopatra's false message is also explained by Diomedes: she feared that Antony, suspecting her of negotiating with Octavius Caesar (which she had been doing), would kill her in a rage. Her calculation miscarried fatally.

anchor_text: Burn the great sphere thou mov'st in
summary: Cleopatra invokes the Ptolemaic model of the universe, in which the sun was set in a crystal 'sphere' revolving around the earth. She calls on the sun to destroy its own sphere and leave the world in darkness, because without Antony the light is meaningless. 'Darkling' means 'in the dark.'
detail: Ptolemaic cosmology placed each planet, including the sun, in a transparent crystalline sphere that carried it around the earth. To ask the sun to 'burn the great sphere thou mov'st in' is to wish the whole mechanical order of the heavens wrecked. The speech moves from cosmic destruction to a private address — 'O Antony, Antony!' — collapsing the universe into one dying man. The line is a formal apostrophe (address to an absent or non-human entity), turning from the advancing Diomedes to the sun in a single breath.

anchor_text: Not Caesar's valour hath o'erthrown Antony
summary: Antony insists that Octavius Caesar — his fellow triumvir and the man who defeated him at Actium — did not beat him in the field; Antony's own failures of judgment and nerve undid him. This is both a wounded soldier's pride and an honest self-reckoning.
detail: The Caesar here is Octavius, not Julius Caesar, who was murdered two decades earlier. Antony's claim echoes Plutarch, who records that after the final sea-battle Antony's cause collapsed because his soldiers deserted rather than because they were overwhelmed. Shakespeare makes the self-defeat more emphatic: the battle Antony really lost was with himself — the man who followed Cleopatra's retreating ships from Actium. The rhetorical device of the negative claim ('Not X, but Y') is classical ring composition, framing the whole dying speech as a refusal of self-pity.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 68-76, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Antony's final military collapse and his self-reproach.

Antony's line 'Not Caesar's valour hath o'erthrown Antony / But Antony's hath triumph'd on itself' plainly states self-defeat, and the reading that this reflects a soldier's self-reckoning consistent with Plutarch is well-supported; the identification of Caesar as Octavius (not Julius) is correct.

anchor_text: I am dying, Egypt, dying
summary: Throughout the play Antony addresses Cleopatra as 'Egypt' rather than by her name — a common Shakespearean practice of naming a person by the country they embody or rule. Here the title carries tenderness and gravity: she is not just his lover but a sovereign, and the repetition of 'dying' gives the line a tolling, incantatory rhythm.
detail: Addressing a ruler by the name of their kingdom rather than their personal name was standard Elizabethan diplomatic and poetic usage (compare 'France' and 'England' in the history plays). For Antony it also collapses public and private: Cleopatra is Egypt — the land, the court, the beauty, and the cause of everything. The dying Antony says 'dying' twice, the repetition (anadiplosis) conveying both urgency and a fading pulse. Plutarch does not record the exact words; they are Shakespeare's invention and among the most famous in the canon.

anchor_text: not the imperious show / Of the full-fortun'd Caesar ever shall / Be brooch'd with me
summary: Cleopatra refuses to descend from her monument to Antony's deathbed because she fears capture by Octavius Caesar — the 'full-fortun'd Caesar' means the Caesar whose fortune is now at its height, his victory complete. 'Brooch'd' means adorned or decorated: she will not become an ornament — a trophy captive — in Caesar's victory. She vows she would sooner kill herself.
detail: This is Octavius Caesar, who defeated Antony at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE and is now the master of the Roman world. A Roman triumph was a ceremonial victory parade in which notable captives were displayed in chains before the cheering crowd; the prospect of being led through Rome in triumph is the specific humiliation Cleopatra refuses to accept. 'Brooch'd' uses the jewellery conceit to make the outrage vivid: she would be worn, displayed, objectified. Lines 2930-31 state her alternative — knife, drugs, or serpents (anticipating the asp of Act 5). Shakespeare follows Plutarch, who records Cleopatra's determination to die rather than grace Caesar's triumph.
