anchor_text: had I great Juno's power, / The strong-wing'd Mercury should fetch thee up, / And set thee by Jove's side
summary: Straining to haul the dying Antony up to her monument, Cleopatra wishes she had the power of Juno, queen of the gods, so that Mercury — the winged messenger-god — could carry Antony aloft and place him beside Jupiter (Jove), king of the gods. The image turns physical effort into divine wish: instead of pulling a dying man up a rope, she imagines apotheosis.
detail: In Roman religion, Mercury (Greek Hermes) was the god of messages and travel, usually depicted with winged sandals and helmet; he could carry souls between worlds (the psychopomp). Juno was Jupiter's queen. By wishing for Juno's authority and Mercury's wings, Cleopatra frames Antony not as a defeated general but as a hero deserving divine elevation — to be set beside Jupiter rather than borne wounded up a monument wall. The three Roman gods (Juno, Mercury, Jove) are all invoked in a single image, marking the scale of what she wishes she could do. No reference card exists for Mercury.

The wish for Juno's power so Mercury might carry Antony to Jove's side is read correctly as an apotheosis image; Mercury's role as winged messenger and soul-guide (psychopomp) is accurate, and the sources cited (Ovid, Virgil) are appropriate for the Roman divine trio.

anchor_text: the false huswife Fortune break her wheel
summary: 'Huswife' (hussey/hussy) here means a woman of loose or deceitful character. Fortune was imagined as a goddess spinning a wheel that raised some up and cast others down without reason or loyalty. Cleopatra wants to scream so loudly that Fortune herself — that false, fickle woman — breaks her own wheel in fright. The image expresses absolute, furious grief at life's injustice.
detail: The personification of Fortune as a woman — often blindfolded, turning a wheel — comes from Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (c. 524 CE) and pervades medieval and Renaissance literature. 'Huswife' was a term for a disreputable or untrustworthy woman, sharpened by the pun on 'hussy'; calling Fortune a false hussey attacks her precisely on her defining trait: she is untrustworthy to everyone. Cleopatra's wish to 'rail so high' that she can shatter Fortune's wheel reverses the normal stoic response (patient endurance of Fortune's turns) with magnificent rage. The same image of Fortune's wheel recurs throughout the play; here it appears for the last time.

anchor_text: a Roman by a Roman / Valiantly vanquish'd
summary: Antony's dying claim that he was 'a Roman by a Roman valiantly vanquish'd' means he was defeated not by Octavius Caesar but by himself — a Roman, conquered by his own Roman hand. He fell on his own sword (the Roman soldiers' customary way of avoiding capture), so he was both the vanquisher and the vanquished. He asks to be remembered as the greatest prince of the world who died without cowardice.
detail: The Roman Stoic ideal held that falling on one's own sword — rather than surrendering to an enemy — was an honorable death that preserved dignity and freedom. Cato the Younger, Brutus, and Cassius all died this way. Antony botched his suicide in the previous scene; he asked Eros to kill him, Eros killed himself instead, and then Antony fell on his sword but did not die immediately, necessitating this scene. His claim that he was 'valiantly vanquish'd' by a Roman — himself — is a final attempt to frame a messy, failed suicide as a noble death in the antique Roman manner. Shakespeare follows Plutarch closely on this self-assessment.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2966

The reading that 'a Roman by a Roman valiantly vanquish'd' means self-defeat (Antony conquered by his own hand/sword) is the mainstream scholarly consensus; the gloss correctly notes the botched suicide in the prior scene and Antony's attempt to frame the messy death in honorable Roman terms, consistent with Plutarch.

anchor_text: The soldier's pole is fallen: young boys and girls / Are level now with men
summary: Cleopatra's lament that 'the soldier's pole is fallen' uses 'pole' in two senses: a military standard (the pole carried in battle around which soldiers rally) and the pole star, the fixed celestial point by which sailors navigate. With Antony dead, the army has lost its rallying point and the world has lost its guiding star. 'Young boys and girls / Are level now with men' means all distinctions of greatness are erased — everyone is equally insignificant without him.
detail: The passage is formally an elegy using the figure of enargeia (vivid evocation of absence): the crown melting, the garland withering, the pole fallen, the moon's wonders exhausted. The double meaning of 'pole' — battle-standard and polestar — works because Antony was both a military commander and a figure who oriented the world around him. 'The garland of the war' is a victory wreath, another image of military achievement now dead. 'Level now with men' carries the force of levelling: if Antony is gone, the distinction between the great and the ordinary collapses. The whole speech (TLN 2973-78) is Cleopatra's most formally controlled elegy in a scene otherwise of raw emotion.

anchor_text: what's brave, what's noble, / Let's do it after the high Roman fashion, / And make death proud to take us
summary: The 'high Roman fashion' of dying means suicide — specifically the Roman Stoic practice of choosing death rather than capture or dishonour. Cleopatra resolves that she and her women will kill themselves in this manner rather than be led as captives in Octavius Caesar's triumph through Rome. The scene ends with the decision that drives Act 5.
detail: The Roman Stoic tradition held that a free person — especially a soldier or ruler — could choose the time and manner of their death to avoid slavery or disgrace. Cato the Younger, Brutus, and Cassius are the canonical examples. Cleopatra's phrasing is striking: she does not say 'die like Romans' (she is Egyptian) but says she will adopt the Roman fashion — a deliberate, performative choice to inhabit that tradition. 'Make death proud to take us' reverses the conventional posture: it is usually mortals who are proud to be taken by death nobly; here death itself is made the subordinate. Plutarch records that Cleopatra resolved on suicide and prepared it carefully, and Shakespeare preserves the deliberate quality of that resolution. This is the specific 'antique Roman' ideal of honorable self-killing.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 82-86, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Cleopatra's resolution to die rather than grace Caesar's triumph, and her preparations for suicide.

Reading 'high Roman fashion' as noble Stoic suicide is the unanimous critical consensus; Cleopatra's explicit list of means (knife, drugs, serpents at TLN 2930-31) and the scene-closing resolve confirm this reading, and the note that she deliberately adopts the Roman tradition rather than claiming it as her own is an apt observation.

anchor_text: The breaking of so great a thing should make A greater crack

The image claims Antony was so great a force that his end should have shaken lions out of the streets and driven citizens into their dens — nature inverted by the fall of a titan.

anchor_text: Not by a public minister of justice, Nor by a hired knife
summary: A 'public minister of justice' was an official executioner. Dercetas distinguishes Antony's death from execution or assassination: neither the state nor an enemy's dagger killed him, but his own hand — the 'self hand / Which writ his honour in the acts it did.' The emphasis on the 'self hand' echoes the Roman Stoic ideal that death by one's own hand, chosen freely, was more honorable than capture or judicial execution. Dercetas's three-part negative — not the executioner, not a hired assassin, but the man himself — is a forensic structure (anaphora) that makes the suicide sound like an affirmative act rather than a failure. He then exhibits the blood-stained sword as proof, turning the weapon into a relic.

anchor_text: a spacious mirror's set before him
summary: Maecenas compares Antony's life to a mirror placed before Octavius Caesar: a man so similar in his strengths, appetites, and imperial scope that Caesar cannot help seeing his own potential self reflected. The 'spacious' mirror is vast enough to hold all of Antony — his greatness and his ruin alike.
detail: The mirror conceit was a Renaissance political and literary commonplace: the 'mirror for magistrates' (the popular genre of moral exempla for rulers) held that the falls of great men served as cautionary reflections. Maecenas is suggesting that Caesar's visible grief — 'Caesar is touch'd' — comes from recognizing a version of himself in what Antony was and what he lost. The image also picks up a motif that runs through the play: Antony and Caesar are doubles throughout, equally imperial, equally consuming, equally driven by rivalries in love and war. Agrippa's remark that Antony had 'A rarer spirit' and the gods give all men 'some faults to make us men' immediately precedes this, framing Caesar's emotion as self-recognition rather than simple grief.

anchor_text: we do lance Diseases in our bodies
summary: To 'lance' a disease means to cut it open with a lance (a surgeon's blade), as in lancing a boil or abscess — painful but necessary to let out the infection. Octavius Caesar apologizes for having had to wound Antony: the war was a surgical necessity, not cruelty. He then adds that he and Antony could not 'stall together in the whole world' — meaning they could not share even the entire world, as two animals too fierce to pen in the same stall.

'Stall together' continues the animal-pen metaphor: a stall is a single animal's compartment in a stable. The metaphor reveals Caesar's self-understanding — he sees the civil war as a natural necessity of two too-large natures in one world, not as personal ambition. Plutarch (Life of Antony 77) reports Caesar saying Antony 'was now the greatest obstacle to a reconciliation with him,' but Shakespeare gives Caesar a more elegiac and self-exculpating framing.

anchor_text: Lest, in her greatness, by some mortal stroke She do defeat us; for her life in Rome Would be eternal in our triumph
summary: Octavius Caesar tells Proculeius to keep Cleopatra alive and calm because if she kills herself she 'defeats' his greatest prize: displaying her alive in his victory procession through Rome. A Roman 'triumph' was a lavish parade of a general's spoils and captives after a major victory; a captured foreign ruler walking in chains was its supreme exhibit. Cleopatra alive, paraded through Rome, would be the final proof of his conquest of the East.
detail: The Roman triumph was awarded by the Senate to a general who met strict criteria of a foreign victory with a large body count. Captured kings and queens were the most prized captives — Julius Caesar had paraded the Gallic chieftain Vercingetorix in his triumph. Caesar's calculation here is bluntly political: Cleopatra's suicide would let her cheat him of that exhibit, and the play's whole fifth act turns on her determination to do exactly that. Plutarch (Life of Antony 83) reports that Caesar assured Cleopatra kindly she would be well treated, while privately planning to exhibit her; Plutarch also says it was Dolabella who secretly warned Cleopatra that Caesar intended to send her to Rome within three days. Caesar's apparent kindness ('Caesar cannot learn / To be ungentle') is therefore theatrical.

anchor_text: How hardly I was drawn into this war; How calm and gentle I proceeded still In all my writings
summary: Caesar invites his officers to read his letters and papers to prove he was reluctant and moderate throughout the war — a piece of deliberate self-presentation. 'Hardly' means with difficulty or reluctantly (not 'harshly'). Historically, Octavius mounted an extensive propaganda campaign before Actium, publishing Antony's will (allegedly found in the Vestals' keeping), portraying Antony as bewitched by a foreign queen and unfit to rule, and framing the conflict as Rome's defensive war against Egypt rather than a civil war between two Romans.

The campaign to characterize Caesar as a reluctant, pacific man forced into war was central to the Augustan political mythology that the historians and poets of the Pax Romana later elaborated. By closing the scene with Caesar demonstrating his paper trail to his generals, Shakespeare shows the cold, calculating aspect of Octavius beneath his expressed grief — the man who has already started to curate the historical record of his own rise. The line anticipates the theme of Caesar's triumphant self-narrative that Cleopatra dreads in Act 5, scene 2.

anchor_text: Not being Fortune, he's but Fortune's knave, / A minister of her will
summary: Octavius Caesar is only Fortune's servant ('knave' means servant or boy, not a villain here), executing her orders. Since he does not control Fortune herself, his victories are not truly his own. This invokes Fortune as the goddess whose wheel raises and throws down the great.
detail: The Roman goddess Fortuna turned a great wheel that lifted and toppled rulers blind to her power. Cleopatra places Caesar below Antony: Antony was Fortune's lord by the size of his nature; Caesar is merely Fortune's errand-boy, elevated by chance. anchor_text: Which shackles accidents and bolts up change; / Which sleeps, and never palates more the dug

anchor_text: Shall they hoist me up, / And show me to the shouting varletry / Of censuring Rome

Captured enemy kings, queens, and commanders were walked in chains before the victor's chariot; after the parade many were strangled in the Mamertine prison. Cleopatra's entire resolve to die rather than be taken to Rome is structured around refusing this fate. The same threat drives her final preparations later in the scene. Cleopatra's Egypt — her homeland, the Ptolemaic kingdom — is represented by the pyramids, among the most ancient monuments on earth. Dying in chains from them would still be dying as a queen of Egypt, not a captive of Rome.

anchor_text: I dream'd there was an Emperor Antony
summary: Cleopatra's speech to Dolabella is a deliberate eulogy for Antony cast as a dream-vision — a rhetorical device that lets her describe a superhuman man she knows is gone. By framing it as a dream she challenges Dolabella to deny that any such man could exist, knowing he cannot.

Its cosmic imagery — a face containing sun and moon, legs straddling the ocean, an arm that 'crested the world' — deliberately exceeds anything nature or dream could supply. The paradox is that Antony was real: 'yet to imagine / An Antony were nature's piece 'gainst fancy, / Condemning shadows quite.' Plutarch's Life of Antony supplied Shakespeare the historical Antony; the eulogy translates him into myth.

anchor_text: his voice was propertied / As all the tuned spheres
summary: Ancient and medieval astronomers imagined the planets as transparent crystal spheres rotating around the earth, each producing a perfect musical tone as it moved — together, the 'music of the spheres.' Antony's voice, Cleopatra says, had the quality of all the spheres playing in harmony at once.
detail: The Pythagorean doctrine held that the planets moved in concentric crystal spheres and that their motion produced perfect musical intervals. Because human ears were impure, we cannot actually hear this celestial music, but it was the standard of cosmic harmony. Antony's voice is placed above all earthly sound: it had the full harmonic range of the universe. The same image appears in The Merchant of Venice 5.1 ('There's not the smallest orb which thou behold'st / But in his motion like an angel sings').

anchor_text: his delights / Were dolphin-like; they show'd his back above / The element they liv'd in
summary: Antony's pleasures were like dolphins — creatures that live in the water but leap above it so their backs shine in the air. His enjoyments rose above the common element of earthly pleasure into something rarer. The image flatters even his vices as a kind of grace.
detail: The dolphin was a symbol of intelligence and playfulness in classical culture, associated with the god Apollo and with the sea. 'The element they liv'd in' is water, yet dolphins breach — they habitually exceed their medium. anchor_text: realms and islands were / As plates dropp'd from his pocket

anchor_text: nature wants stuff / To vie strange forms with fancy: yet to imagine / An Antony were nature's piece 'gainst fancy, / Condemning shadows quite
summary: Cleopatra argues that real nature lacks the material to compete with imagination in inventing extraordinary things — yet imagining an Antony is nature's own masterwork against all fantasy, outclassing the mere 'shadows' (unreality) that fancy produces. Antony was too extraordinary even for the imagination to have invented.

'Condemning shadows quite' means that Antony as reality condemns all mere imaginings as shadows — unreal copies. This is the climax of the dream-speech's logic.

anchor_text: He'll lead me, then, in triumph? ... Madam, he will; / I know it

According to the Roman custom of the triumph, a conquered foreign ruler would be walked in chains before Caesar's chariot through the streets of Rome.

anchor_text: Your scutcheons and your signs of conquest, shall / Hang in what place you please
summary: 'Scutcheons' (also spelled 'escutcheons') were heraldic shields displaying a conquered enemy's coat of arms, hung publicly to advertise victory. anchor_text: Immoment toys, things of such dignity / As we greet modern friends withal

anchor_text: For Livia and Octavia, to induce / Their mediation
summary: Livia was Caesar's wife (later the empress Livia Drusilla, one of the most powerful women in Roman history). Octavia was Caesar's sister and Antony's abandoned Roman wife. Cleopatra's strategy — telling Caesar she kept gifts to bribe their intercession — is a flattery of the two women closest to him.

anchor_text: He words me, girls, he words me, that I should not / Be noble to myself
summary: 'He words me' means he feeds me fine words, he talks me around — Caesar is trying to control Cleopatra with sweet speeches rather than honest dealing. 'Be noble to myself' means to die with the dignity befitting her rank, the same 'high Roman fashion' of honorable suicide.

anchor_text: the bright day is done, / And we are for the dark

anchor_text: saucy lictors / Will catch at us like strumpets
summary: Lictors were the official attendants who walked before Roman magistrates carrying the fasces (a bundle of rods and an axe), symbolizing the power to punish. 'Saucy' means impertinent, disrespectful. Cleopatra imagines these official escorts groping and manhandling her like prostitutes.

anchor_text: scald rhymers / Ballad us out o' tune
summary: 'Scald' means scurvy, contemptible (from 'scald' or 'scabby' — infected with a skin disease, hence low and worthless). Street ballad-singers would produce topical songs mocking Cleopatra and Antony to crude music, singing them out of tune for the common crowd.

The concern is also meta-theatrical: Cleopatra is essentially worried about being turned into bad popular entertainment, which is what she is already becoming in the play the audience is watching.

anchor_text: Some squeaking Cleopatra boy my greatness / I' the posture of a whore
summary: On the Elizabethan stage all women's roles, including Cleopatra's, were played by boy actors whose voices had not yet broken — hence 'squeaking.' Cleopatra imagines a Roman comedian putting a boy in her costume, using his shrill unbroken voice to parody her as a whore for laughs. Shakespeare writes a moment in which the actor playing Cleopatra describes his own theatrical condition.
detail: This is one of the most self-reflexive moments in all Shakespeare. The actor playing Cleopatra is himself a boy ('squeaking') whose cracked voice would mark him as exactly the kind of performer Cleopatra dreads. The line calls attention to the very theatrical convention it is subject to, creating a strange doubling: the fictional Cleopatra fears being played badly by a boy, while a boy is already playing her seriously. Critics since the 19th century have debated whether this meta-theatrical awareness was designed to make the audience more or less convinced by the boys' performances of Cleopatra and Iras throughout.

anchor_text: I am again for Cydnus, / To meet Mark Antony
summary: Cleopatra calls for her royal robes and crown, declaring she is returning to the Cydnus — the river where, in 41 BCE, she first staged her dazzling arrival to meet Antony, sailing in a golden barge dressed as the goddess Venus. Death will reunite her with Antony as their first meeting did: she goes to it as a goddess, not a prisoner.

North, 1579) describes Cleopatra's arrival in elaborate detail — the gilded barge, the purple sails, silver oars, boys like Cupids, women like Nereids — and Enobarbus re-creates it in 2.2's 'barge she sat in' speech. By invoking Cydnus now, as she prepares to die, Cleopatra recasts her death as a return to the moment of supreme theatrical self-presentation: she will dress as a queen and meet death as she met Antony.

anchor_text: when thou hast done this chare, I'll give thee leave / To play till doomsday
summary: A 'chare' (or 'char') is a small task, a household errand. anchor_text: I am marble-constant; now the fleeting moon / No planet is of mine
summary: Cleopatra declares herself fixed and unchanging as marble, no longer subject to the moon. Renouncing the moon, she renounces all change.

anchor_text: Hast thou the pretty worm of Nilus there / That kills and pains not?
summary: The 'worm of Nilus' is the asp — a small cobra (Egyptian cobra, Naja haje) found along the Nile. Cleopatra calls it 'pretty' and 'worm' (archaic English for any snake or serpent) because its bite was believed to bring swift, painless death. The asp was associated with Egyptian royalty and with the goddess Isis.

Plutarch (Life of Antony 86) and Strabo describe Cleopatra's death by asp, noting it was chosen precisely because it was quick and caused little suffering. The asp had sacred status in Egypt: the uraeus, the rearing cobra on the Pharaoh's crown, was a symbol of royal and divine power. Cleopatra dies wearing her crown, applying the very animal that adorned it.

anchor_text: Immortal longings in me: now no more / The juice of Egypt's grape shall moist this lip
summary: 'Immortal longings' are longings for immortality — the desire to join Antony beyond death. She is also done with earthly pleasure: no more wine ('the juice of Egypt's grape') will wet her lips. The phrase fuses spiritual aspiration with the physical act of dying, as the asp will quench the thirst of mortal life.

anchor_text: Husband, I come: / Now to that name my courage prove my title
summary: Cleopatra calls Antony her husband and prepares to die to reach him, proving she has the right to that name by her courage. The two were never formally married by Roman law — Antony was already married to Octavia — but Cleopatra here claims a bond beyond legal ceremony, and death is the proof of it.

Cleopatra may have considered herself his wife by Egyptian royal ceremony, and the play repeatedly treats their bond as marital. 'Prove my title' is language from feudal law — proving one's legal right to a title of ownership or rank by performance. Dying for him is the act that retroactively validates the name.

anchor_text: I am fire and air; my other elements / I give to baser life
summary: Ancient and Renaissance science held that all matter was made of four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. Fire and air were the two lightest and noblest elements, rising upward; water and earth the heavier, lower ones. Cleopatra gives the baser elements (her body, her earthly self) back to the ground, keeping only the noble fire and air — her soul — for reunion with Antony.

anchor_text: The stroke of death is as a lover's pinch, / Which hurts and is desir'd
summary: Watching Iras fall dead, Cleopatra marvels at how quietly she died. She compares the asp's bite to a lover's pinch — something that stings a little but is wanted, a gentle hurt. The line reframes death as erotic, making it intimate and chosen rather than forced.
detail: The image fuses the erotic and the mortal in a way characteristic of the play as a whole. Iras's death proves that the asp kills quickly and without apparent anguish, which reassures Cleopatra. Calling death 'a lover's pinch' also looks back to the Clown's bawdy about dying with the worm, and forward to Cleopatra's own words about the asp as her 'baby at my breast / That sucks the nurse asleep' (TLN 3449-3450) — all part of the scene's sustained eroticization of the death it presents with clinical neutrality.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'stroke': 'a blow, a touch; the act of dying as if by a blow.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3432
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference; the 'stroke' gloss is supportive and the citation is accurate.
The erotic-death ('lover's pinch') reading is the plain meaning of the simile and is a standard reading; the connection to the Clown's bawdy and the nursing image is a defensible thematic pattern.

anchor_text: With thy sharp teeth this knot intrinsicate / Of life at once untie
summary: 'Intrinsicate' is an archaic or Shakespearean form of 'intricate' — complexly knotted. Cleopatra asks the asp to untie the intricate knot of life, imagining the bond between body and soul as a tightly wound cord that only the serpent's teeth can cut. It is a remarkable image for death as a kind of release.
detail: The word 'intrinsicate' appears only here in Shakespeare and may be a nonce-formation (a word coined for the occasion) or a variant of 'intricate' chosen for the meter. The knot-of-life metaphor is rooted in the Parcae (the Roman Fates), who spun and cut the thread of life — here the thread becomes a knot to be bitten through rather than cut. Cleopatra anthropomorphizes the asp as a loving deliverer, speaking to it as if it were both executioner and liberator.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'intrinsicate' (adj.): 'intricate, involved'; rare or dialectal, here used uniquely by Shakespeare.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3442
OED does record 'intrinsicate' as rare/dialectal and used uniquely by Shakespeare; the citation is accurate and supports the archaic-vocabulary claim.

'Intrinsicate' as a Shakespearean nonce-form of 'intricate' is correct; the knot-of-life imagery and Parcae connection are defensible; the annotation responsibly notes the word is unique to this passage.

anchor_text: O eastern star!
summary: Charmian calls the dying Cleopatra 'the eastern star,' almost certainly Venus — the evening and morning star, the brightest in the sky, which rises in the east. The image links Cleopatra to the goddess of love (Venus/Aphrodite), as her barge on the Cydnus also did when she dressed as Venus. It is a brief, radiant elegy.
detail: The planet Venus is the brightest object in the sky after the sun and moon and was identified with the goddess of love. Enobarbus's Cydnus speech describes Cleopatra as surpassing Venus herself ('she did lie / In her pavilion... o'erpicturing that Venus where we see / The fancy outwork nature'). To call her the eastern star as she dies is both an astronomical fact (the morning star is visible in the east at dawn) and a mythological summary: she goes out like the most brilliant of the heavenly bodies.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 2.6 (Venus as the brightest planet, called both morning star Lucifer and evening star Hesperus).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3447
Pliny NH 2.6 does describe Venus as the brightest planet, called Lucifer as morning star and Vesper/Hesperus as evening star; the citation is accurate and supports the astronomical claim.

Identifying 'eastern star' as Venus is plausible but not certain — it could be simply the sun rising in the east or a more generic stellar epithet; the Venus/Aphrodite reading is attractive but the line is brief and the annotation should not present it as the definitive meaning, and the medium confidence assigned is appropriate.

anchor_text: Dost thou not see my baby at my breast / That sucks the nurse asleep
summary: Cleopatra addresses Charmian while holding the asp to her breast and calls it her 'baby' nursing at her as if she were a wet-nurse. The image turns her death into a scene of maternal tenderness: the asp feeds on her while she is lulled to sleep, not tormented. The grotesque reversal — the deadly serpent as an infant — is deliberate and serene.
detail: The 'nurse asleep' image echoes the scene's opening lines, where Cleopatra called death the condition of 'never palating more the dug' (TLN 3101). Now she is the nurse. This nursing image also belongs to the iconography of Isis, who was depicted suckling the infant Horus — a parallel that strengthens Cleopatra's identification with the goddess as she makes her final gesture of sovereign divinity.

sources.name: Plutarch, Moralia: On Isis and Osiris
sources.citation: Plutarch, Moralia, 'On Isis and Osiris' 12-19: Isis as nursing mother to Horus; the iconographic tradition of the divine nursing mother.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3449

Plutarch Moralia 'On Isis and Osiris' chapters 12-19 do cover the Isis-Horus myth including nursing scenes (notably ch. 16); the Isis-as-nursing-mother iconographic tradition is well established in this text and the citation is supportive.

The nursing-asp-as-baby image is the plain text; the Isis-nursing-Horus parallel is a genuine iconographic connection, and the echo of TLN 3101 ('palating the dug') is a real structural link the annotation identifies correctly.

anchor_text: Now boast thee, death, in thy possession lies / A lass unparallel'd
summary: Charmian addresses death directly as if it were a king or conqueror who should be proud to have taken Cleopatra — 'a lass unparalleled,' a girl without equal. The deliberately simple word 'lass' (a young woman, common in northern English dialects) contrasts strikingly with the grandeur of what it describes: the queen is reduced in tenderness, not in dignity.
detail: The line echoes Antony's tribute to Cleopatra elsewhere in the play and is the verbal equivalent of the action that follows it — Charmian straightening the dead queen's crown. Both are acts of service that restore dignity after death. Personified death as a possessor of the beautiful is a topos going back through Donne to classical elegy.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'lass': 'a girl, a young woman; often used tenderly.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3456
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference; 'lass' as 'a girl, a young woman, often used tenderly' is a standard documented sense and the citation supports the gloss.

The reading of 'lass' as deliberately simple and tender against the grandeur of what it describes is a sound and mainstream interpretive point; the personified-death-as-conqueror topos is accurately noted.

anchor_text: Downy windows, close; / And golden Phoebus never be beheld / Of eyes again so royal
summary: Charmian closes Cleopatra's eyelids, calling them 'downy windows' (soft as down, the skin of the eyelids). 'Phoebus' is the sun-god Apollo, the golden sun. The elegy says: let the sun never again be seen by eyes as royal as hers. It is a farewell to the sun from one of the sun's own worshippers.
detail: 'Phoebus' (from Greek Phoibos, 'bright') is Apollo as the sun-god, golden and radiant. Calling the eyes 'windows' was a commonplace figure for them as the soul's outlets. The epithet 'downy' gives the closing of the eyes an intimacy — Charmian touching and closing them as a last act of service. The sun, Egypt's first god and the emblem of royal power (the Pharaohs were sons of Ra/Helios), will never be seen by eyes this worthy again.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.752-779 and 2.1-380 (Phoebus/Apollo as the golden sun-god driving his chariot across the sky).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3457

Ovid Metamorphoses 1.752-779 and 2.1-380 do cover Phaethon and Phoebus/Apollo as the sun-god driving his chariot; the 'golden Phoebus' claim is supported, though the cited passages focus on Phaethon rather than a general Phoebus description — the association is real and the source genuine.

'Downy windows' as eyelids (soft skin) and Phoebus as the sun-god are correct; the annotation's connection of the sun to Egyptian royal ideology (Ra/Helios) is defensible, though the text does not make this explicit, so it is appropriately placed at scholar context.

anchor_text: Caesar's beguil'd
summary: The First Guard reports that Octavius Caesar has been outwitted — 'beguiled' means tricked or cheated. Caesar kept Cleopatra alive to display in his triumph, which was the point of the elaborate surveillance and the seizure of the monument. Her death defeats his greatest public-relations victory.
detail: Plutarch records that Caesar was deeply vexed by Cleopatra's death (Life of Antony 86): he had taken extraordinary precautions to prevent her suicide precisely because he needed her alive for the triumph. Her success in dying deprives him of the single most spectacular element of his planned celebration of his eastern conquest. The triumph he actually celebrated in 29 BCE featured an image of Cleopatra with the asp rather than the queen herself — a substitute that acknowledged his defeat.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 86, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Caesar's frustration at Cleopatra's death and his decision to display her effigy in his triumph instead.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3466
Plutarch Life of Antony 86 (North 1579) does record Caesar's frustration at Cleopatra's death and his use of her effigy in the triumph; the citation is accurate and directly supportive.
'Beguiled' as tricked/cheated is the correct sense; the historical note that Caesar's actual triumph featured an effigy of Cleopatra with the asp is accurate per Plutarch and Dio.

anchor_text: It is well done, and fitting for a princess / Descended of so many royal kings
summary: Charmian's dying words claim that her own death, and Cleopatra's, are entirely proper for women of their rank. The Ptolemaic dynasty descended from Ptolemy I, one of Alexander the Great's generals, and ruled Egypt continuously from 323 to 30 BCE — a lineage of several centuries of royal kings.
detail: The Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by Alexander's general Ptolemy I Soter, produced a line of rulers of Egypt who intermarried, sometimes between siblings, to preserve royal blood. Cleopatra VII (the queen of the play) was the last of the Ptolemies. She was also descended through her dynasty from the Macedonian royal line. Charmian's claim that dying is 'fitting for a princess' asserts the Roman Stoic ethic of noble suicide, but from an Egyptian and royal perspective: the line that never submitted now ends by its own choice.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 86, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): the death of Charmian; Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 1.31-33 (on the Ptolemaic dynasty and Egyptian royal succession).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3469

Plutarch Life of Antony 86 covers the death of Charmian; Diodorus Siculus Bibliotheca Historica 1.31-33 does discuss Egyptian royal succession and the Ptolemaic dynasty; both citations are real and support the historical claims made.

The Ptolemaic dynastic lineage from Ptolemy I Soter is accurate; calling the death 'fitting' for the Roman-Stoic concept of noble suicide applied from an Egyptian royal perspective is a defensible reading.

anchor_text: O sir, you are too sure an augurer; / That you did fear is done
summary: Dolabella calls Caesar 'too sure an augurer' — too accurate a reader of omens and intentions. An augur in Rome was a priest who read the will of the gods from birds' flights, lightning, and entrails. Here the word is used figuratively: Caesar predicted Cleopatra would kill herself, and she has done exactly what he feared.
detail: Roman augury was a formal priesthood that advised the state on divine will; 'augurer' here is used more loosely to mean a man who could foresee what would happen. Caesar throughout the play shows cold, calculating intelligence that amounts to a kind of prophecy — he anticipated Cleopatra's resolve before she acted on it. Dolabella's line implicitly praises and condemns him: he was right, but being right cost him the triumph.

sources.name: Cicero, De Divinatione
sources.citation: Cicero, De Divinatione 1.1-3 (on Roman augury as the official science of reading divine will from natural signs).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3479
Cicero De Divinatione 1.1-3 does introduce Roman augury as the official science of reading divine will from natural signs; the citation is accurate and supportive of the historical-topical gloss.
'Augurer' used figuratively for an accurate foreseer is the plain meaning in context; the historical background on Roman augury is accurate and the annotation correctly notes it is used loosely here.

anchor_text: As she would catch another Antony / In her strong toil of grace
summary: Caesar's elegy on the dead Cleopatra: she looks as if she is still at work, as if she might snare another Antony in the net ('toil') of her charm. 'Toil' in the sense of a net or snare (a hunting word) is combined with 'grace' — her power to charm was both trap and beauty. Even in death he imagines her still dangerous.
detail: 'Toil' as a hunting net appears elsewhere in Shakespeare (Hamlet 3.2: 'the toils of war'). The phrase 'strong toil of grace' brilliantly condenses the paradox that drove the whole play: her charm (grace) was an inescapable trap (toil), and it worked on Antony precisely because it was both. Caesar, who prided himself on never falling under it, nonetheless finds himself using the language of a man who recognizes its power in admiring the dead woman.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'toil' (n., 2): 'a net or snare for catching game'; archaic by the 17th century but common in hunting contexts.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3497
OED does define 'toil' as 'a net or snare for catching game' and notes it as archaic; the citation is real and supports the rhetorical reading.

'Toil' as a hunting net or snare is correct Elizabethan usage; the reading that Caesar uses the language of a man who recognises the power he himself prided himself on being immune to is a subtle but defensible interpretive point.

anchor_text: She hath pursu'd conclusions infinite / Of easy ways to die
summary: Caesar reports that Cleopatra's physician told him she had experimentally tested many methods of painless death — 'conclusions infinite' means countless experiments. This is a direct echo of Plutarch, who records that Cleopatra, after Antony's death, tested various poisons and snake bites on condemned prisoners to find which caused the least suffering.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 71 (North 1579): Cleopatra collected deadly poisons and tested them on condemned prisoners, finding the asp's bite the easiest death.

anchor_text: She shall be buried by her Antony: / No grave upon the earth shall clip in it / A pair so famous
summary: Caesar's closing tribute orders Cleopatra buried beside Antony, in their shared tomb in Alexandria. 'Clip' means to embrace or enclose. Even in death Octavius Caesar, who defeated them, acknowledges that they constitute a pair of unequalled fame. This follows Plutarch's account of their joint burial.
detail: Plutarch (Life of Antony 86) records that Caesar honored Cleopatra's request to be buried with Antony, and that they were interred in magnificent fashion. The location — the Royal Quarter of Alexandria, in a tomb Cleopatra had built in preparation — has never been definitively found. The final lines of the play shift register from elegy to Roman public ceremony, with Caesar ordering the military honors of a state funeral ('solemn show') for the conquered lovers — a recognition that closes the play on a note of grandeur rather than triumph.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 86, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Caesar ordered Cleopatra's body to be buried beside Antony with magnificent ceremony.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3510
Plutarch Life of Antony 86 (North 1579) does record that Caesar ordered Cleopatra buried with Antony with magnificent ceremony; the citation is accurate and directly supportive.

Plutarch's account of the joint burial ordered by Caesar is accurately represented; 'clip' as embrace/enclose is the correct sense; the tonal shift to Roman public ceremony is an accurate characterisation of the scene's ending.
